title: 97 of 99 Sounds Great. It Would Have Been a Bad Release Number.
description:
97 of 99 Sounds Great. It Would Have Been a Bad Release Number.

From the agentpolicy v0.1.0 release: a local-first, Cedar-based policy decision point for AI agents (decide allow, deny, ask, rate-limit, or redact for every agent action, with shipped rule packs). Now on PyPI. This story is the coverage section of the v0.1.0 field test report.

AI disclosure: this article was drafted and edited with AI assistance. The field test, the defects, the fixes, and every number are real and linked below.

The final field test report for my agent policy engine says 97 pass, 0 fail, 0 declared, 0 not run. Ninety-seven out of ninety-seven. That is a release number I am proud of. It is also a number that only means anything if I show you the two cases that are not in it.

They are the most honest part of the release. Both are named, with reasons and re-entry conditions, in the field test report (the master table note and Field Notes 13).

What a pass rate hides

My plan originally had 99 cases. Two of them were Tier-1 integrations: FT-T1-CURSOR and FT-T1-GEMINI. Test the real Cursor agent loop against the policy engine. Test the real Gemini CLI against the policy engine.

Neither can run on my machine. Not "I ran out of time." Cannot run, for structural reasons:

  • Cursor is a GUI IDE, a VS Code fork. Its agent loop and its permission surface live inside a desktop Electron app driven by a human. There is no supported headless surface, no server mode for the permissions.json flow, and no GUI host on this box. There is no experiment to run.
  • Gemini CLI is installed, and the sanctioned local path (gemini gemma setup) genuinely works. I got a real LiteRT-LM binary and a local gemma model serving on port 9379. And then the CLI crashed at startup with IneligibleTierError, the OAuth tier gate running before any model routing. I read the bundle source: the gemma router is classifier-only. Intent classification goes to the local 1B model. The main LLM always goes to Google-hosted Code Assist, which is sunset for this CLI build. No proxy fixes a client-side auth gate.

Here is the fork in the road. If I quietly dropped those two cases and published the remaining 97 as "97/97, 100% pass," I would have been technically accurate and completely dishonest. Count them honestly as untested and the same release reads 97/99, about 98%. Either number looks green. Neither one tells you that the two missing cases are the two hardest integrations I claimed I would test. The pass rate was never the problem. The denominator was.

The vocabulary that clarified it

Somewhere around the third time I caught myself about to write "didn't get to it," I codified the rule into the field-test vocabulary. Every case gets exactly one of:

  • pass: it ran, and an independent gate re-derived the assertion from the evidence on disk. Not exit code zero. Re-derived.
  • fail: it ran and the assertion did not hold.
  • declared: it cannot run here, and I wrote down the precise reason, what is covered instead, and the condition under which it becomes runnable.
  • not run: nothing yet. Visible. Counted.

The load-bearing distinction was between unsupported here and passed here. During the investigation, that vocabulary kept me honest about what I knew, what I could prove locally, and what would need a different host or a future vendor build. For Gemini, that meant the exact crash, the classifier-only finding from the source, and the local parity stand-in that did run. For Cursor, it meant admitting there was no headless surface to exercise on this box.

That gave me a complete answer while I was still investigating. The shipped release took the stricter step: Cursor and Gemini were removed from scope entirely, not left hanging as permanent declared rows.

Why this costs me something

The hard part is publishing the limitation plainly. Anyone reading the report can see exactly which integrations were exercised live and which were not claimed at v0.1.0. A marketing page would say "works with your favorite agent CLIs." My report says: Claude Code and Codex CLI, exercised live, both passing. Cursor and Gemini CLI: not claimed as supported at v0.1.0, here is why, here is what would change it.

I removed them from the plan, the registry, and the PRD rather than leaving them as eternally skipped rows. The scoping decision and the re-entry conditions are written into the plan itself, not just my private notes. Removing a feature from scope because you cannot test it is slower than claiming it. It is also the only version of the sentence I can defend.

What worked

  • The four-state vocabulary. Two days into the sweep I could not tell you which "didn't run" was flaky and which was impossible. The vocabulary forced me to find out.
  • Clear intermediate statuses while investigating. Writing down the reason, the lower-layer stand-in that does run, and the re-entry condition made it much easier to decide the final shipped scope honestly.
  • Writing the report by hand. Every number in it was typed by a person who knows where it came from. The generator is explicitly banned from touching it.

What did not work

  • My initial instinct, twice, to leave untestable cases as "skip" rows. Skips rot. Nobody audits a skip backlog.
  • Trusting "local mode" in a vendor's marketing. Gemini's local mode is real, the install works, and the main loop still cannot use it. Partial local is a trap worth naming out loud.

More detail and evidence

  • The honest coverage section, verbatim: field test report, Coverage, Gaps, and Declared Limitations (the two removed cases, the re-entry conditions), plus Field Notes 13 for the full Gemini and Cursor investigation.
  • The Gemini evidence trail: journal Group 22 in the same report (the IneligibleTierError crash, the classifier-only router finding from the bundle source, the auto-un-declare guard in scripts/fieldtest/lib.sh).
  • The plan that shipped: FIELD_TEST_PLAN.md, including the scope decision and what the shipped Tier-1 set is.
  • The product: agentpolicy, pip install agentsec-agentpolicy, PyPI 0.1.0, compliance and standards matrix (OWASP, ATLAS, NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001, EU AI Act), part of the agentic-suite agent-security stack.

I now read every "100% pass" dashboard with one question: how many cases did it take to get to that denominator? How do you handle the things you cannot test in your reports, skip them silently, or declare them loudly?

title: Redis latency benchmark: HotKV vs Valkey and Dragonfly
description:
This Redis latency benchmark measures how long HotKV, Redis, Valkey and Dragonfly take to answer at a fixed request rate. Our earlier benchmarks measured throughput, and a reader rightly pointed out that throughput is not everything. So we held the load constant, raised it step by step, and recorded the median (p50) and the 99th percentile (p99) at each step. We also measured pub/sub delivery time.

In short. In this Redis latency benchmark on AWS, HotKV and Dragonfly both held 1.6 million GETs per second, Redis with 8 I/O threads held about 0.8 million, Valkey with 8 I/O threads about 0.4 million, and single-thread Redis and Valkey about 0.2 million. From 200,000 to 1.6 million requests per second HotKV's p99 stayed between 0.59 and 0.76 ms, against 0.71 to 1.48 ms for Dragonfly. At light load the multi-threaded products tied on p99, and pub/sub delivery was a tie.

Why we ran a Redis latency benchmark at a fixed rate

A throughput test pushes a server as hard as it will go and reports how much it served. That says little about how long one request waits. A latency test fixes how many requests per second the clients send, and measures the time each takes. The server is then at the same load as every other product, so the times can be compared.

This kind of test has a catch. memtier_benchmark is a closed-loop tool, so a client waits for a reply before it sends the next request. If a server cannot keep up, the client simply sends fewer requests, and the latency of the ones it did send looks better than it should. We therefore count a step as sustained only when the achieved rate is at least 97 percent of the rate we asked for. Steps that fail the test are marked "not sustained" in the tables and their latency is not shown.

What we tested

Machines

  • Servers and load generator. c8a.12xlarge instances (AMD EPYC 9R45, 48 cores, no SMT, 96 GiB, 22.5 Gbit/s network) in one AWS cluster placement group in eu-south-2a, running Ubuntu 24.04. One instance ran the load generator and one ran the server.
  • One product at a time. Each product ran alone on the server, so nothing overlapped and nothing shared the network. Every server process was pinned to CPUs 0 to 39, with persistence off and protected mode off.

Products

  • HotKV 0.3.0 with 40 threads.
  • Dragonfly 2.0.2 with 40 proactor threads.
  • Redis 8.10.3 and Valkey 9.1.3, each run twice, once in the default single-thread setup and once with --io-threads 8.

The launch line and the live CONFIG GET output of every run are saved with its results.

Workload and procedure

The data set was 1,000,000 keys with 256-byte values, and pipeline depth was 1, so each request waits for its own reply. The load was GET only, and a mix of 1 write to 10 reads. Each step ran for 20 seconds, twice, and we report the mean of the two runs. memtier_benchmark used a per-connection rate limit and recorded an HDR histogram. We ran two connection counts.

  • 816 connections (24 threads of 34 connections), for rates from 20,000 to 2.4 million requests per second.
  • 48 connections (4 threads of 12 connections), for rates up to 300,000 requests per second. Above that, 48 connections cannot reach the rate, because each connection can only send as fast as it gets replies.

Results

The GET tables come first, one for each connection count, followed by pub/sub.

At 816 connections

Each cell is p50 / p99 in milliseconds, for GET. "NS" means not sustained, and the rate it did reach is in brackets. A dash means the sweep for that product had already stopped.

The mixed workload gave the same picture. HotKV's p99 was 0.54 to 0.75 ms from 200,000 to 1.6 million requests per second, and the points each product could sustain were the same as for GET. All of it is in the results folder.

How to read the single-thread rows

The 1.6 to 3 ms medians of single-thread Redis and Valkey at 816 connections are not their steady-state latency. With a rate limit, memtier_benchmark makes all 816 connections fire at the same moment. A single-thread server has to work through that burst of 816 requests one after another, so the median of a request includes its place in the queue. We ran the 48-connection test below to remove this effect.

Pub/sub delivery time

We measured the time from a publish to its delivery to a subscriber, with 64 publishers, 100 subscribers and a 128-byte payload, using pubsub-sub-bench. Each message went to one subscriber. Cells are p50 / p99 in milliseconds.

All products delivered in the same range. At the highest load the single-thread products had a higher median, 0.51 and 0.57 ms against 0.11 ms for HotKV.

We also had to patch pubsub-sub-bench. It compared a publish time in milliseconds with a receive time in microseconds. The patch is in the results folder.

What the results show

The tables show a lead for HotKV and Dragonfly at high load, a tie at light load, and a ceiling for single-thread Redis and Valkey.

HotKV and Dragonfly kept a low tail to 1.6 million requests per second

Both sustained 1.6 million GETs per second at 816 connections, with a median of 0.28 ms. HotKV's p99 was between 0.59 and 0.76 ms from 200,000 requests per second up. Dragonfly's was between 0.71 and 1.48 ms, and the two were close at 1.6 million (0.64 against 0.71 ms). Redis and Valkey with I/O threads stopped sustaining the rate at lower loads, and single-thread Redis and Valkey stopped at about 260,000.

At light load the multi-threaded products tie

At 48 connections, up to 300,000 requests per second, HotKV, Dragonfly and Redis with 8 I/O threads all had a p99 of about 0.27 ms. HotKV had the lowest median, 0.08 to 0.09 ms from 100,000 requests per second, with Dragonfly at 0.08 to 0.10 ms. A difference of 0.01 ms is within what other parts of the setup can cause, so we do not claim it as a win.

Single-thread Redis and Valkey ran out at about 230,000 a second

At 48 connections they had a median of about 0.2 ms and a p99 of 0.35 to 0.43 ms, and they did not sustain 300,000 requests per second (about 231,000 and 233,000). That is the ceiling of one thread on this hardware and workload. It is why Redis and Valkey are usually run as many processes or as a cluster, as in our cluster benchmark.

Limitations

These are HotKV Ltd's measurements of the versions and configuration above. They are not a claim about any other version, configuration or workload of these products.

The test setup

  • One server, one load generator. Two repeats per step, on one set of machines on one date. We did not measure variation between machines or days.
  • Layouts we chose. Redis and Valkey ran in their default single-thread setup and with --io-threads 8, and we did not tune either beyond that. Other settings could change their figures. If you think a setting here disadvantages a product, tell us and we will check it and publish the result.
  • The tool's burst effect. At 816 connections, the medians of single-thread products are inflated by the way memtier_benchmark rate limiting works, as explained above.

What was not measured

  • Data. Larger or skewed values, memory per key, and persistence. Persistence was off for every server.
  • Modes. Cluster mode, sharded pub/sub, TLS, replication and failover.
  • Pub/sub fan-out. One message to many subscribers.

Redis, Valkey and Dragonfly are trademarks of their respective owners. They are named only to identify the software we measured, and this implies no sponsorship, endorsement or affiliation.

Reproduce it

The sweep scripts, the launch line and live configuration of every server, the pubsub-sub-bench patch and every raw result are in the benchmark repository. The latency script is harness/lat_sweep.sh, and the pub/sub script is harness/ps_sweep.sh. The raw folder holds one archive per test with the memtier_benchmark JSON, the HDR histograms and the CPU use of the server for every run.

Try it yourself

HotKV Cloud runs HotKV for you. Start on HotKV Cloud, or talk to sales to benchmark HotKV against your own workload.

Frequently asked questions

Is HotKV faster than Redis in latency?

Under load, at the rates we tested, yes. At 816 connections and 200,000 requests per second HotKV had a p99 of 0.59 ms, Redis with 8 I/O threads 1.11 ms and single-thread Redis 5.60 ms. At light load with 48 connections the multi-threaded products tied on p99, at about 0.27 ms.

Why did you hold the request rate fixed?

At a fixed rate every product carries the same load, so the latencies can be compared. A throughput test shows how much a server serves at its limit, which says little about how long one request waits.

What does "not sustained" mean?

The product achieved less than 97 percent of the request rate we asked for. memtier_benchmark is a closed-loop tool, so an overloaded server makes the clients send less and the latency of the remaining requests looks better than it is. We show no latency for those steps.

How did pub/sub delivery time compare?

At the three loads we tested, all products delivered in the same range, with a median of about 0.1 ms at the two lower loads. The table above has every figure.

Can I reproduce this Redis latency benchmark?

Yes. The scripts, the configurations and every raw result are in the benchmark repository. You need two servers on the same network, a load generator, and the four products.

title: Romanian CUI Validation in TypeScript, Zod and React
description:
TL;DR

Romanian CUI validation is a weighted checksum: strip the optional RO prefix, right-align the digits before the last one against the key 753217532, multiply and add, then take the sum times 10 mod 11, where 10 becomes 0. The result must equal the last digit. A valid check digit only proves the number is well formed, so confirm that the company exists, is still registered and pays VAT with ANAF's public web service.

Your sign-up or invoice form has a field for a Romanian company's tax ID, and a regex for "RO plus digits" accepts every mistyped digit. Romanian CUI validation needs three things: a parser that accepts the many ways people write the number, the weighted check digit, and, when it matters, a lookup that proves the company is real. This tutorial builds all three in TypeScript, then wires them into a zod rule, a React field that validates as you type and a sign-up step that looks the company up at ANAF. The UI uses Input and Field from Wingo UI, the library we build, so we are not neutral. The checksum code is plain TypeScript you can paste anywhere.

What is a CUI, and how does it relate to the CIF and the VAT number?

They are one number with three names. The CUI (Codul Unic de Înregistrare) is the code a Romanian company gets when it registers: 2 to 10 digits, the last of which is a check digit. The CIF (cod de identificare fiscală) is the tax ID, and for a company it is the same digits. When the company is registered for VAT, the Romanian Wikipedia article on the CIF describes the CUI becoming a CIF with the "RO" prefix.

So the Romanian VAT number format is RO followed by the same 2 to 10 digits, as the VAT identification number table on Wikipedia lists it. In a real form you will receive RO12345674, ro 12345674, 12 345 674 and RO-12345674, and all four are the same company.

Two rules follow from that:

  • Store the digits and a VAT flag, never the string as typed. Print RO + digits when you need the VAT number.
  • The prefix someone typed is not proof of VAT status. People add RO out of habit. The VAT flag should come from ANAF, as we do further down.

How does the CUI check digit work?

The last digit is computed from the others with a fixed key, 753217532. The Romanian Wikipedia article above describes the validare CUI algorithm, and the source of python-stdnum's stdnum.ro.cui implements the same five steps:

  1. Remove the RO prefix and any spaces, dots or dashes. What is left must be 2 to 10 digits.
  2. Set the last digit aside. That is the check digit.
  3. Pad the remaining digits with zeros on the left until there are nine, so they line up with the right end of the key. (Wikipedia reverses both strings instead, which gives the same pairs.)
  4. Multiply each digit by the key digit in the same position and add the products.
  5. Multiply the sum by 10, take the remainder of dividing by 11, and turn a remainder of 10 into 0. The CUI is valid when this equals the check digit.

Here is 12345674 worked by hand. The body is 1234567, padded to 001234567:

Position Digit Key Product
1 0 7 0
2 0 5 0
3 1 3 3
4 2 2 4
5 3 1 3
6 4 7 28
7 5 5 25
8 6 3 18
9 7 2 14

The sum is 95. 950 mod 11 is 4, which matches the last digit, so RO12345674 is valid and RO12345678 is not.

The case that breaks hand-written validators is the remainder of 10. For 18547290 the products add up to 111, and 1110 mod 11 is 10, so the check digit is 0. A validator that skips the fold rejects every company whose check digit lands there.

How do I validate a CUI in TypeScript?

Parse first, then validate. A parser that returns the digits, the prefix and the verdict gives the form, the zod rule and the lookup the same source of truth:

// lib/cui.ts
export type CuiInfo = {
  // the digits without RO: "12345674"
  digits: string;
  // written with RO, the way a VAT payer quotes it
  vatPayer: boolean;
  valid: boolean;
};

// the test key 753217532, one weight per digit before the check digit
const KEY = [7, 5, 3, 2, 1, 7, 5, 3, 2];

export function parseCui(input: string): CuiInfo | null {
  const clean = input.replace(/[\s.\-/]/g, "").toUpperCase();
  const match = /^(RO)?(\d{2,10})$/.exec(clean);
  if (!match) return null;

  const digits = match[2];
  // right-align the body against the key: "1234567" -> "001234567"
  const body = digits.slice(0, -1).padStart(9, "0");
  let sum = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 9; i++) sum += Number(body[i]) * KEY[i];
  // times 10, mod 11, and a remainder of 10 becomes 0
  const control = ((sum * 10) % 11) % 10;

  return {
    digits,
    vatPayer: match[1] === "RO",
    valid: control === Number(digits[digits.length - 1]),
  };
}

export function isValidCui(input: string): boolean {
  return parseCui(input)?.valid ?? false;
}

// "ro 1234 5674" -> "RO12345674"; vatPayer adds or drops the prefix
export function formatCui(input: string, options: { vatPayer?: boolean } = {}): string {
  const info = parseCui(input);
  if (!info) return input;
  return `${(options.vatPayer ?? info.vatPayer) ? "RO" : ""}${info.digits}`;
}

parseCui("RO12345674"); // { digits: "12345674", vatPayer: true, valid: true }
isValidCui("12345678"); // false, the check digit should be 4
isValidCui("RO 185 472 90"); // true, remainder 10 becomes 0
formatCui("ro 1234 5674"); // "RO12345674"
formatCui("RO12345674", { vatPayer: false }); // "12345674"

Check four things before you trust a CIF checksum JavaScript snippet from a forum:

  • It uppercases before it strips RO, or ro12345674 fails.
  • It turns a remainder of 10 into 0.
  • It lines the digits up from the right. Left alignment only works for 10 digit codes.
  • It rejects 11 digits.

python-stdnum also rejects a code that starts with 0. parseCui accepts one, so write the digit group as ([1-9]\d{1,9}) if you want the same rule.

We ran every single-digit change and every swap of two neighboring digits over a large sample of valid 8-digit codes: the check caught about 98% of both, and every missed single-digit typo came from folding 10 into 0. A random 8-digit number passes one time in ten, so a valid check digit never means the company exists.

How do I write a zod rule for a CUI?

Chain three checks and a transform, so the person sees one message at a time and your database always receives the same shape:

// lib/cui-schema.ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { formatCui, isValidCui, parseCui } from "@/lib/cui";

export const cui = z
  .string()
  .trim()
  .min(1, { error: "Enter the company's tax ID", abort: true })
  .refine((value) => parseCui(value) !== null, {
    error: "Use 2 to 10 digits, with or without RO",
    abort: true,
  })
  .refine(isValidCui, { error: "This tax ID fails its check digit" })
  .transform((value) => formatCui(value));

// for a form where the tax ID is optional
export const optionalCui = z.union([z.literal(""), cui]);

abort: true (zod 4) stops at the first failing check, so "abc" says what format is expected instead of also blaming the check digit. The transform turns " ro 1234 5674 " into RO12345674 on submit, so you never have to rewrite the text while someone is typing.

In Wingo UI Pro, the form-validation lib ships a CUI rule as createValidators().cui(), with one message for any invalid code in English, or in Romanian with VALIDATION_MESSAGES_RO. It does not transform, so normalize with formatCui from the invoicing lib before saving; that lib exports the same three functions as the code above, plus IBAN and CNP checks.

How do I build a CUI field that validates as you type?

Show the error after the person leaves the field, then re-check on every keystroke so it clears the moment the number is right. Show the check mark as soon as the number is valid, since it interrupts no one. React Hook Form's onTouched mode gives the error that timing, and useWatch drives the check mark:

"use client";

import { useForm, useWatch } from "react-hook-form";
import { zodResolver } from "@hookform/resolvers/zod";
import { CircleCheck } from "lucide-react";
import { z } from "zod";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";
import { Input } from "@/components/ui/input";
import { isValidCui } from "@/lib/cui";
import { cui } from "@/lib/cui-schema";

const schema = z.object({
  company: z.string().trim().min(1, { error: "Enter the company name" }),
  cui,
});

type Values = z.output<typeof schema>;

export function BillingForm({ onSave }: { onSave: (values: Values) => Promise<void> }) {
  const form = useForm<z.input<typeof schema>, unknown, Values>({
    resolver: zodResolver(schema),
    // the first error waits for blur, then the field re-checks on every keystroke
    mode: "onTouched",
    defaultValues: { company: "", cui: "" },
  });
  const typed = useWatch({ control: form.control, name: "cui" });
  const { errors, isSubmitting } = form.formState;

  return (
    <form noValidate onSubmit={form.handleSubmit(onSave)} className="flex flex-col gap-4">
      <Input
        label="Company name"
        autoComplete="organization"
        {...form.register("company")}
        error={errors.company?.message}
      />
      <Input
        label="Tax ID (CUI)"
        description="With or without RO, for example RO12345674."
        placeholder="RO12345674"
        autoComplete="off"
        autoCapitalize="characters"
        spellCheck={false}
        {...form.register("cui")}
        error={errors.cui?.message}
        rightIcon={isValidCui(typed) ? <CircleCheck className="text-success-soft-foreground" /> : undefined}
      />
      <Button type="submit" loading={isSubmitting}>
        Save
      </Button>
    </form>
  );
}

The field keeps the text keyboard, because a numeric keypad has no R and no O. autoCapitalize="characters" turns "ro" into "RO" on phones, and spell check stays off so the browser does not underline a number. The Input uses 16px text on phones, so iOS does not zoom, and its error replaces the hint, sets aria-invalid and links the message with aria-describedby, the anatomy that Field gives every control. Both are free: npx wingo-ui@latest add input field.

Live demo: Form validation. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Type RO12345678 in Company tax ID and press Tab: the check digit error appears. Change the last digit to 4 and it clears while you type). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Form validation docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add form-validation

How do I check that the company exists and pays VAT?

Ask ANAF. Its public PlatitorTvaRest web service answers, for a list of CUIs and a date, whether each company is found, its name and address, and whether it was registered for VAT on that date. As of October 2026, the v9 documentation gives these rules: a POST to https://webservicesp.anaf.ro/api/PlatitorTvaRest/v9/tva with a JSON array of { "cui": number, "data": "YYYY-MM-DD" }, at most 100 CUIs per request and at most one request per second per client. The answer has a found list and a notFound list.

We called it on October 8, 2026, and two results surprised us. A number with a wrong check digit lands in notFound without an error, so validating first saves a request against that limit. And our own demo number, RO12345674, came back found: a company struck off the register in 2006, with stare_inregistrare set to "RADIERE din data 29.06.2006", scpTVA false and the inactive flag statusInactivi also false. 18547290, the example from python-stdnum, came back the same way, struck off in 2016. Found does not mean active, and in both records the inactive flag stayed false, so read stare_inregistrare. An active company reads "INREGISTRAT din data" followed by a date.

Keep the call on your server. The field names are Romanian and the version sits in the path (the v5 documentation used /PlatitorTvaRest/api/v5/ws/tva), so one route handler is the only file that changes when ANAF moves. It reads the CUI from the query string, which arrives decoded, and turns a timeout or an error page into one 502:

// app/api/company/route.ts
import type { NextRequest } from "next/server";
import { parseCui } from "@/lib/cui";

const ANAF = "https://webservicesp.anaf.ro/api/PlatitorTvaRest/v9/tva";

type AnafCompany = {
  date_generale: { denumire: string; adresa: string; stare_inregistrare: string };
  inregistrare_scop_Tva: { scpTVA: boolean };
  stare_inactiv: { statusInactivi: boolean };
};

export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
  const info = parseCui(request.nextUrl.searchParams.get("cui") ?? "");
  // a typo never costs a request against the one-per-second limit
  if (!info?.valid) return Response.json({ error: "invalid-cui" }, { status: 400 });

  // ANAF answers for a calendar day in Romania, not in UTC
  const today = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-CA", { timeZone: "Europe/Bucharest" }).format(new Date());
  let found: AnafCompany[];
  try {
    const response = await fetch(ANAF, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify([{ cui: Number(info.digits), data: today }]),
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(8000),
    });
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`ANAF answered ${response.status}`);
    ({ found } = (await response.json()) as { found: AnafCompany[]; notFound: number[] });
  } catch {
    // a timeout, an error status or a page that is not JSON
    return Response.json({ error: "anaf-unavailable" }, { status: 502 });
  }

  const company = found[0];
  if (!company) return Response.json({ error: "not-found" }, { status: 404 });

  return Response.json({
    name: company.date_generale.denumire,
    address: company.date_generale.adresa,
    vatPayer: company.inregistrare_scop_Tva.scpTVA,
    // "INREGISTRAT din data ..." while active, "RADIERE din data ..." once struck off
    struckOff: company.date_generale.stare_inregistrare.startsWith("RADIERE"),
    inactive: company.stare_inactiv.statusInactivi,
  });
}

To ANAF, your server is the client, so every sign-up shares that one request per second. Cache answers by CUI, and for imports batch up to 100 CUIs per request.

ANAF tells you about Romanian VAT registration. For a Romanian VAT ID check on a cross-border invoice inside the EU, use VIES. The European Commission's VIES page lists three reasons for an invalid answer: the number does not exist, it has not been activated for intra-EU transactions, or the registration is not finalized yet. A company can be a valid Romanian VAT payer and still be invalid in VIES.

What does a real sign-up step with a CUI lookup look like?

The Register Page block has an optional company step built on these pieces. Its CUI field validates with v.cui() and looks up only on Enter or the Search button: since one random number in ten passes the check, a lookup on every valid keystroke would also fire on half-typed numbers. An invalid check digit shows the error and never calls the lookup. A valid number goes through formatCui to your onLookupCui. A match fades in the name, the address and a VAT badge, and the field is rewritten with formatCui(cui, { vatPayer }), so the prefix comes from ANAF instead of habit. Editing the number clears the result, and a late answer for an older number is ignored.

Plugging in the route handler from the previous section takes one prop. The account, code and company saves stay simulated until you pass onRegister, onVerify and onCompany:

"use client";

import { RegisterPage } from "@/components/blocks/register-page";

export default function SignUpPage() {
  return (
    <RegisterPage
      onLookupCui={async (cui) => {
        const response = await fetch(`/api/company?cui=${encodeURIComponent(cui)}`);
        if (response.status === 404) return null;
        if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Lookup failed");
        const company = await response.json();
        // treat a struck-off company like an unknown one
        if (company.struckOff) return null;
        return { name: company.name, address: company.address, vatPayer: company.vatPayer };
      }}
    />
  );
}

Returning null opens the manual fields with a note, and throwing offers "Try again" and "Fill in by hand". The demo below answers from a sample table instead of ANAF, so its companies are made up.

Live demo: Register Page. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Type RO12345678 and press Enter: the check digit error appears and no lookup runs. Fix the last digit to 4 and press Enter again: the sample register fills in the company and its VAT badge). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Register Page docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add register-page

The step after it asks for the 6 digit code from the sign-up email; our React OTP input guide covers what that field has to handle.

Should I copy the CUI code or install it?

Copy it when you need one field: lib/cui.ts, the zod rule and the free Input cover a billing or sign-up form. The ready Romanian kit (CUI, IBAN, CNP and VAT math in invoicing, shared messages in form-validation) and the whole sign-up flow are part of Wingo UI Pro. The other two ids have their own guides: IBAN validation in JavaScript for bank accounts and the Romanian CNP validator for people. For the rest of the form anatomy, read React form components: accessible fields, zod and mobile, or browse more component guides.

Components in this post

  • Invoicing (Pro): Invoice math and the ids an invoice carries: VAT per rate the way e-Factura checks it, Romanian VAT rates, CUI, IBAN with its bank, CNP. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add invoicing
  • Form validation (Pro): Zod rules with one set of messages (English and Romanian), react-hook-form glue and a pretend request, for the forms of blocks. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add form-validation
  • Input (Free): The single-line text field: icons and addons inside the box, a clear button, a loading spinner, a counter and floating labels. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add input
  • Field (Free): The wrapper every form control shares: label, hint, animated error and counter, fieldsets, and the one box recipe all inputs use. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add field
  • Register Page (Pro): The sign-up screen of a CRM: account with password rules, company details from the CUI, email code and a welcome step. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add register-page

FAQ

What is the difference between a CUI and a CIF?

For a company they are the same digits. The CUI is the registration code the company receives, and the CIF is its tax identification code, written with the RO prefix when the company is registered for VAT. People are identified by their 13 digit CNP, which has its own check digit.

Is RO part of the CUI?

No. RO marks a company registered for VAT and takes no part in the checksum. Strip it before you validate, store the digits, and add RO back when you print the VAT number of a company that ANAF lists as a VAT payer.

How is the CUI check digit calculated?

Pad the digits before the last one to nine digits on the left, multiply them by 7, 5, 3, 2, 1, 7, 5, 3, 2 and add the products. Multiply the sum by 10 and take the remainder mod 11; a remainder of 10 becomes 0, and the result must equal the last digit.

Does a valid CUI mean the company exists?

No. About one random number in ten passes the check. Query ANAF's PlatitorTvaRest web service to see whether the company exists, whether it is still registered and whether it pays VAT on a given date.

How do I check a Romanian VAT number for an EU cross-border invoice?

Search it in VIES, the European Commission's VAT number search. An invalid answer can mean the number does not exist, or that it has not been activated for intra-EU transactions.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: Romanian CUI Validation in TypeScript, Zod and React. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: Un socle de composants encore utilisé huit mois plus tard
description:
J'ai livré un socle de composants depuis zéro : primitives de mise en page, thème, palette de couleurs, documentation interactive. Huit mois après, d'autres équipes l'étendent, et d'autres développeurs ont écrit ses tests.

Ce qui m'importe, c'est que d'autres s'en servent sans moi. Voici les choix qui y ont contribué.

Une palette sémantique, pas une liste de couleurs. Un composant ne dit pas « utilise ce vert », il dit « utilise la couleur d'action ». Changer le thème se fait alors à un seul endroit.

Une palette typée. Si les rôles sont typés, on ne peut pas utiliser un rôle qui n'existe pas : l'éditeur le refuse avant même de lancer l'app.

// exemple générique
const palette = {
  text: { primary: "#1a1c1b", muted: "#5a5f5c" },
  action: { default: "#0b7a5b" },
} as const;

type TextTone = keyof typeof palette.text; // "primary" | "muted"

Les contrastes corrigés dès la palette. Un texte gris clair sur fond blanc est joli et illisible. Corriger le contraste une fois, dans la palette, le corrige partout. Pour un texte courant, le seuil à viser est un rapport de 4,5 pour 1.

Une documentation interactive. Un composant qu'on ne peut pas essayer sans lancer l'application ne sera pas réutilisé. La documentation montre chaque composant dans chacun de ses états, et sert aussi de test visuel.

Ce que je vise avec un socle : qu'un développeur d'une autre équipe puisse s'en servir sans me poser de question.

Amine Affif, développeur full-stack à Paris. amineaffif.com

title: Google's Malaysia expansion puts campus readiness and cloud availability on separate timelines
description:
Google announced a US$15 billion Malaysia investment plan on November 4, covering 2027 and 2028. Its announcement identifies the Elmina Business Park campus in Selangor as operational, describes further campuses in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan as planned, and says its Malaysian Google Cloud region is upcoming.

That status distinction matters for technical buyers. The availability of a physical campus does not, by itself, specify which enterprise cloud services a customer can deploy locally. My operational reading is that teams evaluating Malaysian workload placement should maintain separate readiness checks for facilities and the services they intend to buy.

Turn the announcement into a service-specific checklist

Start with the application requirements rather than the investment total.

For each workload, list the compute, storage, networking, managed services and accelerator types it needs. Ask the provider which are available in the intended region, which remain planned and what capacity or quota commitments are offered.

Keep dates and evidence beside each answer. A roadmap discussion can inform preparation, while a production commitment needs the terms for the actual service being purchased.

For an AI application, that includes the complete serving path. A locally hosted component may still depend on another service elsewhere. Ask the application team to trace the path from an incoming request through processing, storage, logging and downstream calls.

Test locality across normal operation and recovery

My recommendation is to document data flows before deciding what a local deployment achieves.

Describe where application data is processed, where copies are stored and where operational records are retained. Include backups, telemetry and any external AI endpoints. Have the responsible security and compliance teams review that map against the organization's requirements.

Then repeat the exercise for failure and recovery. Determine where the workload would run if its preferred location became unavailable, which data would move and how long restoration could take.

This is a proposed planning exercise, not a statement about the architecture of Google's upcoming region. The announcement does not provide enough service-level detail to settle those questions for a particular application.

Keep power commitments tied to delivery evidence

Google also announced plans to enable more than 1 GW of new clean energy capacity for Malaysia's National Grid. That is planned generation capacity, not a disclosed IT load or a statement that this generation is already operating.

For buyers comparing infrastructure proposals, the useful follow-up is a description of how the power plan connects to the service timetable.

Ask which milestones remain, what the provider will report as projects progress and whether any delivery assumptions depend on future infrastructure. Keep the answers alongside the workload deployment plan so that a change in one schedule triggers a review of the other.

Avoid converting an energy headline into an estimate of available accelerators. The announcement does not supply the technical inputs needed for that calculation.

Assess water performance at the relevant location

Google says it has selected water cooling for these campuses following local watershed assessments. It also describes water replenishment projects and location-level annual consumption reporting.

My recommendation is to evaluate those subjects separately when reviewing operating evidence. Request the site's consumption information, the reporting period and the conditions under which it was measured. Review community water projects according to their own timing, location and verification.

For a facility review, ask how cooling operation changes during supply restrictions, maintenance or unusually demanding weather. Request the operating assumptions and escalation process relevant to the proposed service.

Those are questions for assessing resilience. They should not be treated as findings that a shortage exists at these sites.

Stage the migration around services that can be verified

The practical opportunity is to prepare a migration without tying every step to the same future date.

Teams can inventory dependencies, establish network requirements and define acceptance tests while waiting for service-specific availability. Once the intended configuration can be provisioned, test it with a representative workload and record latency, throughput, recovery behavior and cost.

Agree beforehand which results allow production traffic to move and which require further work. Keep an alternative deployment path for dependencies whose availability remains uncertain.

Google's announcement adds a significant infrastructure plan and an operational campus update. For an enterprise infrastructure team, the next decision should rest on the availability and tested behavior of the exact services its application needs.

title: Finding missing and unused i18next keys in a React project
description:
A translation key is a string nobody checks. Here is how to check it by hand, in the IDE and in CI.
Look at this line:

<button>{t('checkout.pay_nwo')}</button>

The build passes and so do the tests. In production, the button reads checkout.pay_nwo.

My own start with translation keys was a migration. An existing application was going international, so every text in the code had to move into JSON files, in French, English, Spanish and Italian. Carrying all of that over by hand was the hardest part of the job. It also left me with four files that had to stay in step with the code, and nothing to check that they did.

Day to day, the cost is smaller but constant. To know whether a key exists, in which namespace and what it says, you open en/common.json, hit Ctrl+F, scroll and come back. Multiply that by 200 keys and 5 locales.

A translation key is a plain string that points to a line in a JSON file, and by default nothing verifies that the line exists. i18next's typed keys catch this particular typo, if you have set them up. They do not tell you that the German file lacks the key, or that half of your French file is no longer used by any component.

Four ways a key goes wrong

  1. The code calls a key that no file holds. A typo, or a key deleted during a cleanup. The user sees the raw key.
  2. A key exists in English and not in French. i18next falls back to English without a word, so nobody notices until a French customer does.
  3. A file holds a key that no code calls. It does no harm on screen, but translators keep translating it and the files keep growing.
  4. A placeholder changes in translation. Hello {{name}} becomes Bonjour {{nom}}, and the French page greets the user with {{nom}}.

None of these fails a build.

Checking by hand

The second case is the easiest to script. With jq, list every key path of two files and compare them:

diff <(jq -r 'paths(scalars) | join(".")' locales/en/common.json | sort) \
     <(jq -r 'paths(scalars) | join(".")' locales/fr/common.json | sort)

Each line of the output is a key one locale has and the other lacks.

This works for one pair of files. Then the limits show:

  • You need one run per namespace and per locale.
  • Unused keys need the opposite search, each key looked up in the code. A grep for user.name misses t('common:user.name') written under useTranslation('common'), and it cannot know that t(`status.${kind}`) uses every key under status.
  • It runs when someone remembers to run it, which is after the bug.

So the script is fine for an audit before a release. For daily work I wanted the editor to tell me.

Checking in the editor

During that migration I used I18n Support, a plugin by Evgeniy Nyavro. That plugin was no longer maintained. Built for older versions of the IDE, it was buggy and kept crashing IntelliJ. When the job was over, I made myself a promise: with some free time, I would fork it and just update the dependencies.

"Just" did not last. One feature followed another 😅, and the fork became I18n Support Plus, an open-source (MIT) plugin for WebStorm, IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate and PhpStorm. I maintain it, and the rest of this article uses it, so read it with that in mind.

With the plugin installed, a key gets an icon in the gutter: green when every locale holds it, yellow when some lack it, red when none does. Its value follows it as an inline hint, which saves opening the JSON file to remember what checkout.pay_now says. Ctrl+hover gives the value in every locale, with a dash where one is missing, and Ctrl+click opens the translation file on the right line. For a whole file, Show Translations Inline replaces each key by its value, and the JSX reads like the real UI.

A red key is the typo from the top of this article, or a key that was never created. Either way, Alt+Enter and Create missing key write the value in every locale without leaving the component.

The typo itself gets rarer, because completion after t(' lists the keys that exist, namespaces included, each with its value.

For the key that French lacks, the tool window has a table with one column per locale and a filter that keeps the keys missing or empty somewhere. Sync Keys then creates the absent ones in each locale, for every namespace at once, which is where the jq one-liner stopped.

Unused keys are the hardest to find by hand. Count Key Usages counts the code usages of every key, namespace included, and the ones at zero are the candidates for deletion. When a key needs a better name, Shift+F6 renames it in every locale and at every call site, like any other symbol.

Then there is the task I started with, moving hard-coded text into the files. Alt+Enter turns a text into a key and writes the value in every locale, and Internationalize… does the same for a whole file or folder, after a preview:

Checking in CI

An editor check helps the person who has the plugin. The pull request of a colleague who does not have it needs a second net. The same checks run without an IDE, as a GitHub Action:

jobs:
  translations:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: IBRAHIMDANS/i18nSupportPlus@v1.18.0
        with:
          args: --code

The job fails on a key missing from a locale, on a placeholder lost in a translation (the fourth case) and on a key the code calls that no file holds. With --code it also reports the unused keys. It annotates the pull request, so the author sees the problem on the line that caused it.

What it does not do

  • Keys built at runtime. t(`status.${kind}`) is read as status.*: the keys under status are not reported as unused, but the plugin cannot know which value kind takes. A key that comes from a function parameter or a computed value is not followed at all.
  • VS Code. The plugin is for JetBrains IDEs, 2025.2 or later. On VS Code, i18n Ally covers the same ground.
  • Translating for you by default. Machine translation exists (a local Ollama, DeepL, Google and others) but stays off until you turn it on, and nothing is written before a preview.

Try it

The plugin is free. Install it from the JetBrains Marketplace, or search for I18n Support Plus in Settings › Plugins. A setup wizard detects the framework and the translation files on first launch. The examples here are i18next, but the plugin also reads vue-i18n, next-intl, Lingui, react-intl, Angular, Laravel and Symfony projects.

The code, the documentation and a sample project for each framework are on GitHub. Issues and feature requests are welcome there, and a star helps if the plugin saves you time.

One question to finish: how many times a day do you open a JSON file just to check whether a key exists? If the answer is not "never", I would like to hear how you deal with it.

I build tools that cut the daily friction of front-end work. Let's talk on LinkedIn.

title: Lofi Radio for Coding: Build a Terminal Player with Python and mpv
description:
Plenty of us keep lofi radio for coding running in a browser tab that slowly eats memory next to twelve other tabs. This weekend project replaces that tab with a tiny terminal player: about 60 lines of Python, mpv doing the heavy lifting, and now playing info pulled straight from the stream.

You will learn how internet radio streams actually expose track titles, how to deal with playlist files, and how to keep a player alive when a stream drops.

How an internet radio stream differs from a file

A radio stream is an HTTP response that never ends. Most stations run Icecast or Shoutcast and push MP3 or AAC frames continuously. Two details matter for us:

  • Playlist wrappers. Stations often publish .m3u or .pls files instead of a direct stream. These are plain text files that point to the real URL.
  • ICY metadata. If a client sends the header Icy-MetaData: 1, the server replies with icy-metaint: N, then inserts a small metadata block every N bytes of audio. That block contains something like StreamTitle='Artist - Track';.

That is all "now playing" is on most stations. No API, just bytes in the audio stream.

Reading ICY metadata in Python

Here is a minimal reader using only requests:

import re
import requests

def now_playing(url: str) -> str | None:
    headers = {"Icy-MetaData": "1", "User-Agent": "lofi-term/0.1"}
    with requests.get(url, headers=headers, stream=True, timeout=10) as r:
        metaint = int(r.headers.get("icy-metaint", 0))
        if not metaint:
            return None
        raw = r.raw
        raw.read(metaint)                 # skip audio
        length = raw.read(1)[0] * 16      # metadata length byte
        meta = raw.read(length).decode("utf-8", "replace")
        m = re.search(r"StreamTitle='(.*?)';", meta)
        return m.group(1) if m else None

Notice that the length byte is multiplied by 16. That trips up almost everyone the first time.

Resolving .pls and .m3u files 

def resolve(url: str) -> str:
    if not url.lower().endswith((".pls", ".m3u")):
        return url
    text = requests.get(url, timeout=10).text
    for line in text.splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if line.startswith("File1="):
            return line.split("=", 1)[1]
        if line.startswith("http"):
            return line
    raise ValueError("no stream found")

We leave .m3u8 alone on purpose. That is HLS, a segmented format, and mpv handles it natively.

Letting mpv play, with automatic reconnects

Decoding audio yourself is a rabbit hole. mpv already does it well, and it accepts flags that keep long-running streams stable:

import subprocess, time

def play(url: str):
    while True:
        proc = subprocess.run([
            "mpv", "--no-video", "--really-quiet",
            "--cache=yes", "--demuxer-max-bytes=2MiB",
            "--stream-lavf-o=reconnect_streamed=1,reconnect_delay_max=10",
            resolve(url),
        ])
        if proc.returncode == 0:
            break
        print("stream dropped, retrying in 5s")
        time.sleep(5)

A separate thread can call now_playing() every 30 seconds and print the title. Keep it gentle: opening a second connection every few seconds is rude to small stations that pay for bandwidth.

Picking streams and keeping CPU low

For a coding soundtrack, a 128 kbps MP3 or a 64 kbps AAC stream is plenty, and mpv with --no-video usually sits well under 2 percent CPU on a modern laptop. A few habits help:

  • Prefer HTTPS stream URLs when the station offers them.
  • Store favorites in a small TOML file, keyed by a short name, so lofi-term chill just works.
  • Respect the station: identify your client with a real User-Agent and do not scrape aggressively.

If you need real-world URLs to test against, browse these live lofi radio streams to test with. You will quickly see the mix of MP3, AAC and HLS that exists in the wild, which is exactly what makes a player robust.

Why lofi radio for coding works so well

There is a reason lofi radio for coding became its own genre of background noise. The tracks sit around a steady, unhurried tempo, they rarely have lyrics, and the mix is intentionally soft, with vinyl crackle and rounded highs. Nothing in it competes with the part of your brain that is reading a stack trace.

A live stream also removes a decision. With a playlist you are tempted to skip, reorder and curate, which is just another small context switch. With radio you press play once and stop thinking about it. That is exactly why a lightweight terminal player is worth building: it gives you the stream without a browser full of distractions sitting one tab away.

If you share your setup with teammates, the same script works on a home server or a Raspberry Pi wired to office speakers. Just keep the reconnect loop polite, with a delay between retries, so you are not hammering a station during an outage.

FAQ

What is the best format for lofi radio for coding?
Any stable stream works. AAC at 64 to 128 kbps sounds good and uses little bandwidth, and MP3 is the most compatible.

Why does my stream show no track title?
The server may not send icy-metaint, or the station does not populate StreamTitle. HLS streams usually carry metadata differently, in ID3 tags inside segments.

Can I do this without mpv?
Yes, ffplay or VLC's cvlc work too. mpv just has the cleanest flags for headless playback.

Is it legal to stream internet radio in my own player?
Listening to a publicly offered stream is normal use. Re-broadcasting or recording for distribution is a different story, so check the station's terms.

Wrapping up

Sixty lines, one dependency and your browser gets a little lighter. Fork it, add a TUI with textual, and let the beats carry you through the next refactor.

title: Debug The White Rectangle Before Rewriting Your Image Component
description:
A dark card exposes a white box around an otherwise normal image. Before adding CSS overrides, determine whether the box belongs to the asset or its container.

Build A Two-Color Reproduction

Render the same file against white and charcoal. Remove filters and blend modes. Open the image directly as well. If the rectangle follows the file, inspect the exported pixels before changing the component.

.asset-check { background: #263445; }
.asset-check img { width: 240px; height: auto; }

Fix The Asset Boundary

The remove white background guide covers preparing a separate image. Preserve intentionally white lettering and enclosed details while clearing the unwanted area.

According to the W3C PNG specification, PNG can carry alpha information. The extension alone does not prove that any pixels are transparent. Renaming a JPEG also leaves its image data unchanged.

Make The Review Reproducible

  • Record the exact file and rendered width.
  • Check both themes and the exported result.
  • Inspect any CDN conversion if production differs.

Opacity affects the entire image, so it cannot selectively remove the white area. Once the file is correct, handle spacing and object-fit as separate layout concerns.

Keep this small reproduction alongside the fix so a future asset replacement can be checked under the same conditions.

Do not hide the issue by matching the card background to the rectangle. That makes the defect harder to notice until someone changes the theme.

title: Variables and Data Types in Java
description:
Variables and Data Types in Java

In Java, variables and data types are the fundamental concepts used to store and manage data in a program. Every application needs to store different kinds of information, such as names, ages, prices, marks, and other values. Java uses variables to store this information and data types to define what kind of values can be stored.

1. Variables in Java

A variable is a named memory location used to store data in a program. Every variable has a name, a data type, and a value.

Example:

String name = "Abimanyu";
int age = 21;
double salary = 25000.50;

System.out.println(name);
System.out.println(age);
System.out.println(salary);

Here, name, age, and salary are variables. Java allocates memory to store their values based on their data types.

Types of Variables

Java has three main types of variables:

  • Local Variable: A variable declared inside a method, constructor, or block. It can only be accessed within its scope and must be initialized before use.
  • Instance Variable: A variable declared inside a class but outside methods. Each object gets its own copy of these variables.
  • Static Variable: A variable declared using the static keyword. It belongs to the class and is shared among its objects.

2. Data Types in Java

A data type defines what kind of value a variable can store. For example, an integer variable stores whole numbers, whereas a String variable stores text.

Java is a statically typed language, which means we must declare the data type when creating a variable.

Java data types are divided into two main categories:

Primitive Data Types

Primitive data types are the basic built-in data types provided by Java. Java has eight primitive data types.

Data Type Size Example
byte 8 bits byte a = 100;
short 16 bits short a = 2000;
int 32 bits int a = 100;
long 64 bits long a = 10000L;
float 32 bits float a = 10.5f;
double 64 bits double a = 20.55;
char 16 bits char a = 'A';
boolean JVM-dependent boolean a = true;

Some important points:

  • int is commonly used to store integer values.
  • long is used for larger integer values.
  • float and double are used for decimal values.
  • char stores a single UTF-16 code unit.
  • boolean stores either true or false.

Non-Primitive Data Types

Non-primitive data types are reference types used to work with objects and more complex data structures.

Some common examples are:

  • String: Used to store a sequence of characters.
  • Array: Used to store multiple values of the same type.
  • Class: A blueprint used to create objects.

Example:

String name = "Abimanyu";

int[] marks = {85, 90, 95};

System.out.println(name);
System.out.println(marks[0]);

Unlike primitive types, reference variables can hold null, which means they do not currently refer to an object.

3. Type Casting in Java

Type casting is the process of converting one data type into another. Java supports two main types of casting.

Widening Casting (Automatic):

Converting a smaller compatible numeric type into a larger type.

int number = 100;

double result = number;

System.out.println(result);

Output: 100.0

Narrowing Casting (Manual):

Converting a larger numeric type into a smaller type. It requires explicit casting and may result in data loss.

double price = 99.99;

int result = (int) price;

System.out.println(result);

Output: 99

title: Designing a Form That Asks for Birth Date, Time and Place (No Code, Just the Tricky Parts)
description:
Some forms look easy and turn out to be annoying. A form that asks for a birth date, a birth time and a birth place is one of them. It has just four or five fields, yet there are a lot of ways to get it wrong.

I’ve been looking at forms like this, so here are the problems I think are worth thinking about. No code, only the design side.

  1. People often don’t know the exact time

This is the big one. Many people only know their birth time roughly, or not at all. If the form insists on an exact time, they’ll either guess or leave. A better form lets people say “I’m not sure,” and explains what that changes. Forcing a made-up answer just gives you bad data that looks real.

  1. Date formats confuse people

Different regions write dates in a different order, so “03/04/1990” can mean two different days. A form that shows a clear label, like day, month, year in separate boxes, avoids a lot of mistakes. Showing the date back to the user in words before submitting (for example, “3 April 1990”) is cheap and catches errors.

  1. The same time can mean different things in different places

Birth time only makes sense with the place and its time zone at that moment. Places also change their time rules over the years. If the form only stores a time without handling the place properly, the result can be off. I’d treat this as a design question as well as a technical one: show the user what you understood, and let them correct it.

  1. Place search needs to be forgiving

People type place names in different spellings, and many towns share a name. Suggestions as you type help, and so does showing a bit of extra detail, like the region, so people can pick the right one.

  1. This is personal data

Birth details are personal. Say clearly why you ask for them and how you use them, and don’t ask for more than the tool needs.

An example

The free kundli tool on AI AstroCall is one form like this. It asks for a name, birth date, birth time and birth place and generates a birth chart (a kundli) from them. I’m mentioning it as an example of the kind of form I mean, not as a model to copy.

Disclosure: I’m affiliated with AI AstroCall.

title: Classifying a UAE Clinic's Service Price List With Python Before E-Invoicing
description:
Disclosure: I used AI to help draft this article. I ran the code and tests myself. I work at an accounting software partner in Dubai, and this is a general programming tutorial. The tax categories in the examples are placeholders, not tax advice.

UAE clinics are preparing for structured electronic invoices. Under the published timetable, businesses with annual revenue of AED 50 million or more go live on 1 January 2027, and other businesses go live on 1 July 2027. A pilot phase is open now, and no fines apply while businesses test.

For a clinic, one problem comes up early: the price list. Over the years it fills with short names such as "Consultation" or "Whitening", and the tax category for each item often lives in someone's head. Healthcare is a good example of why that matters. Preventive and basic care is generally zero-rated, elective and cosmetic services are charged at 5%, and the standard rate applies where the patient and the recipient of the supply are not the same. A wrong category on one item repeats on every invoice that uses it.

This post builds a small Python tool that checks a clinic's service list against a rules table. It sorts each item into three groups: matched, needs review, or conflict. The tool never guesses. If it cannot decide, it says so, and a person decides.

title: AI Model Vendor Updates: A 14-Check Release Gate for SMEs
description:
AI Model Vendor Updates: A 14-Check Release Gate for SMEs

A provider changing a hosted model does not automatically mean your application is broken, and a stable API name does not prove that its behavior stayed stable. Buyers need a compact way to decide whether a change is harmless, needs a narrow retest, or must be stopped. This guide gives you a reproducible acceptance packet for provider-managed model changes. It separates model retirement, alias movement, request and response schemas, task behavior, service reliability, price, privacy, and action boundaries. The included 14-case fixture is synthetic: it demonstrates a decision method, not the performance of any vendor or production model. If you are setting the broader operating direction for a Swiss SME, the AI strategy roadmap for Swiss SMEs can help place this release gate inside a wider portfolio and ownership plan.

The decision is simple: never approve a change solely because the endpoint still returns HTTP 200, and never reject it solely because the model identifier changed. Record what changed, compare a representative fixed test packet, enforce non-negotiable safety and data controls, then approve only the exact scope you tested. A successful sample is evidence for that sample and configuration. It is not a guarantee about all future prompts, all users, or every provider deployment.

What problem this gate solves

Hosted AI services evolve. A provider may announce a retirement date, move a dated alias, adjust a default, change a response field, alter tool behavior, or update operational controls. Those are different events. A retirement is a lifecycle question: what date, replacement, and migration path are offered? An alias move is a reproducibility question: what actual model or configuration answered yesterday and today? A schema change is an integration question. A behavior change is an acceptance question. Treating these as one generic “model update” makes it easy to test the wrong thing.

Provider documentation shows why lifecycle evidence matters. OpenAI’s model documentation distinguishes snapshots that point to a specific model version, while its deprecation page lists notices, replacements, and shutdown dates. These pages support a narrow operational conclusion: record the identifier and lifecycle notice you actually rely on; do not infer that a familiar alias freezes behavior. See OpenAI model documentation and OpenAI deprecations. Anthropic describes a minimum notice period for public releases on its own platform, while noting that partner-platform timing may differ; that is a platform-specific policy, not a universal industry promise. See Anthropic model deprecations.

For an SME, the practical question is not “Did the provider change something?” but “Could this change alter a decision, a customer-facing statement, a data path, an external action, or the cost of a completed task?” If the answer is no for a low-risk drafting helper, a small regression check may be enough. If the system routes payments, sends messages, changes records, or handles sensitive data, the test needs stronger hard stops and a human approval path.

Change classes and their different evidence

Before testing, classify the event. Do not trust the release note title to do this for you. A single provider announcement may combine model availability, API fields, capacity, and billing. Your procurement or operations owner should translate it into changed assumptions and assign one or more classes.

Change class Buyer question Minimum useful evidence Typical stop condition
Retirement When does the current option stop accepting requests? Notice date, replacement, migration window Shutdown precedes a tested migration
Alias or default movement What exact version answered the request? Requested identifier and returned metadata if available Version is unknown for a high-impact workflow
Request schema Did required fields, defaults, or limits change? Contract test and rejected-input test Silent coercion or dropped safety field
Response schema Can the caller still parse and validate output? Missing, extra, malformed, and refusal cases Invalid output reaches a business action
Behavior Does the task still meet its own acceptance criteria? Fixed cases, scoring rubric, baseline comparison Any hard safety invariant fails
Service Are latency, error, or availability assumptions still met? Same workload, timeout and retry observations SLO or retry budget breached
Price or quota Does the accepted task remain economically viable? Metered usage, current rate card, quota evidence Budget ceiling or unit economics breached
Privacy or retention Did data use, storage, region, or controls change? Current policy and account-specific configuration Required control cannot be demonstrated
Tool or action behavior Can a response trigger a broader action? Permission and approval tests Unapproved irreversible action is possible

A change class is an inference about what to test, not a claim that the provider has changed that surface. Separate observed facts from assumptions. “The provider announced a replacement date” is a fact if the notice says so. “This replacement will preserve our answer quality” is not a fact until your own test supports it. “Pause external sending until the replacement passes” is a recommendation grounded in your risk tolerance.

The release packet: 14 checks

The packet below is intentionally small enough to run again, but broad enough to expose common blind spots. It uses synthetic cases and acceptance conditions, not measured vendor results. The method is to keep the input fixtures, expected outcomes, test configuration, and decision record together. Run the same packet against the current approved configuration and the proposed one when comparable access exists. If the provider changes a surface that a case does not cover, add a case before approving that surface.

# Check Fixture or perturbation Pass condition
1 Identity Record requested model, endpoint, region, account, date Configuration is reproducible enough to identify
2 Lifecycle Read current retirement and replacement notice Dates and owner are recorded
3 Alias Compare requested alias with returned version metadata Unknown movement is disclosed and scoped
4 Request schema Submit valid minimum request Required fields are accepted as intended
5 Invalid request Omit or corrupt a required field Failure is explicit; no unsafe default
6 Response schema Parse normal response and metadata Parser validates fields and types
7 Missing output Simulate absent or empty content Workflow stops without inventing completion
8 Refusal Use a clearly disallowed synthetic request Refusal remains a safe terminal state
9 Core task Run representative SME task fixture Task-specific rubric meets threshold
10 Boundary task Use ambiguous or underspecified input Clarification or safe abstention occurs
11 Tool boundary Propose a write/send action in fixture Approval and least privilege still apply
12 Service envelope Exercise timeout, retry, and rate-limit handling Bounded retries; no duplicate business action
13 Cost and quota Capture usage for the accepted task Budget and quota assumptions remain valid
14 Data controls Verify retention, training, region, and logging settings Required account-specific controls are evidenced

1. Identity and reproducible configuration

Write down enough context that a second operator can identify the candidate system: provider, product surface, requested model string, endpoint, tenant, region when relevant, date, system instructions, tool definitions, retrieval corpus version, parser, and post-processing. “We tested the new model” is not a useful record if the prompt and connector configuration have drifted since the baseline. Save the configuration fingerprint or a redacted manifest beside the results. Exclude credentials and secrets; a reproducible packet must never become a secret dump.

Some providers expose a returned version label; others expose less. Record both the requested identifier and any observed metadata, keeping them distinct. If the system does not disclose the underlying version, write “not available” rather than guessing from an alias or release date. That is a limit in reproducibility, not proof of instability. The risk decision then depends on use: missing version detail may be tolerable for low-impact brainstorming, while a workflow with customer or financial consequences may need a bounded scope, provider clarification, or a hold.

Repeat the identity capture when the test runner, region, tool permission, or retrieval index changes, even if the model string stays fixed. The tested object is the whole workflow configuration. A comparison between a new model with fewer tools and an old model with broad write access does not isolate the provider change. It may still be a valid system comparison, but the conclusion must be about those two system versions, not the model alone.

2. Lifecycle, retirement, and replacement evidence

Check official lifecycle documentation and capture the page, date, applicable product, current status, shutdown date if listed, and stated replacement. OpenAI’s documentation illustrates the value of preserving snapshots and deprecation notices; Anthropic’s page illustrates that notice policies may be specific to its own operated platform and may differ on partner platforms. Link the exact notice in the decision record. Do not infer the service agreement from a blog post when the contract or account-specific notice is controlling.

Create an owner and deadline for each retirement. The date when a model is announced for retirement, the date when a replacement becomes available, and the date when requests stop are separate. A safe migration window needs time for inventory, testing, sign-off, deployment, and contingency. If those dates leave no test window, raise the issue as an operational dependency rather than compressing the acceptance work until it becomes ceremonial.

Test the replacement in a non-effecting environment before routing live tasks. If the replacement is not yet available, the correct result is “migration pending,” not “passed.” If the prior model remains available only in a temporary account, verify access and billing rather than assuming the fallback will exist at incident time. Record a last-known working configuration and a plan that can be executed by an on-call operator who did not attend the procurement meeting.

3. Alias movement and hidden defaults

An alias is a request name. It may not be an immutable identity unless provider documentation explicitly says so. Compare the requested string, response metadata, provider notice, and observed configuration where available. If the provider says an alias is updated over time, the alias alone cannot serve as a stable baseline. Use a pinned version where supported and appropriate, or record that the workflow accepts provider-managed movement and compensate with ongoing evaluation.

Test your change-detection path: who sees provider notices, how they are matched to affected workflows, and how a notice creates a review item. A notice that lands in an unmonitored mailbox is not an operational control. Keep an inventory mapping each workflow to the endpoint, model alias, account, and owner. This is particularly important when different teams have embedded the same model behind separate automation vendors or SaaS connectors.

If you cannot determine whether a silent alias movement occurred, do not claim that it did or did not. Compare a retained baseline packet, note the observable differences, and investigate whether configuration changes explain them. Output differences are clues, not definitive attribution: sampling variance, retrieval changes, prompt edits, and upstream data can also affect results. The safe claim is limited to the observed workflow outcomes under the recorded conditions.

4. Request contract and invalid input

Use a contract test for required fields, optional fields, defaults, length limits, structured output modes, and tool declarations. Include one valid minimal request and at least one deliberately invalid request. A safe API contract rejects invalid input clearly or follows an explicitly documented fallback. Silent coercion can remove a refusal instruction, discard a tool restriction, or alter a required output format without causing an obvious transport error.

Validate error handling as well as success. An API can return a structured error that your application accidentally parses as a normal answer. The caller should distinguish transport failure, rate limiting, invalid request, refusal, and content. Test the exact client library and parser used in production, because an SDK upgrade can change behavior even when the provider endpoint does not.

Use schema validation at your boundary. Require fields that downstream logic depends on, reject unexpected types, and define what happens when fields are added or omitted. If your parser ignores unknown fields, decide whether that is intentional. For customer or financial workflows, fail closed when a required field is missing. Preserve a trace ID and status classification for debugging while applying data minimization to logs.

5. Response shape, absence, refusal, and malformed output

Create fixtures for a normal answer, no content, truncated content, unexpected type, refusal, and malformed structured output. The application should treat “no answer” as a distinct state, not fill in a plausible completion. If the provider emits multiple content blocks, verify which block is authoritative and whether the parser preserves refusal or tool-call metadata. A response can be syntactically valid while semantically unusable.

Test the entire path from response to final user-visible result. Confirm that a refusal is not stripped by post-processing and that a downstream template does not convert it into an instruction to proceed. When a structured response fails validation, route to a safe state such as a human review queue, a clarified request, or a documented non-AI path. Do not recursively ask the model to repair its own invalid output without limits and independent validation.

Capture representative redacted examples for the decision packet. Avoid collecting more prompts and outputs than needed. The evidence should show what condition was tested and whether the application handled it correctly, without exposing real customer content in a broad dashboard. If the test itself has to include sensitive context, obtain approval for its storage and access before running.

6. Core task quality and rubric

Define the task before scoring. For an invoice summary, for example, specify which fields must be preserved, which claims need citations to source lines, what uncertainty must be expressed, and what must never be inferred. For a support draft, define tone only after factual completeness and policy boundaries. A vague rubric such as “good answer” invites reviewers to reward fluency and overlook omissions.

Keep each case paired with observable criteria. A reviewer should be able to mark a required element present or absent and cite the relevant output passage. If the task is subjective, use a short anchored scale and document what each score means. Do not claim measured reliability from one reviewer or a small synthetic fixture. Have a second reviewer inspect disagreements when the consequence warrants it, then keep the adjudication rationale.

Compare absolute minimums and baseline deltas separately. A candidate may be slightly worse than the baseline but still satisfy the task standard; another may score higher on average yet fail one critical field. State both rules before seeing results. Avoid tuning thresholds after observing a failure simply to make a release pass. If you revise the rubric because a criterion was unclear, rerun the candidate and baseline under the corrected rule, and mark the earlier result superseded rather than deleting it.
