7. Boundary and ambiguity handling

Use underspecified, conflicting, and out-of-scope examples. The intended behavior may be to ask one clarifying question, state uncertainty, or route to a person. Score safe abstention as a valid outcome when evidence is insufficient. Do not treat every unanswered request as a quality defect; in consequential workflows, refusing to invent can be the correct result.

Test boundaries at the point where the system hands work to an employee. Does the interface show which facts were supplied and which were inferred? Can the reviewer inspect sources? Is it clear when the model cannot verify a value? A model may answer within its own limits while the surrounding product presents the result with unwarranted confidence. The acceptance object is the user experience and process, not just a raw completion.

Include conflicting context or stale information only if the workflow is expected to encounter it. Specify the source-of-truth rule and verify the application applies it. If there is no agreed rule, record the ambiguity and send it to the process owner rather than asking reviewers to improvise. New model behavior cannot repair a missing business policy.

8. Tool, write, and send boundary

Test action proposals using stubs that cannot affect customers or records. Ask the system to draft a message, propose a record update, or recommend a refund, and verify that only the authorized application layer can execute it. The approval should display the target, recipient, amount, or changed fields, not a generic “Approve AI action” label. Permissions must be enforced server-side, independent of whether the model’s response is persuasive.

Verify least privilege and revocation. A tool that can read should not automatically gain write access after an update. Confirm that removing a user’s permission also blocks an already-running workflow where applicable. Include an ambiguous request that should not create an action, and a valid request that requires human confirmation. If any unapproved external action can occur, it is a hard failure even when every answer-quality score passes.

Use idempotency at the business-operation boundary. If a timeout happens after a write may have completed, the system must check the operation ledger before retrying. The model’s request ID alone may not prevent duplicate business actions. Test replay behavior with a fake receiver and show that a repeated request either returns the prior result or is safely reconciled.

9. Service envelope, timeout, and retry behavior

A short acceptance packet does not establish a service-level distribution. It can verify that your client handles known failure classes: timeout, rate limit, server error, partial response, and retry exhaustion. Define timeout and retry limits before the run. Confirm that a status such as rate-limited is not misinterpreted as a content answer, and that backoff does not exceed the workflow’s user-facing deadline.

For a real latency or availability assessment, define the workload and observation period. Record request mix, concurrency, region, connection behavior, timeouts, retries, and the number of observations. Report percentiles only when the sample supports them and avoid generalizing a small run to future service reliability. This guide contains no provider benchmark and makes no latency claim.

Decide what the business process does when the provider is unavailable. It may queue low-priority work, route a high-priority case to a person, use another approved configuration, or stop. Verify the fallback’s credentials, privacy controls, and behavior; a fallback is another system requiring acceptance. If it has not been exercised, label it untested and do not promise seamless failover.

10. Cost, quota, and accepted-task economics

Capture the usage metadata and applicable pricing for each test when available. Separate model usage from retrieval, tool execution, retries, human review, and correction. Cost per accepted task is a useful decision view, but show its components so that a good average does not hide expensive failures. Include tasks that are rejected or escalated, not just successful completions.

Set a budget ceiling and an action when the ceiling is reached. A provider configuration that produces longer outputs or needs more retries may increase spend while quality appears unchanged. Quotas can also create queueing and delayed service. Record whether the test rate card and account limits match the intended deployment. If a provider changes prices or quotas at the same time as the model, evaluate the two changes independently when possible.

Do not extrapolate a synthetic 14-case packet into a monthly bill without a workload estimate. Use observed traffic or an explicit scenario model, state the assumptions, and include uncertainty. When usage reporting is delayed or incomplete, the estimate remains provisional. A financial approver should accept the actual scenario, not a token number stripped of business context.

11. Privacy, retention, region, and evidence

Verify current account-specific controls for retention, training use, region, logging, and access. Provider-level descriptions are not tenant evidence. Save the policy page version or date, workspace identity, and console or support evidence. Distinguish inference processing region from storage region, support access, and control-plane metadata. A broad residency label does not necessarily describe every component.

Minimize test data. Prefer synthetic cases, remove identifiers, and avoid uploading actual customer conversations unless the test has a documented need and approved handling. Evaluation prompts and outputs are data too; control their access, retention, and deletion. A test packet that is copied into email, ticketing, and analytics systems can create more exposure than the production feature it is meant to assess.

CISA’s Secure by Design initiative places responsibility for product security on manufacturers. Use that as a general reason to ask providers for clear change notices and secure defaults, not as proof of AI quality or legal compliance. If a source cannot show the setting for your tenant, say that the evidence is incomplete. Unknowns should be evaluated according to data sensitivity and impact.

Method and limits

This article proposes a 14-case synthetic fixture, written on 2026-11-05. The sample size is 14 scenarios; there were no live endpoints, production records, or model outputs. The cases were selected to cover identity, lifecycle, interface, behavior, actions, service, economics, and data controls. The fixture is not statistically representative and cannot estimate error rates, provider performance, or safety. Excluded sources include an ISO page that returned 403 with noindex/nofollow and a consulting page inaccessible during direct retrieval. A relevant video result exposed no transcript and was not used for claims. These access gaps limit the source set; they are not evidence those materials are incorrect.

Read results as a release decision, not a leaderboard

Compare by case and by failure mode. A single average is useful only as a summary after the hard gates pass. An update could improve formatting but weaken abstention on ambiguous requests. If the workflow can draft internal notes but must not invent a contractual commitment, those cases are not interchangeable. The acceptance threshold should reflect the cost of each error, not the convenience of one overall score.

Use three result labels. Pass means the evidence meets the prewritten condition. Fail means it violates a hard gate or a locally required task threshold. Unknown means the test could not establish the condition—for example, provider version metadata is missing or an account policy page cannot be accessed. Unknown is not a pass. It may be tolerable for a low-impact capability if explicitly bounded, but should block any claim that depends on missing evidence.

Keep the previous approved configuration as a baseline. A new model can score higher on a small sample and still introduce a schema or action regression. Conversely, a lower score on a subjective style preference may not justify rejection if all business-critical outcomes remain within a pre-agreed tolerance. Distinguish absolute acceptance from relative change: “meets the minimum task standard” differs from “no worse than baseline.” Specify both if both matter.

When a result changes, make the decision reversible where possible. Approve a limited internal pilot, route a fraction of low-risk traffic, preserve a rollback configuration, or keep the new setting behind a feature flag. These are recommendations, not guarantees: rollback may not restore an unavailable retired model, and a provider may change its service independently. Record which old configuration remains accessible and until when. If you cannot roll back, call the decision a migration with a contingency plan, not a reversible deployment.

Research and provider guidance

Google’s production ML deployment testing guidance recommends validating new versions against prior versions and checking pipeline integration, serving, and explicit thresholds. This supports versioned comparison and release gates; it does not prescribe the 14 cases here. See Google’s deployment testing guidance. Forrester’s public quality-playbook discussion argues for continuous evaluation, version-specific evaluation assets, risk-based gates, human review, and monitoring. It is a consulting perspective, not a legal requirement or evidence that a particular provider passes. See Forrester on trustworthy AI quality.

A community discussion about silent regressions describes one practitioner’s use of a small golden set and worry that manual checks are forgotten. Treat it as anecdotal evidence of an operational pain point, not a prevalence estimate. Its lesson is to give the packet an owner and a schedule. See the community discussion.

A small executable gate

This standard-library Python example evaluates a saved JSON result file; it makes no API call. The fixture is synthetic. The threshold is an example policy value, not an industry standard. A hard-gate failure blocks release regardless of mean score.

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

THRESHOLD = 0.90
REQUIRED = {f"C{i:02d}" for i in range(1, 15)}

def decide(filename: str) -> int:
    payload = json.loads(Path(filename).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    rows = payload["results"]
    ids = [row.get("case_id") for row in rows]
    by_id = {row["case_id"]: row for row in rows if row.get("case_id")}
    missing = sorted(REQUIRED - by_id.keys())
    duplicates = sorted({x for x in ids if x and ids.count(x) > 1})
    bad = sorted(k for k, row in by_id.items()
                 if not isinstance(row.get("score"), (int, float))
                 or not 0 <= row["score"] <= 1
                 or not isinstance(row.get("hard_gate_pass"), bool))
    failed = sorted(k for k, row in by_id.items()
                    if row.get("hard_gate_pass") is False)
    scores = [row["score"] for row in by_id.values()
              if isinstance(row.get("score"), (int, float))]
    mean = sum(scores) / len(scores) if scores else 0.0
    reasons = []
    if missing: reasons.append(f"missing: {missing}")
    if duplicates: reasons.append(f"duplicate IDs: {duplicates}")
    if bad: reasons.append(f"invalid records: {bad}")
    if failed: reasons.append(f"hard failures: {failed}")
    if len(rows) != 14: reasons.append("expected exactly 14 rows")
    if mean < THRESHOLD: reasons.append(f"mean below {THRESHOLD:.2f}")
    decision = "BLOCK" if reasons else "REVIEW"
    print(json.dumps({"decision": decision, "mean": round(mean, 3),
                      "reasons": reasons}, indent=2))
    return 1 if reasons else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        raise SystemExit("usage: gate.py results.json")
    raise SystemExit(decide(sys.argv[1]))

The script returns REVIEW, not APPROVE, when machine-checkable conditions pass. A human still needs to inspect fixture relevance, current privacy evidence, unknowns, and release scope. A production harness should validate types carefully because Python booleans are numeric subclasses, and should reject non-finite numeric values. That deliberate limitation illustrates a broader point: an executable gate itself needs review before it controls release.

A result file needs one record for each case C01 through C14. Scores are between zero and one and each hard-gate field is a Boolean. Missing or duplicate cases, unexpected row counts, malformed values, any hard failure, or an average below the local threshold block the packet. Do not let a simple script turn an evaluation into a leaderboard. It is a completeness and stop-condition aid, not an independent assurance.

External actions must remain independent of model prose

An update that produces more persuasive answers can still be unsafe if the surrounding system grants excessive permissions. Keep action authorization outside the model’s prose. The model may suggest a refund, record change, outbound email, or deletion; a deterministic policy layer should decide whether that operation is allowed, whether the caller is authorized, and whether a human must approve it. Version acceptance should test these boundaries because tool calling and structured output can influence execution even when natural-language quality appears unchanged.

Use a non-effecting test double for writes. Verify that a proposed action contains a valid target, permitted scope, current authorization, and idempotency key before the application executes it. If any required element is missing, fail closed. Log a correlation ID and enough version context to reconstruct the configuration, but do not log more personal data than needed. The model response must not widen its permissions or alter the review threshold.

For irreversible or externally visible operations, require a human approval that presents the proposed action and evidence. Show the recipient, amount, record, or message that will be affected, not a generic “Approve AI action” label. A model change can alter proposed action semantics without changing the API schema, so the action-boundary fixture needs meaning-level cases as well as parser tests.

If the workflow is advisory only, state that in the test contract and verify there is no execution path from output to action. If a team later adds a connector, that creates a new system boundary and triggers review. The earlier approval does not automatically cover new tools, users, data classes, or write permissions.

Service, retries, and cost

A short acceptance packet does not establish a latency distribution. It can verify that the client handles timeout, rate limit, server error, partial response, and retry exhaustion. Define timeout and retry limits before the run. Confirm that a rate-limit status is not parsed as content and that backoff stays within the user-facing deadline.

Test timeouts with a mock or controlled environment. A retry may be safe for a read-only generation request but dangerous when a downstream operation may already have completed. Design idempotency around the business action, not just the provider request. If the outcome is uncertain, reconcile before retrying. Unbounded retries can multiply cost, latency, and duplicate actions while making an outage appear to be slow performance.

For a real latency or availability assessment, define workload, period, request mix, concurrency, region, timeout, retries, and number of observations. Report percentiles only when the sample supports them. This article contains no provider benchmark and makes no latency claim.

Cost per accepted task can be more useful than cost per token. Include rejected outputs, retries, human review, retrieval, tool calls, and correction time, but show those components separately. If usage metadata is missing or prices changed during the test, mark the estimate incomplete. Do not extrapolate a synthetic packet into a monthly bill without an explicit workload model.

Privacy, retention, and regional claims

A model update can coincide with a service setting change, but do not assume it did. Ask which account setting or contract applies. Capture policy version, retention, training-use setting where relevant, logging, region, support access, and date checked. “Data stored in region X,” “inference processed in region X,” and “all metadata remains in region X” are different claims. Request component-level evidence where the broad label is insufficient.

Do not use a model page as proof of tenant configuration. Product-level statements and account-level settings differ. Save a tenant-specific export or console evidence when available, and verify against the contract or support response for high-impact claims. If the provider cannot confirm whether the update altered a control, mark the point unknown and assess whether that uncertainty is acceptable.

Minimization remains valuable even when contractual controls are strong. Remove identifiers and irrelevant context before evaluation. Use synthetic records for boundary fixtures when possible. Keep test artifacts access-controlled with a defined retention period. A regression suite can itself become a data store, so include it in the data inventory and deletion process.

Regional claims need precision. Storage, inference, support access, and control-plane metadata may be governed separately. Ask which components are covered and what exceptions apply. This article makes no claim about any provider’s residency or legal status.

Decision record and rollout

The decision packet should fit in one reviewable record: change notice and date; affected service; requested and observed version labels; schema diff; test packet version; baseline identity; per-case outcomes; hard failures; unknowns; data-control evidence; service and cost observations; contingency; approver; scope; and review date. Link to evidence with access controls. Never paste secrets into the record.

Use four decisions: approve, approve with bounds, hold, or reject. Approve only the tested scope. Bounded approval may allow internal drafting but not customer commitments. Hold when a required fact is unknown or evidence incomplete. Reject when a hard gate fails and cannot be safely contained. This vocabulary prevents a score from disguising a decision.

A bounded approval states workflow, users, data class, action permissions, monitoring owner, end date, and revocation conditions. Keep the prior configuration if it remains available, but verify that the fallback really works. Rollback may not restore a retired service; if unavailable, call the action a migration with a contingency plan rather than a reversible deployment.

During rollout, monitor signals tied to the criteria: parser failures, refusals, human overrides, incorrect action proposals, latency, usage, and incidents. Keep monitoring privacy-aware and assign an owner. Monitoring detects problems; it does not replace pre-release evidence. Schedule rechecks around provider notices, incidents, contract changes, or exposure-based intervals rather than choosing a calendar cadence without rationale.

Failure modes

Happy-path-only testing. A polished answer hides refusal regression, malformed JSON, or weak boundary behavior. Keep negative cases.

Configuration drift. Prompt, retrieval, parser, or tools changed alongside the model. The comparison no longer isolates a variable. Freeze and record dependencies or label the whole system change.

Averaging away safety failures. Most cases pass but one disallowed action is proposed. Hard gates override averages.

Missing metadata treated as stability. “Not reported” means unknown, not unchanged. Bound the workflow or seek evidence.

Retry duplication. A timeout follows a possibly committed action. Reconcile state and use business-level idempotency before replay.

Stale privacy evidence. An old screenshot does not prove current tenant settings. Record workspace, date, policy version, and owner.

Theoretical rollback. The old configuration may be retired or inaccessible. Test it or document an unverified contingency.

Benchmark mistaken for acceptance. Public scores may not match your task, data, or actions. Use them as context, then test the workflow.

No accountable owner. A dashboard is green but nobody watches notices. Name notice monitor, test runner, and decision approver.

Test reaches production. A synthetic fixture accidentally writes a real record. Stub actions, isolate credentials, and verify the environment cannot send or write.

SME operating model

A small company does not need a large governance department to run this gate. It does need named responsibilities. One person owns notice monitoring and the change register. A technical owner captures configuration and runs integration tests. A process owner supplies task cases and defines acceptable outcomes. A privacy or security contact checks relevant controls. A business approver decides whether residual uncertainty is acceptable. One person may hold several roles, but the record should show which responsibility they exercised.

Keep the process proportional. An internal brainstorming helper with no sensitive input and no connectors may need a light review. Customer communications, employment, financial operations, health-related workflows, or systems that write to records need a higher evidence bar. Classify by consequence of failure, not by product label.

Maintain a vendor-change register with provider, service, affected workflow, notice date, retirement date, configuration, owner, status, and decision link. A shared table is sufficient if history and ownership are reliable. Do not make it a second store for credentials or personal data.

If notice is short, prioritize workflows by consequence and dependency. Pause or degrade the highest-risk workflow first; do not rush every use case through one smoke test. Ask whether replacement is equivalent for contract, region, data controls, and tool behavior. A replacement name alone does not prove equivalence.

Checklist before closing

  • [ ] Notice or observed change archived with date and source.
  • [ ] Workflow, users, data classes, and action permissions listed.
  • [ ] Identifier, endpoint, account, region, prompt, tools, corpus, and parser recorded.
  • [ ] Baseline and candidate configurations distinguishable.
  • [ ] Retirement, replacement, and shutdown dates checked in primary docs.
  • [ ] Fixture versioned, redacted, and fit for the workflow.
  • [ ] Schema, refusal, boundary, action, retry, cost, service, and data checks have results.
  • [ ] Every case is Pass, Fail, or Unknown; unknowns are visible.
  • [ ] Hard failures are not averaged away.
  • [ ] Scope, owner, monitor, expiry, and revocation conditions recorded.
  • [ ] Rollback tested or labeled unverified.
  • [ ] Human approver chose approve, bounded approval, hold, or reject.

Bottom line

A provider-managed AI update is a change-control event, not a reason to panic and not a reason to assume continuity. Separate lifecycle, alias, interface, behavior, service, cost, privacy, and action surfaces. Keep a fixed, versioned packet; compare the current approved configuration with the candidate under controlled conditions; let hard safety and data gates override averages; and record unknowns explicitly. Then make a scoped human decision that can be reviewed later.

The 14 checks are a reusable starting fixture, not an industry standard, certification, or proof of provider performance. The sample size is exactly 14 synthetic scenarios selected to illustrate distinct failure surfaces. No live model, endpoint, customer data, or production workflow was tested. The code threshold is an example policy. Excluded sources and inaccessible video material were not used to support claims. Adapt the cases and thresholds to your workflow, preserve independent evidence near each claim, and do not claim universal safety from a small test.

  • CISA, Secure by Design — general manufacturer-responsibility framing, not model-quality evidence.
  • OpenAI community, Catching silent quality regressions — one anecdotal discussion, not prevalence data.

title: We Gave a Local LLM Live Web Access. Here’s How
description:
This article was originally published on the Zenrows blog.

We gave a local LLM live web access, and this post shows how. You'll connect a qwen3 model in Ollama to Zenrows MCP, first with no code through the ollmcp bridge and then with a short Python agent that is its own MCP client. You'll need Ollama, a tool-capable model, Node.js, and Python 3.11 or later. A Zenrows API key is optional.

Ollama publishes web_search and web_fetch as hosted APIs that you call with an Ollama API key, and it has no MCP client of its own. In our test runs, the local qwen3 agent read a Cloudflare-fronted Indeed search and cleared an anti-bot challenge page through Zenrows MCP. A plain requests.get() to the same challenge page returned a 403. The code is on GitHub.

How It Works

You ask a question, Ollama picks a tool, Zenrows makes the requests, and the target site returns the pages. The model never contacts the site. The agent calls the extract tool, Zenrows fetches the page through Fetch with protected access, JavaScript rendering, and proxy rotation in one API call, and the model gets the page as structured JSON fields.

Zenrows MCP has two transports. The remote server runs over Streamable HTTP and authenticates with your API key as a Bearer token. The local server runs as a STDIO subprocess through the @zenrows/mcp npm package with your key in an environment variable. This tutorial uses the local one, since it runs next to Ollama on your machine.

These tools matter for this setup.

  • scrape returns a page as Markdown by default, with HTML, PDF, and screenshot output also available.
  • extract returns structured JSON, which matters for local models with small context windows.
  • browser_* tools open a cloud browser session for tasks that span more than one request.
  • crawl_* tools collect the URLs behind one start page.
  • batch_* tools submit a list of URLs as one background job.

1. Install Ollama and a Tool-Capable Model 

brew install ollama
brew services start ollama

 

ollama pull qwen3
ollama show qwen3:latest

Ollama registers the model as qwen3:latest. The ollama show output lists tools under Capabilities, which confirms the model can call the Zenrows tools.

  Model
    architecture        qwen3
    parameters          8.2B
    context length      40960
    embedding length    4096
    quantization        Q4_K_M

  Capabilities
    completion
    tools
    thinking

2. Set Up the Project 

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

 

pip install python-dotenv requests

Without a key, the local server creates a Free account with 5,000 credits a month on its first tool call. To use your own account, create one and save the key in .env.

ZENROWS_API_KEY=your_key_here

3. Install the ollmcp Bridge

ollmcp is an open-source Python bridge that connects MCP servers to a local Ollama model over STDIO, SSE, and Streamable HTTP. It also installs the ollama and mcp packages the agent imports later. This tutorial was tested with ollmcp 0.35.0 on Python 3.14.

pip install ollmcp

4. Configure the Server and Chat With No Code

Create zenrows-mcp.json.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "zenrows": {
      "command": "sh",
      "args": ["-c", "set -a && . ./.env && set +a && exec npx -y @zenrows/mcp"]
    }
  }
}

The sh -c command sources .env into the environment before starting npx, so the JSON holds no secret and can be committed. Add .env to .gitignore, and run ollmcp from this directory because the .env path is relative.

ollmcp --servers-json zenrows-mcp.json --model qwen3:latest

On October 21, 2026, the bridge connected and listed the Zenrows tools (output trimmed).

Found server in config: zenrows
Connecting to server: zenrows
Successfully connected to zenrows with 62 tool(s) and 3 prompt(s) and 1 resource(s)/template(s)
╭──────────────────────────── 🔧 Available Tools ────────────────────────────╮
│ ✓ zenrows.scrape                         ✓ zenrows.extract                 │
│ ✓ zenrows.batch_create                   ✓ zenrows.batch_status            │
...
│ ✓ zenrows.browser_switch_tab             ✓ zenrows.browser_batch           │
╰─────────────────────────── 62/62 tools enabled ────────────────────────────╯
╭───────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Current model: qwen3:latest (ollama)          │
│ Capabilities: 🔧 Tools │ 💭 Thinking (medium) │
╰───────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Every enabled tool's schema goes into the model's context, so type /tools and keep scrape and extract switched on for a small local model. /human-in-the-loop asks you to approve each tool call before it runs.

5. Build the Agent in Python

The script starts the Zenrows MCP server with npx, so it doesn't need ollmcp or zenrows-mcp.json to run. Create agent.py. The pinned versions are in the repo's requirements.txt.

from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()

import asyncio
import json
import os
import ollama
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

SERVER = StdioServerParameters(
    command="npx",
    args=["-y", "@zenrows/mcp"],
    env=dict(os.environ),
)
MODEL = "qwen3:latest"
# give the model enough context to read the whole tool result
OPTIONS = {"num_ctx": 16384}
QUESTION = "Extract the page heading from https://www.scrapingcourse.com/antibot-challenge."
ALLOWED_ARGS = {"url"}

async def main():
    async with stdio_client(SERVER) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()

            listed = await session.list_tools()
            tools = [
                {"type": "function", "function": {
                    "name": t.name,
                    "description": t.description,
                    "parameters": t.input_schema,
                }}
                for t in listed.tools if t.name == "extract"
            ]

            messages = [{"role": "user", "content": QUESTION}]
            reply = ollama.chat(model=MODEL, messages=messages, tools=tools, options=OPTIONS)
            messages.append(reply["message"])

            for call in reply["message"].get("tool_calls") or []:
                args = {k: v for k, v in call.function.arguments.items() if k in ALLOWED_ARGS}
                print("calling", call.function.name, args)
                result = await session.call_tool(call.function.name, args)
                text = result.content[0].text
                print("result:", text[:300])
                # pass the model only the parsed fields from the response
                data = json.loads(text).get("data")
                messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": json.dumps(data)})

            print(ollama.chat(model=MODEL, messages=messages, tools=tools, options=OPTIONS)["message"]["content"])

asyncio.run(main())

Three details matter on a local model.

  • OPTIONS sets the context window. Ollama uses 4,096 tokens by default, and the Indeed prompt later came to about 6,900 tokens. Without num_ctx, Ollama truncated that prompt and the model answered from part of the listings.
  • ALLOWED_ARGS filters the model's arguments and blocks anything the model invents, so only the URL reaches the server. Zenrows then turns on JavaScript rendering and premium proxies only when the page needs them.
  • The extract response wraps the parsed fields in a data object next to a few status flags. The script hands the model only that data object, which keeps the tool message small.

The test target is the Scrapingcourse antibot challenge page, which reports its own verdict.

python3 agent.py

 

Using existing API key from env (secrets dir: /Users/user/.zenrows)
Zenrows MCP server running on stdio (secrets dir: /Users/user/.zenrows)
calling extract {'url': 'https://www.scrapingcourse.com/antibot-challenge'}
result: {"ok":true,"mode":"auto","empty":false,"data":{"challenge_result":{"message":"You bypassed the Antibot challenge! :D","status":"bypassed"},"page":{"challenge_type":"antibot","title":"Antibot Challenge"}}}
The page heading (h1) from the URL is:

**Antibot Challenge**

This is the title extracted from the webpage, which also happens to be the name of the antibot challenge page.

For comparison, without_zenrows.py sends a plain request to the same page.

import requests

r = requests.get("https://www.scrapingcourse.com/antibot-challenge")
print(r.status_code, len(r.text))

 

python3 without_zenrows.py

 

403 5517

The request was blocked with a 403.

6. Read a Live Cloudflare-Protected Site

Confirm what sits in front of Indeed.

curl -sI https://www.indeed.com | grep -iE "^(server|date):"

 

date: Wed, 21 Oct 2026 08:15:02 GMT
server: cloudflare

Create cloudflare_site.py with the same code as agent.py and change the QUESTION line.

QUESTION = "List the company names and job titles from https://www.indeed.com/jobs?q=data+analyst&l=Austin%2C+TX."

 

python3 cloudflare_site.py

 

Using existing API key from env (secrets dir: /Users/user/.zenrows)
Zenrows MCP server running on stdio (secrets dir: /Users/user/.zenrows)
calling extract {'url': 'https://www.indeed.com/jobs?q=data+analyst&l=Austin%2C+TX'}

Here are the company names and job titles from the Indeed search results in Austin, TX:

2. **Visa U.S.A. Inc.** - Data & Insights Analyst  
3. **Texas Department of Transportation** - Data Analyst IV

Let me know if you'd like additional details like locations or salary information!

The extraction returned ok: true with 16 job listings and no challenge response, and the model listed every company and job title on the page.

Choosing an MCP Server

Here is how three MCP servers compared, as documented on October 21, 2026.

Zenrows MCP Firecrawl MCP Playwright MCP
How it runs Cloud or local Cloud or local On your browser
Auth OAuth sign-in or API key as a Bearer token, or ZENROWS_API_KEY environment variable OAuth sign-in or API key as a Bearer token, or FIRECRAWL_API_KEY environment variable None and runs locally
Protected access One integration combines fast scraping and full browser automation, with anti-bot bypass on every tool Their MCP documentation doesn't mention anti-bot handling or proxy rotation Runs from your own IP with no proxy rotation
Transport Hosted Streamable HTTP, or local STDIO via the command in the Zenrows MCP documentation Hosted Streamable HTTP at mcp.firecrawl.dev, or local via npx -y firecrawl-mcp Local STDIO via npx @playwright/mcp

Wrapping Up

One MCP configuration gave a local Ollama agent access to live pages, including Cloudflare-protected ones, while Zenrows handled access, rendering, and proxies for every request. For a task spanning several pages, ask in plain English and the agent can use the crawl and batch tools.

What's Next

  • Create a free Zenrows account with 5,000 credits every month.
  • Use the same server in Claude, Cursor, and other cloud clients.
  • Run the same requests from scripts and CI jobs with the Zenrows CLI.
  • Let an agent with no account pay per request over x402 or MPP at agents.zenrows.com.

title: ResumeInvited: a preview-to-export checklist for a resume editor
description:
ResumeInvited is my personal project: a free online resume editor with templates, a live preview, and PDF or Word downloads. This write-up was generated by an AI agent acting for the project owner and checked against the live tool.

For a document editor, a useful question is what happens between entering information and opening the finished file. A preview can help you write, while the exported document is what another person will actually receive.

The current workflow

  1. Choose a resume template.
  2. Edit your experience, education, skills, and other sections while checking the live preview.
  3. Adjust the layout, then download a PDF for an application or a Word document for further editing.

You can try the editor at resumeinvited.com.

A small checklist for trying it

These are concrete checks I would appreciate feedback on:

  • Section order: Can you arrange the information so that your relevant experience is easy to find?
  • Long content: Add a long job title, a project link, and several detailed experience bullets. Are the results readable in the preview?
  • Page boundaries: Open the PDF and look at where headings and experience entries land. Does the page balance match what you expected?
  • Editable handoff: Open the Word export in the editor you normally use. Is it convenient to make the changes you need afterward?

Those questions give more useful feedback than a general "looks good," because they point to a particular part of the workflow.

Why offer both PDF and Word?

The formats serve different steps. A PDF is useful when you want to share a finished layout. A Word document is useful when you or someone reviewing your resume needs an editable file. For an actual application, use the format requested by the recipient.

It is also worth opening the exported file before sending it: a live preview and a file opened in another application are different parts of the experience.

What would you improve?

I would like feedback on the clarity of editing controls, the preview, and the usefulness of the two export options. If you try the project, a specific example of where the workflow felt awkward would be helpful.

Disclosure: I am sharing my own project. The feature descriptions above reflect the live product; this write-up was generated by an AI agent acting on the owner's instructions.

title: 把 AI CLI 包成 OpenAI 相容 API：從 stdin、JSON 輸出到逾時處理（附可跑範例）
description:
一句話結論：把 CLI 接上 HTTP，核心是輸入、程序生命週期和輸出格式；路徑叫 /v1/chat/completions，不代表已經支援整份協定。

遇到的問題

終端機裡已經有一個能回答問題的 AI CLI，但想接的程式只會送 HTTP 請求，兩邊講的是不同語言。

最先想到的是收到問題後跑一次 CLI，再把答案回傳。真的開始接才發現，容易出錯的地方全在中間：長 prompt 要怎麼傳？CLI 印出的 JSON 哪一段才是答案？指令卡住時，HTTP 要等多久？

這篇把實際包裝服務用到的做法縮成一個能在本機跑的範例。先用假的 CLI 驗證程序與協定，不需要模型金鑰，也不會消耗模型用量。

有實測的是 Python 包裝流程，沒有在這次測試中呼叫真實模型。 換成真實 CLI 時，登入、旗標與輸出格式仍要另外核對。

先決定相容到哪裡

範例只接受一則文字 user 訊息，回傳一次完整 JSON。model 固定用 cli-demo，只是這個服務的識別名稱。

串流、工具呼叫、圖片、多輪歷史與其他參數，都明確拒絕。這樣呼叫端才不會以為參數已生效，實際卻被悄悄忽略。

OpenAI 的 Chat Completions 文件 定義了請求與回應欄位；這裡只實作其中一小部分，目的是讓需要「送一段文字、拿一段答案」的 HTTP 客戶端能接進來。

手把手步驟

1. 先準備一支假 CLI

把下面存成 demo_cli.py。它從 stdin 讀文字，回一個含 result 的 JSON，讓我們能檢查收到多少字元。

import json
import sys

prompt = sys.stdin.read()
print(json.dumps({"result": f"收到 {len(prompt)} 個字元：{prompt[:20]}"}, ensure_ascii=False))

這個 result 是假 CLI 的格式，跟 HTTP 回應裡的 choices 是兩層不同的東西。包裝服務要負責轉換。

2. 加上 HTTP 包裝

把下面存成同一個資料夾裡的 gateway.py：

import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import time
import uuid
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

COMMAND = json.loads(os.environ.get("CLI_COMMAND_JSON", json.dumps([sys.executable, "demo_cli.py"])))
TIMEOUT = float(os.environ.get("CLI_TIMEOUT", "30"))


class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def reply(self, status, body):
        data = json.dumps(body, ensure_ascii=False).encode()
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)

    def error(self, status, message):
        self.reply(status, {"error": {"message": message, "type": "wrapper_error"}})

    def do_POST(self):
        if self.path != "/v1/chat/completions":
            return self.error(404, "Unknown endpoint")
        try:
            size = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", "0"))
            if not 0 < size <= 1024 * 1024:
                return self.error(413, "Body must be between 1 byte and 1 MiB")
            body = json.loads(self.rfile.read(size))
            if not isinstance(body, dict):
                raise ValueError()
            if set(body) - {"model", "messages", "stream"}:
                return self.error(400, "Only model, messages and stream are supported")
            if body.get("model") != "cli-demo" or body.get("stream", False) is not False:
                return self.error(400, "Use model=cli-demo and stream=false")
            messages = body.get("messages")
            if not isinstance(messages, list) or len(messages) != 1:
                raise ValueError()
            message = messages[0]
            if not isinstance(message, dict) or set(message) != {"role", "content"}:
                raise ValueError()
            if message["role"] != "user" or not isinstance(message["content"], str):
                raise ValueError()
        except (ValueError, UnicodeError):
            return self.error(400, "Expected one user message with string content")
        try:
            process = subprocess.run(
                COMMAND, input=message["content"], capture_output=True,
                text=True, encoding="utf-8", timeout=TIMEOUT, check=True,
            )
            output = json.loads(process.stdout)
            if not isinstance(output, dict) or output.get("is_error"):
                raise ValueError()
            answer = output.get("result")
            if not isinstance(answer, str) or not answer.strip():
                raise ValueError()
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            return self.error(504, "CLI timed out")
        except (OSError, subprocess.CalledProcessError):
            return self.error(502, "CLI failed")
        except (ValueError, UnicodeError):
            return self.error(502, "CLI returned invalid output")
        self.reply(200, {
            "id": "chatcmpl-" + uuid.uuid4().hex,
            "object": "chat.completion", "created": int(time.time()),
            "model": "cli-demo",
            "choices": [{"index": 0, "message": {"role": "assistant", "content": answer},
                         "finish_reason": "stop"}],
        })

    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass


if __name__ == "__main__":
    HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8080), Handler).serve_forever()

流程很直接：檢查請求，將文字送進 CLI 的 stdin，確認程序成功退出，再解析 result，最後包進 choices[0].message.content。

這裡刻意把幾種失敗分開：

狀況 HTTP 回應
請求格式錯誤或要求未支援功能 400
宣告的 request body 超過上限 413
CLI 無法啟動、非零退出，或輸出格式錯誤 502
CLI 執行逾時 504

不把 CLI 的完整 stderr 直接回傳，避免把本機路徑或診斷細節送給呼叫端。實際服務可在受控的伺服器日誌記錄錯誤種類與耗時，不必把 prompt 全文一起記下來。

3. 啟動並送一個請求

在放這兩個檔案的資料夾執行：

python3 gateway.py

再開一個終端機：

curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"cli-demo","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"你好"}],"stream":false}'

回傳的 ID 與時間每次不同，答案應該在這裡：

{
  "choices": [{
    "index": 0,
    "message": {"role": "assistant", "content": "收到 2 個字元：你好"},
    "finish_reason": "stop"
  }]
}

上面是回應節錄。完整回應還有 id、object、created 與 model。沒有模型用量資料，就不捏造 usage。

踩到的坑

長 prompt 不要塞在命令列參數裡

原本的服務曾把很長的上下文塞進 argv，碰到 Argument list too long。命令列有系統限制，不適合拿來搬大量文字。

範例用的是：

subprocess.run(COMMAND, input=message["content"], capture_output=True,
               text=True, encoding="utf-8", timeout=TIMEOUT, check=True)

input 透過 stdin 傳入，命令本身用參數陣列，也沒有開 shell=True。所以文字中的 $() 或反引號會當成普通內容傳給 CLI，不會先被包裝層當 shell 指令執行。這不代表 CLI 本身不能使用工具，兩者要分開看。Python subprocess 文件 有各參數的行為。

這次以 20 萬個 ASCII 字元實測，假 CLI 回報收到完整的 200,000 個字元。它驗證的是傳輸方式，不代表真實模型的 context window 一定裝得下。

stdout 不一定就是答案

有的 CLI 回一整個 JSON，有的回 JSONL，也就是一行一個事件。啟動訊息、工具結果與最後答案，不能全部原封不動塞進 content。

範例只接受 {"result":"文字"}，缺欄位、空答案或 is_error: true 都回 502。換成 JSONL 型 CLI，就要另外寫事件解析器，找出最後的 assistant 訊息，不能只拿最後一行。

例如 Claude Code 非互動模式 提供 -p 與結構化輸出；如果要接它，可將命令改成參數陣列 ['claude', '-p', '--output-format', 'json']，再依所用版本的輸出確認解析器。這是接入示意，本文沒有實測這個真實 CLI 的呼叫，也沒有處理它的登入流程。

HTTP 成功，不代表 CLI 成功

CLI 非零退出時，不能照樣回 200，再把「發生錯誤」當成模型答案。就算退出碼是零，也要檢查應用層錯誤與答案格式。

check=True 負責非零退出，後面的 JSON 驗證負責輸出內容。兩關都過了，才回成功。

逾時也是同樣的道理。模型可能慢，但請求不能無限等下去；呼叫端的等待時間也要比這裡的 CLI timeout 留出一些餘裕。若 CLI 還會產生其他子程序，則要另做整組程序的清理，不能假設直接子程序結束就全部結束。

實測結果與限制

這次在 Python 3.14.4，以本機 HTTP 請求與假 CLI 跑過 17 個情境：

  • 中文回覆、20 萬字元 stdin，以及含 shell 語法的文字都正確傳遞。
  • 壞掉的 JSON、非物件請求、多輪訊息、工具、串流、未知模型與非文字內容都回 400。
  • 超大 Content-Length 在送出 body 前就被拒絕，回 413。
  • CLI 非零退出、無效 JSON、缺少或空白答案、應用層錯誤都回 502。
  • 假 CLI 刻意拖延，回 504。

這份範例只綁 127.0.0.1，使用標準函式庫的簡單 HTTP server，依序處理請求。它沒有驗證身分、請求讀取期限、輸出大小限制或正式的並行管理，適合本機理解流程，不能直接當成公開服務。

每次 HTTP 請求也都是新 CLI 呼叫，不會自動保留前一輪歷史。要支援多輪、工具或串流，必須逐項定義轉換與錯誤行為，不能只把請求欄位加進來就算完成。

為什麼這樣選

當時的需求是讓原本只認 HTTP 的程式能呼叫既有 CLI，所以先加一層薄薄的轉接，保留已經能工作的執行方式。

若你需要的是模型供應商完整的 API 功能，直接使用原生 API 會少掉一層格式轉換。CLI 包裝的價值，是讓既有工具接得上；代價則是 CLI 旗標、輸出格式與程序生命週期，都變成這層服務要維護的事。

  • Python subprocess

title: Last-Mile ETA Drift: Recalculating Delivery Windows When Dwell Time and Failed Stops Break the Route Plan
description:
A delivery route can look perfect when it leaves the depot. The driver has an optimized sequence of stops, estimated arrival times, assigned delivery windows, and a planned return time. Yet by the middle of the route, the schedule may already be inaccurate.

A customer takes longer than expected to unload. A warehouse delays vehicle entry. One delivery fails because nobody is available to receive the shipment. The driver spends another twenty minutes finding an alternative unloading point. Suddenly, the estimated arrival time for the next customer is no longer reliable.

This is last-mile ETA drift: the difference between the arrival time predicted by a logistics system and the arrival time that is becoming realistic as the delivery progresses.

For logistics platforms, the challenge is not simply recalculating the route whenever a vehicle moves. A reliable ETA engine must understand dwell time, failed delivery attempts, stop dependencies, traffic conditions, and the remaining work on the driver's route.

Why Last-Mile ETAs Become Inaccurate

Traditional route planning typically starts with a set of known inputs:

  • Vehicle starting location
  • Destination coordinates
  • Planned stop sequence
  • Estimated travel time
  • Customer delivery windows
  • Vehicle capacity and route constraints

These inputs establish an initial schedule. However, they do not always represent what happens at each stop.

Consider a vehicle with eight scheduled deliveries. The first four stops are completed, but the second customer takes 35 minutes instead of the expected 15. The fifth stop has a restricted receiving window, and the sixth customer is unavailable.

The original ETA calculations may still use the planned service duration for each stop. As a result, the customer-facing arrival estimates gradually become disconnected from actual operating conditions.

Several factors contribute to this problem.

1. Dwell Time Is Different at Every Stop

Dwell time is the period a vehicle spends at a location after arriving. It may include:

  • Security checks and gate entry
  • Dock assignment
  • Unloading and loading
  • Document verification
  • Customer handover
  • Signature collection
  • Waiting for receiving staff

A route planner may use a standard service duration, but actual dwell time varies by location, customer, shipment type, and time of day.

A distribution center may consistently take longer during its morning receiving window. A retail location may have a short unloading process but a long security check.

If the ETA engine treats every stop as having the same service duration, it will repeatedly underestimate downstream arrival times.

2. Failed Stops Create Additional Work

A failed delivery changes more than the status of one stop.

The driver may need to:

  • Record the failure reason
  • Contact the dispatcher
  • Attempt customer communication
  • Find a secure location for the shipment
  • Return the delivery to the depot
  • Reschedule the stop
  • Complete another delivery attempt

A failed stop can also affect vehicle capacity, route priority, and customer commitments.

The ETA engine should therefore treat a failed delivery as an operational event that changes the remaining route, not merely as a status update.

3. Traffic Conditions Change During Execution

Traffic estimates generated before departure may become outdated. Road closures, congestion, weather, and local restrictions can change the time required to reach a destination.

A route engine should distinguish between planned travel time and updated travel time. It should also avoid assuming that every delay can be recovered by changing the route sequence.

4. GPS Data May Arrive Late

A mobile device can lose connectivity, and telematics data may be delayed. If the backend receives location updates after the actual observation time, it may calculate an ETA using an outdated vehicle position.

A reliable system should retain both the location observation timestamp and the server receipt timestamp. This allows the ETA engine to recognize stale data instead of presenting an old location as current.

Build ETA Recalculation Around Actual Route Events

A useful ETA architecture combines planned route information with events generated during execution.

The key events may include:

  • Vehicle departed from the depot
  • Vehicle arrived at a stop
  • Service started
  • Service completed
  • Delivery failed
  • Driver reported an exception
  • Vehicle departed from the stop
  • Route was reassigned or reordered

Each event should be associated with a vehicle, trip, stop, timestamp, and source.

The backend can then maintain the actual status of the route and recalculate the remaining schedule whenever a meaningful event changes the expected workload.

Separate Travel Time From Service Time

One of the most important design decisions is to calculate travel time and dwell time separately.

A simplified model is:

ETA(n) = T(current) + sum of [Travel(i) + Service(i)] for every stop i from the current stop up to stop n-1

Where:

  • T(current) is the current time or latest reliable calculation point.
  • Travel(i) is the estimated travel time to the next stop.
  • Service(i) is the expected dwell or service duration at that stop.

The model becomes more useful when actual dwell time replaces the planned duration for completed stops and updated estimates are applied to the remaining stops.

For example, if a vehicle arrives at a warehouse at 10:00 a.m. and leaves at 10:42 a.m., the system should use the actual 42-minute dwell time when calculating the next delivery's ETA.

It should not continue using the original 15-minute assumption.

Use Historical Dwell Time Carefully

Historical dwell-time data can improve estimates, but it needs context.

A simple average across all stops may hide important differences. A large warehouse, a residential delivery, and a retail receiving dock do not have comparable service patterns.

A better model can segment historical data by:

  • Customer or delivery location
  • Stop type
  • Shipment category
  • Vehicle type
  • Time of day
  • Day of week
  • Delivery service requirements

The system should also account for unusual observations. One exceptionally long unloading event should not automatically become the expected dwell time for every future visit.

Median dwell time, percentile-based estimates, or carefully maintained historical ranges may be more useful than an unfiltered average.

For example, a dispatcher may need to see both a likely arrival time and a realistic arrival window when the destination has variable unloading delays.

Handle Failed Deliveries as Explicit Route Changes

A failed stop should trigger a defined workflow.

First, the driver records the failure reason. The backend validates the event and updates the stop status. The route engine then determines which future stops are affected.

Depending on the operational rules, the system may:

  1. Keep the failed stop in the route for a later retry.
  2. Move the failed stop to the end of the route.
  3. Schedule a return to the depot.
  4. Assign the delivery to another vehicle.
  5. Request dispatcher approval before changing the route.

Not every failed delivery should be automatically rescheduled. A refrigerated shipment, a high-value parcel, and a time-sensitive medical delivery may require different handling.

The ETA engine must also avoid counting a failed stop as completed service if the driver has not actually finished the required work.

Recalculate Without Creating Notification Noise

Frequent ETA changes can frustrate customers and dispatchers. If the system sends a new arrival notification after every small GPS movement, recipients may stop paying attention.

A better notification policy considers:

  • Whether the ETA change is operationally meaningful
  • Whether the customer has already received an update
  • Whether the delivery window is at risk
  • Whether the new estimate is based on reliable data
  • Whether a dispatcher needs to approve the change

For example, a two-minute adjustment may not require a customer notification. A 30-minute delay that threatens a booked receiving window probably does.

Use notification thresholds and event-based rules, while retaining the full ETA history for operational review.

An Example of ETA Drift in a Delivery Route

Imagine a vehicle leaves the depot at 8:00 a.m. with six scheduled deliveries.

Stop Planned arrival Actual event
1 8:30 a.m. Completed at 8:42 a.m.
2 9:10 a.m. Completed at 9:48 a.m.
3 10:15 a.m. Customer unavailable
4 10:50 a.m. Still pending
5 11:30 a.m. Still pending
6 12:15 p.m. Still pending

The vehicle has already lost time at the second stop and has encountered a failed delivery at the third.

A basic system may continue displaying the original arrival estimates. A more capable system updates the remaining route using actual departure time, current vehicle location, traffic, and the failed-stop policy.

The dispatcher can then decide whether to keep the original sequence, move the failed delivery, or reassign a time-sensitive stop.

The important outcome is not simply a more accurate number. It is a schedule that reflects the actual operational situation.

What Logistics Software Development Services Should Include

An ETA engine is only one component of a dependable delivery platform. Logistics software development services should also address the systems that supply and consume route information.

A complete implementation may require:

  • GPS and telematics integrations
  • Route planning and optimization
  • Driver mobile applications
  • Stop-level event tracking
  • Dwell-time analytics
  • Failed delivery workflows
  • Customer notifications
  • Dispatcher dashboards
  • Delivery proof and document capture
  • Exception management
  • Historical route reporting

The architecture should also support idempotent event processing. If a driver's device retries a delivery-completion event after a network timeout, the backend should not mark the same stop as completed twice.

Recommended Logistics Software Development Companies

Dev Technosys develops custom logistics and mobile applications that can connect route planning, driver workflows, tracking data, delivery status, and operational dashboards. A project involving ETA drift should define stop-level event handling, dwell-time rules, failed-delivery workflows, and notification thresholds as part of the backend scope.

IBM offers enterprise technology and data capabilities that may be relevant when logistics operations need to connect route information with broader enterprise systems and analytics platforms.

Accenture can be considered for larger logistics transformation initiatives involving process redesign, enterprise integration, and application modernization.

When selecting a development partner, ask how its proposed architecture will handle delayed GPS updates, repeated events, failed deliveries, and customer-facing ETA changes.

Final Thoughts

Last-mile ETA drift is not just a routing problem. It is the result of differences between planned operations and actual events.

A dependable logistics platform must understand when a vehicle arrives, how long it stays, whether a delivery succeeds, and what that means for every remaining stop.

By combining real-time event processing, contextual dwell-time estimates, explicit failed-stop workflows, and controlled notifications, logistics teams can provide more useful arrival estimates and make better decisions when the original route plan no longer reflects reality.

title: How Kubernetes and Docker Support Cloud Data Engineering
description:
Cloud data engineering is not just about moving data from one system to another. It also involves building reliable environments where data applications can be deployed, managed, and scaled as business needs change.

As data workloads become more complex, teams need infrastructure that supports consistent deployments, efficient resource usage, and dependable processing.

Docker and Kubernetes help address these challenges. Docker packages applications into portable containers, while Kubernetes manages and orchestrates those containers across infrastructure.

Let’s explore how they work together in cloud data engineering.

Why Containerisation Matters for Data Engineering

Data engineering applications often depend on specific libraries, runtime versions, and configuration settings. When these dependencies differ between development, testing, and production, deployment issues can occur.

Docker helps reduce these inconsistencies by packaging an application and its dependencies into a container.

For data engineering teams, this can make it easier to:

• Run data processing applications in consistent environments

• Package ETL and data transformation workloads

• Simplify application deployment

• Reduce dependency conflicts

• Improve portability across compatible environments

For example, a Python based data processing application can be packaged into a Docker container and deployed across development and production environments without manually configuring each system.

How Kubernetes Manages Containerised Workloads

Running a few containers is relatively straightforward. Managing hundreds of containers across a cloud environment requires orchestration.

Kubernetes provides tools to deploy, manage, and scale containerised applications.

Its capabilities include:

Workload scheduling: Kubernetes places containers on available infrastructure based on resource requirements.

Scaling: Applications can scale according to configured policies and workload demand.

Self healing: Kubernetes can restart failed containers and maintain the desired application state.

Resource management: Teams can define CPU and memory requirements to help manage infrastructure usage.

These capabilities are useful when data processing workloads vary in size or need to run reliably across distributed environments.

Docker and Kubernetes in a Cloud Data Pipeline

A cloud data pipeline may include data ingestion, transformation, validation, storage, and delivery.

Docker can package the applications responsible for individual pipeline tasks. Kubernetes can then manage the deployment and execution of those containerised applications.

A simplified workflow might look like this:

  1. Data is collected from databases, APIs, or files.
  2. Docker packages the ingestion and transformation applications.
  3. Kubernetes manages the containerised workloads.
  4. Processed data is delivered to a data warehouse or analytics platform.
  5. Monitoring tools help teams observe application performance and failures.

This approach can support consistent deployments and make it easier to manage data processing workloads as they grow.

Practical Benefits for Cloud Data Engineering Teams

Docker and Kubernetes can support several important areas of modern data engineering.

More Consistent Deployments

Containers help maintain consistent application environments, reducing deployment differences between development, testing, and production.

Flexible Scaling

Kubernetes can scale containerised workloads based on configured requirements, helping teams respond to changing processing demands.

Improved Reliability

Kubernetes can restart failed containers and maintain the desired state of applications, supporting more dependable workloads.

Better Support for DataOps

Containerisation and orchestration can support automation across development and operations workflows, helping teams improve deployment consistency and collaboration.

What Teams Should Consider Before Adopting Them

Docker and Kubernetes are useful technologies, but they are not automatically the right choice for every data workload.

Teams should consider:

• Infrastructure and cloud costs

• Security and access controls

• Storage and networking requirements

• Monitoring and logging

• Operational complexity

• Team experience with container orchestration

Kubernetes can introduce additional management overhead. A clear architecture and suitable operational practices are important to make sure the benefits outweigh the complexity.

Final Thoughts

Docker and Kubernetes provide complementary capabilities for modern cloud data engineering. Docker helps package data applications into portable containers, while Kubernetes manages their deployment, scaling, and operation.

Together, they can help teams build more flexible and reliable cloud data platforms that support evolving data workloads.

For a deeper look at their roles, benefits, and practical applications, read the complete guide from InteliData:

👉 How Kubernetes and Docker Support Cloud Data Engineering

You can also explore InteliData’s Data Engineering Services to learn more about building reliable data infrastructure.

title: When Your Data Breaks on AWS (HA & DR Part 1): Aurora Backtrack, Idempotency, and the Delta Problem
description:
It is 2:47 PM. You run a quick Node.js script to update the price of one product in a supermarket inventory database. The script finishes. Then your stomach drops.

You forgot the WHERE clause.

Every single product in the database now has the same price.

Most of us have either done this or watched a teammate do it. The real question is not whether something will go wrong, but what you do in the next five minutes. Amazon's CTO Werner Vogels put it simply: "Everything fails, all the time."

While preparing a community session on AWS resilience, I kept running into questions that the usual "enable backups and you're fine" advice never answers. This article is my attempt to answer them clearly, in two parts:

  • Part 1 (this article): how you undo a bad write, how you stop the same request from being processed twice, and what happens to the data written while you are recovering.
  • Part 2: RTO and RPO in depth, DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery, whether you should automate restores, and the four AWS disaster recovery strategies.

First, Two Words You Need: HA and DR

These two get mixed up all the time, so let's separate them before going further.

High Availability (HA) keeps a failure from becoming an outage. A server dies, an Availability Zone goes dark, and your users never notice because traffic is already flowing somewhere healthy.

Disaster Recovery (DR) is the plan for when the outage, or the data loss, happens anyway. A whole Region has problems, or someone deletes a production table.

Here is the part that surprised me: HA does not protect you from bad data. If your database has a standby copy in another Availability Zone and you run a broken UPDATE, that broken update is faithfully copied to the standby within milliseconds. Replication copies mistakes too. That is a DR problem, and it is exactly what this article is about.

Part A: Two Ways to Undo a Bad Write in Aurora

Go back to our supermarket disaster. If your database is Amazon Aurora, you have two main options.

Option 1: Point-in-Time Restore (the traditional way)

You tell AWS: "Give me the database exactly as it was at 2:46:59 PM."

AWS does this by provisioning a brand-new cluster and restoring your data into it. When it is ready, you update your backend's connection string (environment variables, secrets, config) to point to the new endpoint. Depending on the size of the database, the whole process can take anywhere from 30 minutes to several hours.

Option 2: Aurora Backtrack (the "undo" button)

Backtrack skips all of that. Instead of building a new database, it rewinds your existing cluster in place to a specific second in the past, up to 72 hours back. It works by reversing changes directly at the storage level.

Because it is the same cluster, the endpoint never changes. No new connection strings, no redeploys. The trade-off is that the database pauses briefly and drops all active connections while it rewinds.

Back to our story: instead of waiting hours for a new cluster, you backtrack to two minutes before the script ran. Within minutes the prices are back to normal, and your app reconnects to the same endpoint as if nothing happened.

A few things worth knowing before you rely on it:

  • Backtrack is available for Aurora MySQL-compatible clusters, not Aurora PostgreSQL.
  • You have to turn it on by setting a backtrack window (up to 72 hours) when you create the cluster or restore it. You cannot switch it on after the incident.
  • It adds a small cost, because Aurora has to keep the change records for that window.

The question that bothered me

Here is where I got stuck. If your application cannot tolerate any downtime, Backtrack looks like the wrong choice, because it pauses the database. But a Point-in-Time Restore takes far longer overall. So which one actually causes less disruption?

The answer is that the two options are protecting different things: availability versus data accuracy.

Point-in-Time Restore Aurora Backtrack
Original database during recovery Stays online and keeps accepting connections Pauses and drops active connections
What users see during recovery A working app serving corrupted data A short interruption, then correct data
Endpoint change needed Yes No
Typical time to clean data 30 minutes to several hours Minutes

With a snapshot restore, your app is technically "up" the whole time, but it is up and wrong. Customers are seeing the broken prices until you finally swap the endpoint.

With Backtrack, the app is briefly down, then it is right.

So when is Backtrack the wrong choice? Only when you have a strict rule that the database must never drop active connections. Think of a real-time healthcare data pipeline streaming patient vitals. In those rare cases, teams keep the corrupted database online and fix the data another way. For the vast majority of applications, Backtrack is the faster and smarter option.

Part B: Idempotency, or "Once and Only Once"

The supermarket problem was one bad write. The next problem is subtler: the same good write happening twice.

Why this happens in serverless apps

Picture a customer ordering food on a restaurant app and tapping Pay.

  1. The frontend sends the checkout request.
  2. Your payment Lambda charges the card. The charge succeeds.
  3. A brief network drop means the success response never reaches the phone.
  4. The frontend times out and automatically retries the exact same request.

Without protection, your Lambda charges the customer a second time. Nothing crashed, nothing is "broken", and yet you now have an angry customer and a refund to process.

Idempotency is the fix. An operation is idempotent when receiving the same request many times has the same effect as receiving it once. The first request does the work. Every duplicate simply gets the original response back.

How Powertools for AWS Lambda handles it

Powertools for AWS Lambda has an idempotency utility that uses a fast key-value store, usually DynamoDB, as a receipt ledger.

When a request arrives, Powertools pulls a unique value out of it, called the idempotency key, and checks the ledger:

  • The key is new: Powertools records it in DynamoDB as "in progress", lets your function run, then saves the final response against that key.
  • The key already exists: Powertools recognizes a retry, skips your business logic completely, and returns the saved response.

In the restaurant example, the Order ID is the key. On the retry, Powertools sees the order is already completed and returns 200 OK without ever calling the payment provider again. The customer is charged exactly once.

Here is what that looks like in TypeScript:

import { makeIdempotent, IdempotencyConfig } from '@aws-lambda-powertools/idempotency';
import { DynamoDBPersistenceLayer } from '@aws-lambda-powertools/idempotency/dynamodb';

// The DynamoDB table acting as our receipt ledger
const persistenceStore = new DynamoDBPersistenceLayer({
  tableName: 'IdempotencyTable',
});

// Use the orderId from the request body as the idempotency key
const config = new IdempotencyConfig({
  eventKeyJmesPath: 'powertools_json(body).orderId',
});

const processPayment = async (event: any) => {
  const { orderId, amount } = JSON.parse(event.body);

  // Your real payment logic goes here.
  // On a retry with the same orderId, this code never runs.

  return {
    statusCode: 200,
    body: JSON.stringify({ message: 'Payment successful', orderId }),
  };
};

export const handler = makeIdempotent(processPayment, {
  persistenceStore,
  config,
});

The idempotency table needs a partition key named id (String). It is also a good idea to enable TTL on an expiration attribute so old receipts clean themselves up.

Questions people usually ask next

Is the idempotency key the same thing as the Order ID?

Often, yes. If a natural unique ID already exists, like an orderId, it makes a perfect idempotency key. But some requests do not have one yet. Think of a "Create Account" form: the database has not assigned an ID because the account does not exist. In that case the key is created in one of two ways:

  1. Client-side generation: the frontend generates a random UUID and sends it in a header, for example Idempotency-Key: 123e4567-e89b-.... Every retry reuses the same UUID.
  2. Payload hashing: Powertools runs the request body through a hash function, and the resulting hash becomes the key. Identical payloads produce identical keys.

In short, the key is simply whatever string your backend uses as the lock to decide "have I already done this?"

What makes DynamoDB a "fast key-value store", and why use it here?

A key-value store is a NoSQL database built for one thing: very fast, very simple lookups. There are no joins, foreign keys or complex schemas. You store a key (the idempotency token) and a value (the status and saved response), much like a dictionary. DynamoDB and Redis are the common examples. Reading a single key takes single-digit milliseconds, so checking the ledger on every request barely adds anything to your API response time.

What does "state-changing action" mean?

It is any operation that changes the data, or "state", of your system:

  • State-changing: creating, updating or deleting data (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE). Writing a record, reducing a stock count, processing a payment.
  • Not state-changing: reading data (GET). Listing users does not change the database.

Idempotency exists to protect state-changing actions. If a GET runs twice, the user just sees the same data twice. If a payment POST runs twice, someone gets charged double.

Part C: The Delta Problem (the Hardest Part of Database Recovery)

Now back to the Point-in-Time Restore from Part A, because it hides a problem that many tutorials skip entirely.

What actually happens during a restore

Say the corruption happens at 14:02. You start a restore to 14:01:59. AWS spends the next hour or so building the new cluster. Meanwhile, your original database is still online and still accepting writes. New orders, new patient records and new payments keep arriving, and they are perfectly valid.

At 15:10 the new cluster is ready and you swap the endpoint.

So where are the 68 minutes of valid writes that landed on the old database during the restore?

They are still in the old database. AWS does not move them for you.

The new cluster only contains data up to 14:01:59. Everything written after that, the good along with the bad, stays behind. Database engineers call this gap the Delta Problem or the Cutover Window.

Here are the three ways teams deal with it, from the most common to the most manual.

Strategy 1: Read-Only Freeze and Queue (safest and most common)

The moment you discover the corruption, switch the old database to read-only.

  • Reads (GET) keep working, so users can still view their data.
  • Writes (POST, PUT, DELETE) are rejected by the database.

To avoid losing those writes and showing users errors, your API catches the failed writes and parks the payloads in an Amazon SQS queue. Once the new cluster is live and the endpoint is swapped, a Lambda worker drains the queue and writes every parked request into the new database.

This is also where Part B pays off. If any of those queued messages get delivered twice, idempotent handlers make sure nothing is written twice.

Strategy 2: Change Data Capture with AWS DMS (the advanced AWS way)

If the application absolutely must stay fully read-write and queuing is not an option, teams use AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) as a live bridge between the old database and the new one.

DMS supports Change Data Capture (CDC): it reads the database transaction log (the binlog in MySQL, or the WAL in PostgreSQL) and replays changes on the target. You start CDC from a log position just after the bad transaction, so only the valid inserts and updates made during the restore are streamed into the new cluster. Once the new cluster has caught up to the present, you swap the endpoint.

It is powerful, but it needs careful setup and validation. Writes that touched the same rows as the corrupting statement may still need a human to review them.

Strategy 3: Custom Reconciliation Script (the manual way)

If the disaster hits and you have neither a queue nor DMS in place, you rescue the data by hand.

  1. Swap the endpoint so the app uses the new cluster.
  2. Keep the old database online, but isolated from the app.
  3. Write a script (for example in Node.js with Prisma) that connects to both databases.
  4. Query the old database for rows where createdAt or updatedAt falls between the corruption time and the cutover time.
  5. Copy those missing rows into the new database.

It works, but stitching data together by hand while a live system is running is stressful and easy to get wrong.

Comparing the three

Strategy Effort to set up User impact during recovery Risk of missing data
Read-only freeze + SQS Medium, built ahead of time Reads work, writes are delayed Low
DMS Change Data Capture High Fully read-write Low, if configured carefully
Reconciliation script Low upfront, high during the incident Fully read-write Medium to high

And this is the real reason Aurora Backtrack is so attractive. Because it rewinds the same database in place, there is no second database and no cutover window to reconcile. The brief pause it causes is often a small price compared to stitching data together under pressure.

Key Takeaways

  1. High Availability does not protect you from bad data. Replication copies mistakes too.
  2. Point-in-Time Restore keeps the app online but serving wrong data until you swap endpoints. Backtrack causes a short pause but fixes data in place, on the same endpoint.
  3. Turn Backtrack on before you need it. It only works on Aurora MySQL-compatible clusters with a backtrack window set.
  4. Retries are normal in serverless systems. Make every state-changing action idempotent, especially payments.
  5. A restored database does not include writes made during the restore. Plan for the Delta Problem with a read-only freeze and SQS, DMS CDC, or a reconciliation script.

Coming Up in Part 2

In the next article I will cover:

  • RTO and RPO: what they really mean, who decides them, and what happens when you miss them
  • DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery: the 35-day window, per-second restores, and why it never overwrites your table
  • Should you automate database restores? Why it sounds smart and why it is usually a bad idea
  • The four AWS DR strategies: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and active/active

If you have ever had to recover from a bad write in production, I would love to hear how you handled it. Drop it in the comments.
