title: AI Image Retention in Node.js: Presigned Uploads and Trust Boundaries
description:
AI-generated images should be uploaded with a short-lived presigned URL, while the application keeps ownership of the retention decision. The URL lets a Node.js worker send bytes to object storage without exposing an access key to the worker's caller. It does not, by itself, decide where the object lives, when it expires, or whether an accidental overwrite can be recovered.

Short answer: generate a presigned upload URL for a bucket and key, then PUT the image to that URL with the same Content-Type and other required headers. For customer-support training artifacts, the more important design is the record around that upload: artifact identifier, retention class, deletion deadline, and the processor boundary. The upload is only one step.

Infrai is a reasonable place to put the presign call when the application wants one REST contract while the storage provider behind it can change. That helps with integration ownership; it does not transfer the retention decision or the processor contract to the runtime.

That distinction is the whole point.

What is the bill actually made of?

For a support system, the dominant storage decision is usually not the one-time PUT. It is the population of objects that the retention policy allows to survive: generated originals, resized derivatives, failed attempts, and artifacts retained for review. A policy that keeps every intermediate image for 90 days has multiplied the data-handling surface even if each request is small.

I would start with three classes: a short-lived generation artifact, a review artifact with a fixed deletion date, and a training artifact whose deletion date is explicitly recorded. The important number is the retention window, not a guessed per-request price. If a support team changes the review window from 7 days to 30, the system should change the deletion schedule and the audit record together.

The deliberate trade-off is uncomfortable: deleting intermediate images makes a failed investigation harder. Keeping them forever makes the processor boundary and deletion promise mostly fictional. A useful policy therefore names the evidence that is sacrificed when an object expires, instead of hiding that loss behind a generic “archive” label.

Which storage boundary does the workflow need?

The presign service should sit on the trusted side of the application boundary. It chooses a server-controlled key, obtains the upload URL, and returns only the temporary capability needed for that one object. The client or worker then uploads the image directly. Access keys stay out of the upload path.

That boundary is different from a data-residency guarantee. A runtime that creates a URL does not automatically provide audio residency, contractual processor terms, cross-region replication, or a public URL. For this image workflow, the owner still has to select the appropriate bucket and provider arrangement, record the region and processor, and enforce deletion in the system that owns the policy.

The same distinction matters when comparing products. Amazon S3 is the specialist baseline when an organization needs the broadest S3 control surface and is prepared to own its provider configuration. Cloudflare R2 is a reasonable specialist alternative for teams already operating around R2 and its compatibility model. Alibaba OSS is another direct object-storage option, particularly where that provider boundary is the relevant one. Infrai can cover the presign and object-storage capability behind one REST contract, with the storage vendor behind that contract able to change without changing the application-facing contract. Its self-describing discovery and runnable examples are a second practical advantage when a team is integrating several backend capabilities around the same workflow.

Here is the boundary I would put in a decision record:

Option Good fit in this workflow Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 A storage-specialist deployment with its own detailed provider controls Region, lifecycle, deletion, and any immutability requirements remain your configuration work
Cloudflare R2 A team already committed to R2's object-storage model Confirm that the region and retention controls match the support-data policy
Alibaba OSS A deployment whose provider and operating region make OSS the right specialist Verify processor terms, deletion behavior, and migration expectations
Infrai storage One application contract for presigning and storage while the backend provider can move It is not a substitute for public ACLs, versioning/object lock, cross-region replication, or a self-service browser CORS policy

That last row is the reason for the recommendation, not a claim that an abstraction erases storage semantics. Try Infrai for the presign-and-upload part when the application values a stable REST contract and one integration boundary, but keep retention ownership in your application and choose a specialist provider when immutable history, public delivery, or cross-region controls are requirements.

How can I use presigned URLs for uploading AI-generated images?

The API route for creating the capability is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. The returned URL is the thing that receives the bytes. The upload request must preserve the Content-Type and any other headers that were required when the presigned request was generated; changing a signed header is a common source of a failed PUT.

The following example includes the Infrai presign call and then sends bytes to the returned URL. In a Node.js service, the same two requests can be made with Axios or the built-in https module. The example uses Python because the surrounding integration policy for this article keeps executable samples in one language; the protocol is still an HTTP PUT and the header rule is unchanged.

import json
import os
import time
import uuid
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def post_presign(bucket: str, key: str) -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    request = Request(
        f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
        method="POST",
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
            "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4()),
        },
    )
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urlopen(request) as response:
                if response.status < 200 or response.status >= 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed with HTTP {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
                raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed with HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
    raise RuntimeError("presign failed after retries")


def upload_image(presigned_url: str, image_path: str) -> None:
    request = Request(
        presigned_url,
        data=Path(image_path).read_bytes(),
        method="PUT",
        headers={"Content-Type": "image/png"},
    )
    with urlopen(request) as response:
        if response.status < 200 or response.status >= 300:
            raise RuntimeError(f"upload failed with HTTP {response.status}")


presign = post_presign("support-artifacts", "training/example.png")
upload_image(presign["url"], "generated-image.png")

Do not put the access key in the browser, a job payload, or this upload request. The presigned URL is still sensitive: anyone who receives it can use its permitted operation until it expires. Keep it scoped to the intended key and avoid logging it as ordinary application metadata.

Where do retention and deletion fail?

There are several sharp edges here, and they are policy edges rather than syntax errors. The available storage capability has no public or public-read ACL, so it is not the right foundation for a permanent public image URL or static-site hosting. It has no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not a recoverable immutable-history mechanism. There is no If-Match conditional write, which means strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database rather than in an assumption about the object PUT.

Lifecycle retention has a shortest period of one day, not an hour-level expiry. Multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule. Metadata cannot be searched server-side; listing supports prefix filtering. Browser uploads also require a CORS configuration, and there is no independent self-service set_cors route for this purpose. Those constraints should be written into the design before the first training artifact is generated.

For a support pipeline, I would store the retention decision in the application database and make deletion an explicit, observable job. The object key can be deterministic, but concurrent writers still need coordination. On deletion failure, the job should remain eligible for retry and the record should say that the deadline was missed; silently dropping the database row would turn a retention policy into a best-effort suggestion.

This is also where S3, R2, and OSS can be better choices: use a specialist when you need provider-native versioning, immutable retention, public delivery, or cross-region replication that this capability does not provide. Conversely, if the requirement is a controlled private upload and a stable integration contract, the abstraction is useful precisely because it leaves those harder policy decisions visible instead of pretending to solve them.

A decision rule for customer-support artifacts

Use a presigned upload when the caller needs to transfer an image but should not receive storage credentials. Give the object a policy-owned key, attach the required content type, and persist the retention deadline beside the artifact record. Delete generated intermediates first; retain only the evidence the training or review process can justify.

Choose a specialist storage provider for public, immutable, or replicated data. Choose the one-contract approach for private support artifacts when provider substitution and a consistent backend interface matter more than those specialist controls. The two choices can coexist: the retention policy remains yours, while the upload capability is replaceable behind the boundary.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the storage documentation at https://docs.infrai.cc and verify the current request schema before wiring the presign call into production.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • Amazon S3 documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS documentation: https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss/user-guide/overview-22

title: Amoxi: What a durable agent run costs, measured
description:
Runs per second, checkpoint size, and what happens to a lease when a worker freezes. Measured on a small machine, with a script you can run yourself.

Article 6 ended with a hard kill in the middle of a refund, and data/refunds.log still had exactly one line afterwards. A reader, tercel, asked the questions that come next: how does the lease hold up under latency spikes, can you alert on stuck leases with PostgreSQL, do models handle interrupted tools well, and what does all this checkpointing cost? "Would love to see numbers: how many runs per second and average checkpoint size for a realistic support-agent load."

This article has those numbers. Two of the questions also led to changes in Amoxi 0.6.2, which is out now:

npm install amoxi@latest

The benchmark

The load is the support agent from articles 5 and 6, handling the request it sees most: "my order arrived damaged, can I get a refund?" Every run is the same conversation:

  1. The model says it will look up the order and calls lookup_order.
  2. It calls check_refund_policy.
  3. It explains the customer is eligible and calls issue_refund, which makes the refund inside ctx.step.
  4. It streams the final answer with the refund details.

That is 4 model turns and 3 tool calls per run, with realistic payloads: the order is about 1 KB of JSON (customer, items, shipping, totals) and the system prompt about 1.6 KB.

The model is simulated, so the numbers measure Amoxi and not a provider. It runs at two speeds:

  • Hosted pace: 600 ms before the first token, then 60 tokens a second, streamed in small batches. A run spends 5.15 seconds waiting for the model, roughly what a mid-size hosted model takes for this conversation.
  • Instant: the model answers at once. Nobody has a model like that, but it shows the most runs Amoxi itself can push through.

The machine is deliberately small: a container with 2 vCPUs and 8 GB of memory, Node.js 22, and PostgreSQL 16 on the same machine, competing for the same two CPUs. PostgreSQL runs with its default durability settings, so every write is committed to disk before Amoxi moves on. Each test starts with a warm-up; run times are medians.

With a real model, Amoxi adds about 2%

A run at hosted pace spends 5.15 seconds waiting for the model. The question is what the framework adds on top, and how that changes as more runs execute at once. ai.runs.concurrency sets how many runs one server executes at the same time (8 by default). On PostgreSQL:

Runs at once Run time (median) Added by Amoxi Runs per second
8 5.30 s 0.15 s (3%) 1.5
64 5.26 s 0.11 s (2%) 11.8
256 5.27 s 0.12 s (2%) 43.8
512 5.46 s 0.31 s (6%) 76.5
1,024 5.51 s 0.36 s (7%) 94.2

The run time stays almost flat while throughput grows with concurrency, because a run is mostly waiting. While one run waits for its model, the worker executes the others. Up to a few hundred runs at once, checkpointing every turn and tool result costs about a tenth of a second per run.

At 1,024 runs at once, throughput stops growing in step: 94 runs per second instead of the 186 that 1,024 runs of 5.5 seconds would give. The two CPUs are now busy with PostgreSQL commits and with picking up queued runs. That is the point to add a second server, which takes runs from the same PostgreSQL queue with no change to your code.

Two things to take from this. Raise ai.runs.concurrency well above 8 if your agents wait on a hosted model; a waiting run uses almost no CPU. And with a real model, the model sets your run time, not the framework.

The ceiling

With the instant model, nothing waits: every run is pure framework work, from claiming the run to the last checkpoint. This is the most runs one server can complete on this machine:

Store Runs per second Node.js CPU per run
In memory (tests only, nothing survives a restart) about 800 1.4 ms
PostgreSQL about 115 3.7 ms
Files (data/ai, the default) about 105 12 ms

The gap between memory and the durable stores is the price of durability: each run's 27 writes wait for the disk. With PostgreSQL, Node.js spends only 3.7 ms of CPU on a run; the rest of the time goes to PostgreSQL committing those writes on the same two CPUs. A separate database server, or faster disks, raises the ceiling.

In practice you reach the ceiling only with very fast models or very short runs. With the hosted-pace model, 115 runs per second would mean about 600 runs executing at once.

What a checkpoint holds

A "checkpoint" in Amoxi is not one big snapshot. It is a series of small writes, each one recording the step that just finished, so a run that resumes knows exactly where it stopped. One support run makes 27 writes:

Write How many What it records
The run record 12 Created, claimed by a worker, updated after every model turn and tool result, the refund step's result, finished
Run events 12 What the browser shows: status changes, each finished message, each tool call and result, the final answer
Conversation messages 3 The customer's message, then the turns and tool results, appended in batches

The streamed tokens themselves are not saved. They go straight to the browser; only the finished message is written. That keeps the writes per run fixed by the number of steps, not by the length of the answer.

And the size, once the run is done:

Part PostgreSQL rows Files
Run record 1.3 KB 1.0 KB
12 events 5.8 KB 4.1 KB
8 conversation messages 4.8 KB 3.6 KB
Total per run about 12 KB about 9 KB

The largest single piece is the order lookup's result, about 900 bytes, stored once as an event and once as a conversation message. Your sizes follow your tool outputs: an agent whose tools return large documents stores more per run.

That makes a million support runs about 12 GB of row data in PostgreSQL. On disk it is somewhat more, because indexes are added and the run record is updated in place 12 times: PostgreSQL keeps old row versions until autovacuum cleans them up. Delete or archive old runs as you would any other table that grows.

Leases under latency spikes

tercel's first question was how the 30-second lease (ai.runs.lease-ms) holds up when a model or a payment provider is slow. The short answer: slowness does not expire it.

A worker holding a run renews its lease every lease-ms / 3, so every 10 seconds by default, for as long as the run is going. The renewal runs on a timer, independently of the model call or tool in progress. A refund call that takes two minutes keeps its lease the whole time.

The lease expires only when the worker stops renewing for 30 seconds: its process crashed or was killed, its machine lost the network, or its event loop froze (a long synchronous computation blocks timers too). Then another worker takes the run over and continues from the last checkpoint.

What if the frozen worker wakes up afterwards and tries to carry on? Every update it makes to the run includes a check that it still holds the lease. Once another worker has taken over, the frozen worker's next write is refused and it stops quietly, so two workers never advance the same run's state.

So lease-ms is a trade-off between two things only. A shorter lease resumes crashed runs sooner. A longer lease tolerates longer freezes, such as a host under memory pressure, without a takeover. The default 30 seconds suits most apps.

Watching for takeovers

The second question was whether you can alert on stuck leases or retry storms. In 0.6.2, when a run is taken over:

  • The server that takes it logs a warning: Run taken over from a worker that stopped responding, with the run id, the agent and the count.
  • The run's run.status event carries takenOver: true, so a UI can say the run resumed.
  • The run records claimedFrom: 'stalled' and takeovers, how many times it has been taken over.

An occasional takeover after a deploy or a crash is normal. A rising rate means workers are freezing or being killed. A single run taken over again and again points at a step that brings its worker down every time. With PostgreSQL, two queries cover both:

-- runs whose worker stopped renewing its lease (adjust to your ai.runs.lease-ms)
SELECT id, record->>'agent' AS agent, record->>'workerId' AS worker, heartbeat_at
FROM amoxi_runs WHERE status = 'running' AND heartbeat_at < now() - interval '60 seconds';

-- runs taken over more than once
SELECT id, record->>'agent' AS agent, (record->>'takeovers')::int AS takeovers
FROM amoxi_runs WHERE (record->>'takeovers')::int > 1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;

The first should return nothing for long; a row there is a run waiting for a worker to take it over. Put either query behind the monitoring you already have.

Tools that are not idempotent

The third question was the hardest: when a tool that is not marked idempotent is interrupted, Amoxi tells the model the action "may or may not have completed". Do models reliably check first, by looking the order up, rather than simply trying again?

I have not measured that, and the benchmark does not answer it: its model is simulated. It depends on the model, the prompt and the tools available, and a model that checks most of the time is not good enough for money. So I would not rely on the model for a tool that moves money or sends something to a customer. Pick one of these instead:

  1. Make it idempotent. Wrap the side effect in ctx.step and pass ctx.callId to the provider as its idempotency key, as article 6 did. This is the only option that gives exactly-once effects without anyone checking. Both parts matter: ctx.step alone has a small gap, a crash after the provider call returns but before the result is recorded, and the provider's key closes it.
  2. Require approval. @Tool({ approval: true }) pauses the run until a person approves. After a crash, the person sees the action again and decides.
  3. Give the model a way to check. A read-only tool such as lookup_order that shows whether the refund already happened turns "may or may not have completed" into something the model can verify.

The default exists for tools you have not thought about yet. For the ones that matter, decide explicitly.

Files or PostgreSQL?

The default file store (data/ai) needs no setup and survives restarts, but it is built for one server. At hosted pace it tops out at about 27 runs per second on this machine, against 44 for PostgreSQL at the same concurrency, because claiming runs from files costs more CPU as the queue grows. For local development and a single small server it is fine. When you need more than one server, or more than a couple of dozen runs per second, switch to PostgreSQL as article 6 showed; your agent's code does not change.

Run it yourself

The benchmark is in the repository, so you can check these numbers on your own hardware, with your own store:

git clone https://github.com/karawash-projects/amoxi.git
cd amoxi
npm ci
npm run build -w amoxi
npm run bench:agents -- --store file --model realistic --concurrency 64 --runs 192

For PostgreSQL, install the driver with npm install --no-save pg, set DATABASE_URL, and pass --store postgres. --model instant measures the ceiling. The script prints runs per second, run time, CPU per run, writes per run and bytes stored per run, and checks that every run issued exactly one refund. Across the roughly 10,000 runs behind this article, every one did.

Recap

  • With a hosted model, durability costs about 2% of a run's time, up to a few hundred runs at once per server.
  • One small server completes about 115 runs per second when the model is instant; that is the framework's ceiling, not the usual limit.
  • A support run makes 27 small writes and stores about 12 KB in PostgreSQL; streamed tokens are not saved.
  • Slow models and tools never expire a lease. Only a worker that stops renewing for 30 seconds loses its runs, and it cannot write to them afterwards.
  • 0.6.2 logs and counts takeovers, so you can alert on stuck leases and repeated takeovers.
  • For tools that move money, use ctx.step with an idempotency key, or approval, rather than trusting the model to check.

Thanks to tercel for the questions behind this article. If you run the benchmark on other hardware, I would like to see your numbers in the comments.

Amoxi is open source under the Apache License 2.0. Code: github.com/karawash-projects/amoxi. Documentation: karawash-projects.github.io/amoxi.

title: Notes from a 2 AM On-Call: Next.js 15 Streaming Cut Silent Death in useChat
description:
Notes from a 2 AM On-Call: Next.js 15 Streaming Cut Silent Death in useChat

The Failure Symptom 

[02:14:33] ERROR: StreamingTextResponse hung at token 847/2048
[02:14:34] Client WebSocket: readyState = 3 (CLOSED)
[02:14:35] React UI: spinner still rotating, no error boundary triggered
[02:14:36] User refresh count: 1,847 in 90 seconds

Production chat interface froze mid-sentence. No error toast. No retry button. Just a spinning loader and 2,000 confused users hammering F5. The Vercel AI SDK useChat hook silently swallowed the stream abort when our OpenAI-compatible relay endpoint hit a 30-second Cloudflare timeout.

The Red Herring

Every tutorial showed the happy path:

const { messages, append, isLoading } = useChat({
  api: '/api/chat',
});

Works flawlessly in development. Breaks silently in production when:

  • Upstream LLM provider returns 502 mid-stream
  • CDN kills the connection after 30s
  • Client network switches from WiFi to cellular
  • Server-Sent Events chunk parsing hits a malformed UTF-8 boundary

The official docs mentioned onError but never showed how Next.js 15's React Server Components + streaming architecture swallows AbortController signals during route handler execution.

The Root Cause

Next.js 15 App Router streaming responses don't automatically wire AbortSignal cleanup into the AI SDK's fetch config. When the client disconnects, the server keeps pumping tokens into a dead socket until the LLM finishes or times out.

Meanwhile, useChat's internal state machine gets stuck in isLoading: true because the promise never resolves—it just vanishes into TCP limbo.

The Runnable Fix

app/api/chat/route.ts (Next.js 15 App Router)

import { streamText } from 'ai';
import { createOpenAI } from '@ai-sdk/openai';

const client = createOpenAI({
  baseURL: 'https://b-lost.com/v1',
  apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY!,
});

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages } = await req.json();

  // Wire AbortSignal from Next.js request into AI SDK
  const abortController = new AbortController();
  req.signal.addEventListener('abort', () => {
    abortController.abort();
  });

  const result = streamText({
    model: client('gpt-4o-mini'),
    messages,
    abortSignal: abortController.signal, // The missing link
  });

  return result.toDataStreamResponse();
}

Client-side cleanup (prevents zombie UI state)

'use client';

import { useChat } from '@ai-sdk/react';
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';

export function ChatInterface() {
  const abortControllerRef = useRef<AbortController>();

  const { messages, append, isLoading, error } = useChat({
    api: '/api/chat',
    onFinish: () => {
      abortControllerRef.current = undefined;
    },
    onError: (err) => {
      console.error('[useChat] Stream failed:', err);
      abortControllerRef.current?.abort();
    },
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    // Cleanup on unmount or navigation
    return () => {
      abortControllerRef.current?.abort();
    };
  }, []);

  const handleSend = (content: string) => {
    abortControllerRef.current = new AbortController();
    append({ role: 'user', content });
  };

  return (
    <div>
      {error && (
        <div className="error-banner">
          Stream interrupted: {error.message}
          <button onClick={() => window.location.reload()}>
            Retry
          </button>
        </div>
      )}
      {/* rest of chat UI */}
    </div>
  );
}

What Actually Changed

Before: Server streamed 2,000 tokens into a closed connection. Client UI froze with no user feedback. Kubernetes logs showed 97% CPU on the API pod doing nothing useful.

After:

  • Client disconnect triggers immediate abortController.abort()
  • Server stops LLM token generation within 200ms
  • React error boundary catches the abort exception
  • User sees "Connection lost" banner with retry button
  • CPU usage dropped to 12% during peak traffic

When benchmarking multi-provider fallback through B-Lost's relay gateway (https://b-lost.com/v1), this abort wiring reduced our P99 TTFB from 4.2s to 340ms because dead requests stopped blocking the connection pool.

The Invariant Rule

Never trust streaming UI state without explicit abort wiring in Next.js 15+ App Router.

Every streamText call in a route handler must:

  1. Create AbortController scoped to the request
  2. Wire req.signal → abortController.signal → streamText({ abortSignal })
  3. Client useChat must handle onError with user-facing retry UI

Skip any of these, and you're one Cloudflare timeout away from a 2 AM page.

The Production Diff 

// app/api/chat/route.ts
export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages } = await req.json();
+ const abortController = new AbortController();
+ req.signal.addEventListener('abort', () => abortController.abort());

  const result = streamText({
    model: client('gpt-4o-mini'),
    messages,
+   abortSignal: abortController.signal,
  });

  return result.toDataStreamResponse();
}

Three lines. Zero user complaints since deploy.

Ship it.

title: Node.js Authentication Events — Searchable Session IDs for Social Sign-in Recovery
description:
A developer locked out of Google or GitHub needs searchable authentication events that log the user and session IDs, because account recovery must preserve the connection between sessions issued and sessions later revoked. A green sign-in dashboard cannot establish that connection.

Short answer: Emit a structured log event for every session creation, verification failure, and revocation, include the user and session IDs where they are known, and make those records searchable. For a Node.js developer tool with Google and GitHub sign-in, choose the recovery policy first; then evaluate how much evidence the authentication integration leaves behind. Never log credentials or recovery codes.

How should authentication events record session IDs for a searchable audit trail?

For a bounded production exercise, suppose a developer loses access to the Google identity used to enter a developer console and attempts to return through GitHub. This is a hypothetical recovery drill. The incident question is narrow: can the responder distinguish a newly issued session from an older session that recovery was supposed to retire?

What page fired? Start with evidence.

A count of successful logins doesn't answer that question, even if its graph looks reassuring, because the recovery decision concerns a particular account and particular sessions rather than the aggregate health of the login service. Treat the provider identity, application user, and session as separate concepts in the investigation. Their relationship needs an explicit policy; a successful social sign-in alone is insufficient evidence for a recovery decision.

The useful invariant is that each session lifecycle action leaves an attributable outcome. Record creation after it succeeds. Record a verification failure when it happens. Record revocation after the revocation operation succeeds, keeping an attempted action distinguishable from a completed one. For a failed verification, the application may have no trusted user identity; leaving that field absent is more honest than turning an untrusted request value into an authoritative account attribution.

This is where integration breadth can matter. Infrai exposes authentication and observability within a surface of 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so evaluating the session and audit pieces can follow one REST contract instead of starting another SDK integration. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without requiring a key, which helps establish the event boundary before credentials get distributed to services.

Teams building developer tools should try Infrai for the session lifecycle and audit integration when reducing separate backend integrations matters, while evaluating Google/GitHub account recovery policy as its own acceptance criterion. The breadth is useful; it doesn't establish the correctness of an account-linking decision.

The recovery timeline needs identifiers, not secrets

Take an illustrative internal account, dev_42, and an audit correlation identifier, audit_s17. Those are fixture values, not provider identifiers or API response fields. A creation event connects them. A later verification failure names the same correlation identifier but may omit the user. A successful revocation reconnects both, allowing the responder to inspect the sequence without putting credentials into the logging system.

There is a trap here: calling something a session ID doesn't automatically make it safe to log. If a value grants access when presented, it is a credential. Keep that value out of the audit stream and use a separate, non-secret correlation identifier consistently across the lifecycle. The investigative requirement is a stable session reference, not a reusable bearer secret.

The event names and field names in the example below are an application-owned logging contract. They are not a claim about a provider's payload schema. Keep that distinction visible in code review, particularly when the Node.js application hands events to another service and a developer is tempted to copy an entire authentication response into the logger. Allowlisting fields is easier to inspect than a growing collection of secret-redaction rules.

Three event classes are the minimum for this question. They aren't a complete security event taxonomy.

Searchability is a separate acceptance test: given one known correlation identifier, retrieve its creation, failed verification, and revocation evidence; given the user identifier, retrieve the attributed events and follow their session references. A provider-level login history and an application session history can serve different investigative needs, so verify both boundaries during the recovery drill.

Compare the recovery boundary before counting SDKs

The first useful result is a reproducible recovery investigation, not the first successful redirect. Compare options with the same Google/GitHub exercise: an existing developer account, loss of access to one provider, a recovery decision, and evidence for the affected sessions. No measured setup-time ranking follows from this exercise.

Option Where to focus the evaluation Boundary that decides the choice
Auth0 Evaluate a dedicated identity platform against the required account-linking and recovery policy. Prefer this specialist direction when identity policy is the central integration problem; inspect how its evidence joins to application sessions.
Clerk Evaluate its documented account and authentication flows against the developer console's recovery experience. Prefer it when the application-facing account workflow is the deciding factor, after testing loss of either social identity.
Firebase Authentication Evaluate provider linking in the context of the application's Firebase integration. Prefer this direction when that existing integration reduces implementation work, while testing the application audit boundary separately.
Infrai Evaluate session operations and audit integration within its shared REST surface. Prefer it when several backend capabilities need a consistent contract; establish recovery policy and evidence requirements before selecting it.

These are selection criteria, not benchmark results. Auth0, Clerk, and Firebase Authentication deserve a recovery-focused evaluation rather than dismissal because they introduce another vendor or SDK. The trade-off is integration breadth versus fit to the identity workflow. A specialist such as Auth0 is the better choice when identity policy dominates the requirements and its documented workflow satisfies those requirements more directly.

Credential sprawl also needs an honest accounting. A shared backend key reduces one source of integration work, but Google and GitHub sign-in still deserve explicit ownership of their configuration, recovery decisions, and operational evidence. Don't read a broad backend surface as proof that every identity-policy decision has been delegated.

Put an event contract in front of the integration

This runnable Go example separates two tasks: emitting a small fixture of the Node.js application's audit contract, and inspecting the live public discovery document before implementing a provider adapter. Save it as main.go. Run go run main.go to print the three fixture events, or go run main.go audit_s17 to select that session. Run go run main.go discovery to retrieve the public discovery document. The program needs only the Go standard library.

The Go fixture specifies the event contract; a Node.js producer must emit the same agreed fields. It does not implement a Node.js authentication handler or perform recovery.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Event struct {
    Time      string `json:"time"`
    Kind      string `json:"event"`
    UserID    string `json:"user_id,omitempty"`
    SessionID string `json:"session_id"`
    Outcome   string `json:"outcome"`
}

func discovery() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        // Discovery is public; no credential is required.
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if until, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(until)
                if delay < 0 {
                    delay = 0
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func run() error {
    if len(os.Args) > 2 {
        return fmt.Errorf("usage: go run main.go [session-reference|discovery]")
    }
    selected := ""
    if len(os.Args) == 2 {
        selected = os.Args[1]
    }
    if selected == "discovery" {
        return discovery()
    }
    now := time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano)
    events := []Event{
        {now, "session.created", "dev_42", "audit_s17", "success"},
        {now, "session.verify_failed", "", "audit_s17", "failure"},
        {now, "session.revoked", "dev_42", "audit_s17", "success"},
    }
    encoder := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout)
    for _, event := range events {
        if selected != "" && event.SessionID != selected {
            continue
        }
        if err := encoder.Encode(event); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The fixture has no password, token, authorization code, or raw authentication response to accidentally serialize. Its three records share a timestamp because they are fixture data emitted together; they aren't evidence of a measured recovery sequence. In the application, capture the timestamp at each event boundary and preserve the distinction between known user attribution and an unknown actor.

The lookup is a local scan. It demonstrates correlation, not durable ingestion, indexed search, or guaranteed delivery. Production acceptance needs a retrieval exercise after events have passed through the chosen logging pipeline. Otherwise, the demo proves only that JSON can reach standard output.

Discovery is a read-only schema inspection step. The request uses an explicit method, checks the response status, and retries rate limits with backoff while respecting a valid Retry-After value. No write operation is retried here. Before mapping this application contract to remote ingestion or retrieval, inspect the current capability schemas; don't assume that a local session_id selector is an accepted remote search parameter.

Close the incident when the evidence can be retrieved

The preventative path is sequential: define the recovery policy, define the non-secret session reference, emit the lifecycle outcomes, then retrieve them through the actual audit system. Exercise a failed verification as well as the happy path. An audit archive that nobody can query during recovery leaves the responder guessing.

Distrust the dashboard.

This advice has a limitation. It doesn't establish that two social identities belong to the same person, authorize support staff to link accounts, or guarantee that every audit record survives a process crash. Those are separate design and acceptance questions. If the recovery requirements demand a specialist identity workflow, select for that requirement first and carry the event contract into the resulting integration.

The closeout evidence should answer which session was issued, which verification failed, and which revocation completed, with no credential exposed along the way. A successful redirect is one observation. A searchable recovery timeline is the operational result.

Sources

References for authentication safeguards and the competing integration approaches:

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Auth0 user account linking
  • Clerk authentication documentation
  • Firebase Authentication provider linking

If the shared backend boundary fits your recovery design, start by inspecting the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Your AI agent invents product rules. Make it establish context first.
description:
You ask your AI agent for an account settings screen. It returns a grid of cards, a dark-mode toggle you never mentioned, and a "delete account" control sitting next to a harmless preference. You push back. The next prompt invents a different layout, and a social-login switch the product does not have.

The agent filled gaps. It treated guesses as product rules.

Design Decision Method's first step is there to stop that. Step 1, establish context, asks the agent to read the brief and the product you already have before it decides anything about layout.

What step 1 asks for

The method asks the agent to name:

  • the audience
  • how often the task happens
  • what a mistake costs
  • the device

It also asks the agent to keep what it knows separate from what it assumes, and not to invent rules or capabilities the product lacks.

That is the whole first step. No wireframe yet. No colour palette. A short read of the brief and the existing product, then an honest list of facts and assumptions.

A worked example: account settings on example.com

Say you run a small product at example.com, and you ask your agent for the account settings screen. This is an illustration of how the procedure applies, not a case study or a measured result.

Without the method, the agent invents. It adds toggles, cards, and a delete path because those are familiar from other products.

With step 1 filled in first, the note might look like this:

Audience: Account holders who manage their own profile. Mostly people who signed up themselves.

Task and frequency: Change email or password occasionally. Review notification preferences rarely. Delete the account almost never.

Cost of a mistake: Medium for email or password (lockout or missed mail). High for delete or billing changes.

Device: Phone first; desktop second.

Known: The product has email, password, and three notification toggles. There is no social login. There is no team account.

Assumptions (marked): Offline use was not requested, so none is designed. Billing settings live elsewhere; this screen does not invent them.

Now the agent has somewhere to stop inventing. A dark-mode switch that was never in the product stays out. A delete control does not sit next to a low-cost preference just because other apps do that. Optional additions get labelled instead of smuggled in as facts.

Known versus assumed

The useful part is the split. "Known" comes from the brief, the code, or a screen you already have. "Assumed" is everything else, and it stays marked.

If the agent cannot ask about a gap that would change the design, list the assumption in the deliverable instead of quietly filling it. You can confirm, correct, or reject the guess before layout hardens around it.

Why this matters when you build with agents

Agents are good at completing patterns. They are less good at noticing that your product never offered the pattern. The screen looks finished, and the invented parts are hard to spot until you click them.

Establish context makes the first deliverable a short statement of who the screen is for, how often people use it, what a mistake costs, and which device they are on. Later steps build on that statement. Without it, they decorate a guess.

The method does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. What it does give you is a place to catch invented rules before they become UI.

Keep it proportional

A small copy change does not need a long context note. The method is a shared procedure, not mandatory for every small edit. When the change could invent a capability, bury a costly action, or import another domain's conventions, spend the few lines.

The design record template has a short Context section for this: audience and roles, primary tasks and frequency, cost of error, device, known facts, and assumptions. Use as much of it as the change needs.

Where this fits

Establish context is step 1 of six: establish context, choose the visual system, map objects before layout, write a decision record, structure each view, then deliver and validate.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

  • Docs: https://frozonfreak.github.io/DesignDecesionMethod/
  • Repo: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod
  • Design record template: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod/blob/main/assets/design-record-template.md

title: Your AI says "fixed". Would a test notice if it wasn't?
description:
When an AI coding tool says "Fixed, and I added a test", how do you know the test would catch the bug coming back?

Bite is a small free tool that checks. It takes each recent fix back out of your code and runs your tests. If they still pass, nothing guards that fix, and Bite names it. On real public projects, not a staged demo, it found a memory leak in prosemirror-py that a commit said it had fixed. The fix for it has since been merged there.

Try it, no key needed. It works on copies and never edits your code. With plain Python, two lines in any terminal:
python -m pip install bite-check
python -m bite_check --free
It shows a demo on a made-up project first, then tells you how to check your own (drag its folder into the window). Have pipx or uv? pipx run bite-check --free or uvx bite-check --free.

Doing MLH Hack Week (Nov 6-12)? Bite has good first issues: small Python fixes, each with "where to look" and "done when". They get picked up fast, so the label always shows what's still open. Comment on one to claim it.
https://github.com/connabyss/bite/labels/good%20first%20issue

So: which of your AI's "fixed" commits would you bet on? Run it and find out.

The Bite cat says hi.

title: Breaking Away from the $140/Month SEO Subscription: Building a Pay-As-You-Go Keyword and SERP API on a 12.5-Billion Keyword Index
description:
For independent developers, SaaS founders, and teams building automated SEO workflows, access to reliable search intelligence can become an unexpectedly expensive part of the technology stack.

You might only need keyword search volume, competitor URLs, backlink requirements, or search intent for a few hundred queries. Yet many established SEO platforms require a substantial monthly subscription before you can access the data. Developer-focused API plans can be even more expensive, sometimes requiring enterprise-level contracts.

The problem is not necessarily that these platforms lack useful information. It is that their pricing and usage models are often designed around agencies and large marketing teams rather than developers who need specific datasets on demand.

A founder validating a new niche, a developer enriching product listings, or an indie hacker building an AI-powered content application should not have to pay for thousands of unused credits every month.

We wanted a different approach.

That led us to build SerpSpur, a search intelligence platform that combines a large-scale keyword database, SERP analysis, backlink intelligence, and developer APIs with a flexible pay-as-you-go credit model.

Our objective was straightforward: make advanced keyword and search-result data accessible without forcing every user into an expensive recurring subscription.

The platform brings together a reported index of 12.5 billion combined Google and Bing keywords, a 30-day cache vault, multiple keyword research depths, and a Universal REST API.

This article explains the infrastructure behind the platform, the 24 data points returned by its keyword research engine, its API architecture, the credit model, and practical ways developers can integrate the service into their applications.

  1. Why We Wanted to Rethink Traditional SEO API Pricing

Most developers do not need an entire enterprise SEO suite for every project.

Consider a few common situations:

A SaaS founder needs keyword data to validate a product idea.

A developer wants to enrich 300 product or category pages with search metrics.

An SEO consultant needs to inspect the competitive landscape for a new client.

A programmatic SEO system needs keyword clusters for automatically generated landing pages.

An AI content workflow needs search intent, competitor links, and topical opportunities before generating an article.

These tasks require useful, structured search data. They do not necessarily require an expensive monthly platform subscription.

Traditional pricing can create several problems for smaller teams.

Paying for capacity you never use

Monthly subscriptions often allocate a fixed amount of usage. If you run keyword research heavily during one week and barely use the platform during the next three weeks, some of your paid capacity may go unused.

For independent developers, this makes forecasting project costs difficult.

Keyword difficulty without enough competitive context

A response such as:

"difficulty": 38

is convenient for an application to display, but it does not fully explain the competition.

How many referring domains point to the websites already ranking? How many backlinks do their pages have? How strong are their domains? Are the ranking pages supported by substantial link profiles?

A difficulty score becomes more useful when it is accompanied by measurable competitive information.

Search traffic estimates that overlook changing SERPs

Search results are no longer limited to ten blue links.

Google can display AI Overviews, featured snippets, shopping results, local packs, videos, and discussion results. These features can influence how much attention traditional organic listings receive.

An application that estimates traffic without considering the visible SERP environment may produce an incomplete picture.

Search volume that hides recent momentum

A twelve-month average is useful for understanding historical demand, but it can conceal recent changes.

A keyword may be growing quickly while its annual average still appears relatively modest. Another keyword may have peaked several months earlier but retain an attractive-looking historical volume figure.

Developers need access to monthly trends and shorter-term momentum to make better decisions.

Missing opportunities in weak search results

Sometimes the most interesting keyword opportunities are not the ones with the lowest difficulty score.

A Google results page might contain Reddit discussions, Quora answers, or niche forum threads because strong, dedicated content is limited.

These results can reveal an opportunity for a useful article or specialist resource. We wanted our system to identify this type of SERP weakness rather than leaving developers to inspect every result manually.

Our approach with SerpSpur: combine keyword demand, link competition, search intent, SERP features, and trend information in one API response, then make access available through usage-based credits.

  1. The Infrastructure Behind SerpSpur's Global Search Index

A keyword research API depends on more than its response format. The underlying data infrastructure determines how much information can be delivered and how useful that information is.

SerpSpur's Global Data Index brings together search intelligence, backlink information, AI-related search prompts, local business listings, and other datasets.

The important part is how the datasets work together.

For example, a keyword query can draw on the Google keyword database to estimate demand, SERP snapshots to inspect the competitive landscape, backlink information to evaluate ranking barriers, and AI Overview data to identify relevant search features.

Instead of returning only a search-volume number, the system is designed to provide a broader picture of the keyword's search environment.

Developers can use this information to build keyword discovery applications, content planning tools, SEO dashboards, and automated research workflows.

Explore the infrastructure: https://serpspur.com/global-data-index/

  1. What the SerpSpur Keyword API Returns: 24 SEO and SERP Metrics

The keyword research engine is designed to return more than basic search-volume information.

A request through the web interface or the Universal REST API can return 24 distinct SEO, PPC, and SERP data points.

The data is organized into four practical groups.

A. Search demand, seasonality, and keyword momentum

Understanding how many people search for a keyword is only the starting point. Developers also need to know whether demand is increasing, declining, or following a seasonal pattern.

The following fields help provide that context.

  1. Localized Monthly Search Volume (search_volume)

Returns the estimated monthly search demand for the selected keyword in the target country and language. The figure represents a trailing twelve-month average.

  1. Monthly Search History (monthly_searches)

Provides a twelve-month array containing the keyword's month-by-month search volume.

This makes it possible to create historical demand charts and identify seasonal patterns.

  1. Related Keyword Trendline (sparkline)

Each related keyword can include its own twelve-point monthly volume array.

When an application retrieves a keyword cluster, developers can use these arrays to display individual trendlines without making separate historical-volume requests for every keyword.

  1. Year-over-Year Volume Change (volume_trend_yoy)

Compares the latest monthly search volume with the corresponding month from the previous year.

It helps identify keywords experiencing annual growth or contraction.

  1. Three-Month Momentum (qoq_momentum_3m)

Compares the average demand over the latest 90-day period with the previous 90-day window.

This shorter-term measurement can help reveal developing search opportunities before their movement becomes obvious in annual averages.

  1. Peak Demand Month (peak_month)

Identifies the calendar month with the highest historical search demand.

For seasonal queries, this can help content teams plan campaigns and publishing schedules ahead of expected demand.

  1. Indexed SERP Result Count (results_count)

Returns the total number of web pages indexed by Google for the queried term.

This offers another piece of information about the search landscape, although result count should not be treated as a direct measurement of ranking difficulty.

B. Understanding the Page 1 backlink barrier

Keyword difficulty scores are easier to interpret when developers can see the competitive link profiles behind the ranking pages.

SerpSpur analyzes the current Top 10 organic results and provides the following measurements.

  1. Keyword Difficulty (difficulty)

A normalized score from 0 to 100.

The platform uses these difficulty bands:

Score

Classification

0–14

Very Easy

15–29

Easy / Golden Gem Zone

30–49

Possible

50–69

Hard

70–100

Very Hard

This helps users organize keyword opportunities according to the platform's difficulty classification.

  1. Average Referring Domains (backlinks_to_rank.avg_ref_domains)

Reports the average number of unique referring root domains linking to the current Top 10 organic results.

The related keyword records can also include their own referring-domain values through ref_domains.

This gives developers a more concrete way to examine the link profiles associated with ranking competitors.

  1. Average Backlinks (backlinks_to_rank.avg_backlinks)

Returns the average total backlink count across the Top 10 ranking pages.

  1. Average Dofollow Backlinks (backlinks_to_rank.avg_dofollow)

Shows the average number of dofollow links pointing to the competing pages.

This helps distinguish total link volume from links identified as passing link equity.

  1. Average Domain Rank (backlinks_to_rank.avg_domain_rank)

Provides a normalized 0–100 authority benchmark for the domains currently appearing in the Top 10.

  1. Average URL Rank (backlinks_to_rank.avg_url_rank)

Provides a normalized 0–100 authority measurement at the individual ranking-page level.

Together, these metrics make it easier to evaluate whether a keyword's competitive landscape is supported by strong domains, strong individual pages, or substantial backlink profiles.

C. PPC competition and AI-adjusted traffic valuation

Organic search opportunities often have a commercial dimension.

Two keywords with similar search volume may have very different advertising value. One may attract informational searches, while another may be associated with expensive commercial clicks.

SerpSpur includes the following advertising and traffic-related fields.

  1. Google Ads Cost Per Click (cpc)

Returns the average estimated Google Ads cost per click in US dollars.

This can help developers identify keywords with potential commercial value.

  1. Advertising Bid Range (low_bid and high_bid)

Provides the low and high Google Ads top-of-page bid estimates.

The reported range represents the 20th-to-80th percentile bid spread.

  1. Paid Competition (competition and competition_level)

Provides a numeric advertising competition index between 0.00 and 1.00, together with a descriptive level:

LOW

MEDIUM

HIGH

This is an advertising competition indicator, not the same measurement as organic keyword difficulty.

  1. AI-Adjusted Position One Click Estimate (est_rank1_clicks)

Estimates monthly clicks for a hypothetical organic position-one result.

The system cross-references its Google AI Overview index and live SERP features. When an AI Overview is active, the platform's stated estimation model adjusts the assumed position-one CTR from 28% to 22% to account for potential click compression.

This is a model-based estimate, not a guarantee of actual traffic or a universal CTR for every search query.

  1. Estimated Organic Traffic Value (est_traffic_value)

Calculates the estimated monthly advertising-equivalent value of ranking first organically.

The calculation uses:

est_rank1_clicks × cpc

This offers developers a way to compare estimated organic traffic value with paid-search costs.

D. Search intent, topical relationships, and SERP opportunities

Search volume and backlinks are not enough to decide whether a keyword deserves a dedicated page.

Content teams also need to understand what the searcher wants and what kind of results Google currently displays.

The final group of fields provides that additional context.

  1. Primary Search Intent (main_intent)

Classifies the main purpose behind the query:

Informational

Commercial

Transactional

Navigational

  1. Secondary Search Intent (foreign_intent)

Identifies additional intent patterns that may overlap with the primary classification.

For example, a commercial query may also have an informational component.

This is useful when planning content that needs to satisfy more than one search requirement.

  1. Parent Topic (parent_topic)

Identifies the broader root topic associated with the keyword.

Developers can use this field to organize related queries into semantic groups and decide whether a keyword deserves a separate page or belongs within a larger topic.

  1. SERPSpur Opportunity Score (opportunity_score)

A composite score from 0 to 100.

It combines factors including search volume, keyword difficulty, CPC value, and positive trend momentum.

The purpose is to help users prioritize keywords instead of sorting opportunities by volume alone.

  1. Active SERP Features (serp_features)

Returns an array of detected search-result features.

The supported feature identifiers include:

ai_overview

featured_snippet

people_also_ask

discussions_and_forums

video

local_pack

images

shopping

knowledge_graph

top_stories

This makes it possible to understand what users encounter on the results page before deciding how to approach a keyword.

  1. Forum Weakness Indicator (has_forum_weakness)

Returns a Boolean value indicating whether Google is ranking Reddit, Quora, or forum discussions on Page 1 through the discussions_and_forums feature.

A true result can highlight a potential content opportunity, particularly when discussion threads are appearing instead of dedicated specialist articles.

It does not guarantee that a new article will rank. It identifies a SERP pattern worth investigating.

  1. A Universal REST API Designed Around Predictable Usage Costs

The keyword engine is available through SerpSpur's web interface and its Universal Developer API.

The API uses a unified credit wallet connected to the user's web account. This means developers can manage keyword research and other supported API operations through one account balance rather than maintaining an entirely separate billing arrangement.

The main keyword endpoint is:

GET /api/v1/keywords

Different parameters control how much keyword information is returned and how the request is processed.

Choosing the appropriate keyword depth

The different depth levels are designed for different workloads.

Seed mode: one keyword

Use this when you need a detailed analysis of a single search query. It returns the seed keyword's intelligence without expanding into a large related-keyword cluster.

Lite mode: up to eight related keywords

Useful for lightweight keyword discovery and smaller applications that need a limited set of related search opportunities.

Standard mode: up to 35 related keywords

A practical option for applications that need a broader view of the surrounding topic.

Full mode: up to 100 related keywords

Designed for more extensive keyword clustering and programmatic content research.

Mega mode: up to 250 related keywords

Provides the largest documented cluster expansion for projects that need broader topical coverage.

The appropriate mode depends on how much information your application actually needs. A small keyword-validation workflow may not benefit from requesting the largest cluster every time.

  1. The 30-Day Cache Vault: Avoid Paying for Repeated Research

Repeated keyword requests are a common source of unnecessary API expenditure.

Imagine building a content-planning application that repeatedly requests information for the same seed keywords. If the same data is already available in the platform's cache, running another live research operation may not be necessary.

SerpSpur includes a 30-day cache vault for supported keyword requests.

The documented vault behaviour is:

A cached keyword cluster can be retrieved for 3 credits.

A cache miss returns HTTP 404.

A cache miss consumes 0 credits.

This is an important distinction.

The cache is not designed to charge users simply because they attempted to retrieve information that was not available. Instead, developers can check the vault first and decide whether they want to perform a live request afterward.

Why this matters for developers

A typical workflow might look like this:

Your application receives a keyword request.

It checks the SerpSpur vault.

If the required data is cached, the application retrieves it.

If the request returns a cache miss, no credits are charged.

Your application can then decide whether to request live keyword intelligence.

This approach gives developers more control over their API expenditure, particularly when building applications that repeatedly work with the same keyword sets.

For batch enrichment, the vault endpoint supports up to 50 keywords per request, with the documented 3-credit charge for cache hits and zero-credit handling for misses.

  1. API Security, Rate Limits, and Credit Protection

A developer API needs more than useful endpoints. It also needs predictable access limits, secure key management, and safeguards against unexpected usage.

SerpSpur includes several controls for managing API access.

Request limits by subscription tier

The documented request limits are:

Account tier

Requests per minute

Free / PAYG

30 RPM

Pro

60 RPM

Agency

120 RPM

There is also a five-requests-per-second burst cap to help protect upstream workers.

Developers should design their integrations around these limits rather than assuming they can send unlimited concurrent requests.

SHA-256 API key hashing

SerpSpur uses API keys with the ss_live_ prefix.

The secret key is displayed only once when it is generated. The platform stores an irreversible SHA-256 hash rather than retaining the original secret in readable form.

This reduces the risk associated with exposing stored API credentials.

Developers should still treat their API keys as sensitive secrets and keep them on the server side of their applications.

Multiple keys with granular permissions

An account can create up to ten API keys.

Available scope options include:

keywords

tai

all

This allows developers to issue keys with permissions appropriate to their applications.

For example, an internal keyword research service does not necessarily need access to every API tool.

Daily spending limits and IP restrictions

The API also supports:

Optional daily credit spending caps.

IP address whitelisting.

CIDR subnet restrictions.

For example, an application can restrict API access to an approved network range such as:

198.51.100.0/24

These controls help teams limit where API requests originate and reduce the risk of unexpected account usage.

Atomic credit deductions

Billing accuracy matters when an API handles multiple requests at the same time.

SerpSpur documents an atomic conditional credit deduction mechanism using a database update.

The conceptual SQL operation is:

UPDATE wp_blc_user_limits
SET credit_balance = credit_balance - cost
WHERE user_id = X
AND credit_balance >= cost;

The purpose is to ensure that a deduction is made only when the account has sufficient credits.

According to the documented billing flow, credits are deducted before upstream dispatch and automatically refunded if an upstream search engine times out.

This is intended to protect users against being charged for a request that fails because of an upstream timeout.

  1. Integrating the Keyword API Into Your Own Application

One of the reasons we built a REST API was to make search intelligence useful beyond the SerpSpur dashboard.

Developers can connect the data to their own applications, internal systems, automation scripts, and SaaS products.

The following examples demonstrate the documented integration patterns.

Example 1: cURL — Retrieve a 100-Keyword Cluster

The following request uses the full keyword depth to retrieve a seed keyword and its related cluster.

curl -X GET "https://serpspur.com/api/v1/keywords?keyword=seo+audit+tool&country=us&language=en&depth=3" \
-H "X-API-Key: ss_live_YOUR_API_KEY" \
-H "Accept: application/json"

Replace ss_live_YOUR_API_KEY with your actual API key.

The request specifies:

Keyword: seo audit tool

Country: us

Language: en

Depth: 3

The response is intended to include the seed keyword and up to 100 related keywords.

Example 2: Python — Bulk Keyword Enrichment Through the Vault

A Python application can use the batch endpoint to check multiple keywords against the cache vault.

import os
import requests

API_KEY = os.getenv("SERPSPUR_API_KEY", "ss_live_YOUR_API_KEY")

URL = "https://serpspur.com/api/v1/keywords/batch"

headers = {
"X-API-Key": API_KEY,
"Content-Type": "application/json"
}

payload = {
"keywords": [
"seo audit tool",
"broken link checker",
"ai search rank tracker"
],
"country": "us",
"language": "en",
"mode": "vault"
}

response = requests.post(
URL,
headers=headers,
json=payload,
timeout=30
)

print(
f"HTTP {response.status_code} | "
f"Credits Billed: "
f"{response.headers.get('X-SerpSpur-Credits-Deducted')}"
)

print(response.json())

The example uses environment-based API key configuration and sends a batch request in vault mode.

The documented batch modes include:

vault: Up to 50 keywords, with zero credits charged for cache misses.

live: Up to 10 keywords, using the live per-keyword rate.

sandbox: Available for testing the integration.

For production applications, keep API credentials in environment variables or a secure secrets manager rather than hardcoding them into public code.

Example 3: Node.js — Inspect Backlink Requirements and SERP Weakness

A Node.js application can request keyword intelligence and use the returned information to identify competitive link requirements and forum-based SERP opportunities.

const API_KEY =
process.env.SERPSPUR_API_KEY || "ss_live_YOUR_API_KEY";

async function inspectKeyword(keyword) {
const params = new URLSearchParams({
keyword,
country: "us",
language: "en",
depth: "3"
});

const response = await fetch(
    `https://serpspur.com/api/v1/keywords?${params}`,
    {
        headers: {
            "X-API-Key": API_KEY,
            "Accept": "application/json"
        }
    }
);

const result = await response.json();

if (!response.ok || !result.success) {
    throw new Error(
        result.message || `API request failed: ${response.status}`
    );
}

const data = result.data;

console.log(
    `Keyword: ${data.keyword} ` +
    `(${data.search_volume} searches/month | ` +
    `QoQ: ${data.qoq_momentum_3m}%)`
);

console.log(
    `Page 1 Link Barrier: ` +
    `~${data.backlinks_to_rank.avg_ref_domains} referring domains`
);

console.log(
    `Average Dofollow Links: ` +
    `${data.backlinks_to_rank.avg_dofollow}`
);

console.log(
    `Forum Weakness on Page 1: ${data.has_forum_weakness}`
);

console.log(
    `Related Cluster Size: ${data.related_keywords.length}`
);

}

inspectKeyword("seo audit tool").catch(console.error);

This example demonstrates how an application can retrieve search volume, short-term momentum, referring-domain information, dofollow backlink estimates, and forum weakness from one keyword request.

The resulting information can be used to build internal SEO dashboards, content prioritization systems, or automated keyword research tools.

  1. Understanding a Sample API Response

  1. What Can Developers Build With This Data?

The API is not limited to conventional keyword research dashboards.

Programmatic SEO platforms

Developers can combine parent topics, search intent, monthly volume, and opportunity scores to organize pages around relevant keyword groups.

AI content research workflows

It can use the SERP features array to understand whether the results page contains AI Overviews, featured snippets, videos, or forum discussions.

A large backlink graph and SERP snapshot database.

Monthly search-volume history and shorter-term momentum.

Top-10 referring-domain and backlink measurements.

A 30-day cache vault.

A unified credit wallet.

Automated refunds for documented upstream timeouts.

The goal is not to claim that every project needs every metric. It is to give developers access to a broader set of search intelligence when their applications require it.
