title: 45 System Tables: What an AI-Native Backend Foundation Looks Like
description:
If you use an AI coding assistant for backend work, you have probably seen this pattern: it generates a CRUD endpoint in seconds, then you spend days aligning authentication, permissions, menus, dictionaries, audit logs and reports.

The endpoint was never the hard part. The hard part is the foundation underneath it.

The foundation keeps getting rebuilt

Most enterprise backends contain two kinds of tables:

  • Business tables: customers, orders, projects. They differ from product to product.
  • System tables: users, organizations, roles, permissions, menus, dictionaries, logs, workflows, reports. They are almost identical in every product.

When an AI starts from an empty repository, it invents the second category again. One generation calls the user table sys_user; the next calls it t_user. One puts permission checks in an interceptor; another puts them in every controller.

The code runs. But three problems show up later:

  1. Inconsistency with the existing system. You already have a user table and a permission model. The AI created a second one.
  2. Missing cross-cutting constraints. Rules like "only editors can see the export button" live in the backend, the route config and the menu config at the same time. The AI only sees the file you pasted.
  3. Handover cost. A codebase with no history and no conventions has to be understood before it can be maintained.

The expensive part is not the number of lines. It is keeping those lines consistent across modules.

What 45 system tables actually cover

GewuMind Boot ships a baseline schema for the parts every admin system needs:

  • identity: users, organizations, roles, positions
  • access control: menus, buttons, data scopes, role bindings
  • configuration: dictionaries, parameters, scheduled jobs
  • operations: audit logs, login logs, online sessions
  • collaboration: workflows, messages, attachments
  • reporting: report definitions and data sources
  • integration: open APIs, webhooks, external identity

The exact table list matters less than what it represents: a set of decisions already made. Naming, audit fields, soft deletes, permission resolution, dictionary translation and menu registration follow one convention instead of being reinvented per project.

That is also why the number alone is not the selling point. A foundation is valuable when the conventions are consistent and documented, not when the count is large.

Why conventions beat generation speed

Consider a request that sounds simple: "different departments should see different data."

Built from scratch, the work looks like this:

  1. create an organization table
  2. model the hierarchy
  3. write a recursive query for visible child organizations
  4. apply that filter to every business query
  5. add a role bypass for administrators
  6. translate organization ids in the UI

With a foundation, the same request becomes configuration:

  • the organization tree already exists
  • a helper resolves the current user's visible scope
  • the role model already supports bypass
  • the component layer already knows how to render dictionary values

The AI still writes business logic. It just does not rebuild identity, permissions and navigation first.

The AI-native part

An AI-native backend is not "a backend with a chat box". It is a backend whose primitives are stable enough that an agent can target them reliably.

Three properties make that possible:

Explicit contracts. Tables, scripts and page components have documented shapes. The agent does not guess where permissions live.

Idempotent publishing. Changes are packaged and applied as a bundle, so a failed run can be retried without duplicating menus or tables.

Reversible operations. Every publish creates a version that can be rolled back.

Without those properties, AI output is fast but fragile. With them, generated modules can be reviewed, versioned and rolled back like any other change.

A note on licensing

The core of GewuMind Boot is Apache License 2.0. Some enterprise capabilities, including SSO, the workflow engine, module management, Redis/shared sessions, MQTT, Kafka, SSE, TCP and WebSocket, are enabled at runtime by a commercial offline license key. Without a valid key those capabilities run in a 30-day trial or stay disabled. The license key is a feature entitlement, not a change to the source code license.

That distinction matters if you plan to self-host or embed the platform.

What to look for in an AI backend foundation

If you are evaluating this category, ask four questions:

  1. Does it define the system tables I would otherwise rebuild?
  2. Are permissions and menus part of the same model, or separate afterthoughts?
  3. Can an agent publish changes repeatedly without creating duplicates?
  4. Can I roll back a bad publish?

The answers tell you more than a feature list.

Closing

AI coding tools are good at producing code. They are less good at preserving the conventions a codebase depends on. The practical fix is not a better prompt. It is a better starting point.

If you want to see the schema and the publishing model, the project is at gewumind.github.io. The repository, documentation and commercial terms are linked there.

title: SQL INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN vs RIGHT JOIN vs FULL OUTER JOIN: Differences With Examples (Tested in MySQL 8.4 and SQLite)
description:
INNER JOIN returns only the rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, with NULL where the right table has no match. RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image: every row from the right table. FULL OUTER JOIN returns every row from both tables, matched where possible. On my four customers and five orders, those joins returned 4, 5, 5 and 6 rows. MySQL doesn't support FULL OUTER JOIN at all, so there you combine a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN with UNION ALL.

Joins are where a lot of SQL bugs hide. A report silently drops customers who never ordered, a WHERE clause quietly turns a LEFT JOIN back into an INNER JOIN, or MySQL happily runs a "FULL JOIN" that isn't one. I'll show each of those with real output.

Every query below ran against the same two tables on MySQL 8.4.8 and SQLite 3.46.1, and the result tables are pasted straight from the mysql and sqlite3 command-line clients.

In this guide:

  • INNER vs LEFT vs RIGHT vs FULL OUTER JOIN at a glance
  • The two tables used in every example
  • INNER JOIN: only rows that match
  • LEFT JOIN: keep every row from the first table
  • RIGHT JOIN: keep every row from the second table
  • FULL OUTER JOIN: keep everything from both sides
  • How to do a FULL OUTER JOIN in MySQL
  • The MySQL "FULL JOIN" trap
  • Find rows with no match (the LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL pattern)
  • The WHERE clause trap that turns LEFT JOIN into INNER JOIN
  • COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) after a LEFT JOIN
  • Why joins can multiply rows (and what CROSS JOIN does)
  • Which join should you use?
  • Frequently asked questions

INNER vs LEFT vs RIGHT vs FULL OUTER JOIN at a glance

Join Rows it keeps Unmatched side shows Rows in my test MySQL 8.4 SQLite
INNER JOIN Only rows that match in both tables Not returned 4 Yes Yes
LEFT JOIN All left rows + matching right rows NULL in right columns 5 Yes Yes
RIGHT JOIN All right rows + matching left rows NULL in left columns 5 Yes Yes (3.39.0+)
FULL OUTER JOIN All rows from both tables NULL on whichever side is missing 6 No (use UNION ALL) Yes (3.39.0+)
CROSS JOIN Every left row paired with every right row No matching at all 20 Yes Yes

LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN are the same thing; the word OUTER is optional. The same goes for RIGHT and FULL. And a plain JOIN means INNER JOIN. RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN arrived in SQLite with version 3.39.0, as the SQLite 3.39.0 release notes put it: "Add (long overdue) support for RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN."

The two tables used in every example

Here's the schema and data. It runs unchanged on both MySQL and SQLite:

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  city VARCHAR(50)
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT,
  total       DECIMAL(8,2),
  status      VARCHAR(20)
);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES
  (1, 'Ayesha', 'London'),
  (2, 'Ben',    'Leeds'),
  (3, 'Chloe',  'London'),
  (4, 'Dev',    'Bristol');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES
  (101, 1,    25.00, 'paid'),
  (102, 1,    40.00, 'refunded'),
  (103, 2,    15.50, 'paid'),
  (104, 3,    60.00, 'paid'),
  (105, NULL, 12.00, 'paid');

The data is built to show every edge case:

  • Ayesha has two orders, so she can appear twice in a join.
  • Ben and Chloe have one order each.
  • Dev has no orders at all.
  • Order 105 has no customer (customer_id is NULL), like a guest checkout.

A NULL never equals anything in SQL, not even another NULL, so order 105 can never match a customer through o.customer_id = c.id.

INNER JOIN: only rows that match

An INNER JOIN pairs each customer with each of their orders and throws away anything without a partner on the other side:

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

MySQL 8.4.8:

+--------+----------+-------+
| name   | order_id | total |
+--------+----------+-------+
| Ayesha |      101 | 25.00 |
| Ayesha |      102 | 40.00 |
| Ben    |      103 | 15.50 |
| Chloe  |      104 | 60.00 |
+--------+----------+-------+

Dev is gone because he has no orders, and order 105 is gone because it has no customer. Ayesha appears twice because she matches two orders. That's normal: a join returns one row per matching pair, not one row per customer.

Use INNER JOIN when a row is only meaningful with its partner, like "orders with the customer's name". The MySQL 8.4 JOIN reference notes that in MySQL, JOIN, CROSS JOIN and INNER JOIN are syntactic equivalents, though standard SQL treats them differently.

LEFT JOIN: keep every row from the first table

Swap INNER for LEFT and every customer stays, with or without orders:

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

+--------+----------+-------+
| name   | order_id | total |
+--------+----------+-------+
| Ayesha |      101 | 25.00 |
| Ayesha |      102 | 40.00 |
| Ben    |      103 | 15.50 |
| Chloe  |      104 | 60.00 |
| Dev    |     NULL |  NULL |
+--------+----------+-------+

Dev is back, with NULL in every column that comes from orders. Here's the same query in SQLite 3.46.1 using .mode table:

+--------+----------+-------+
|  name  | order_id | total |
+--------+----------+-------+
| Ayesha | 101      | 25    |
| Ayesha | 102      | 40    |
| Ben    | 103      | 15.5  |
| Chloe  | 104      | 60    |
| Dev    |          |       |
+--------+----------+-------+

The rows are identical. Two display differences are worth knowing: the SQLite shell shows NULL as an empty cell by default (run .nullvalue NULL to change that), and SQLite has no true DECIMAL type, so 25.00 prints as 25.

LEFT JOIN is the join you'll write most after INNER JOIN. Any time the question is "all X, plus their Y if they have any", it's a LEFT JOIN.

RIGHT JOIN: keep every row from the second table

RIGHT JOIN flips the rule. Now every order is kept, even the guest order with no customer:

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY o.id;

+--------+----------+-------+
| name   | order_id | total |
+--------+----------+-------+
| Ayesha |      101 | 25.00 |
| Ayesha |      102 | 40.00 |
| Ben    |      103 | 15.50 |
| Chloe  |      104 | 60.00 |
| NULL   |      105 | 12.00 |
+--------+----------+-------+

Order 105 appears with a NULL name, and Dev has disappeared, because nothing on the right side points at him.

Any RIGHT JOIN can be rewritten as a LEFT JOIN by swapping the table order: FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON ... returns the same rows. The MySQL manual even recommends using LEFT JOIN instead of RIGHT JOIN to keep code portable. Most teams follow that, because queries are easier to read when the "keep everything" table always comes first.

FULL OUTER JOIN: keep everything from both sides

A FULL OUTER JOIN is a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN combined. SQLite 3.46.1 runs it directly:

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total
FROM customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

+--------+----------+-------+
|  name  | order_id | total |
+--------+----------+-------+
| Dev    |          |       |
| Ayesha | 101      | 25    |
| Ayesha | 102      | 40    |
| Ben    | 103      | 15.5  |
| Chloe  | 104      | 60    |
|        | 105      | 12    |
+--------+----------+-------+

Six rows: the four matches, Dev without an order, and order 105 without a customer. Dev sorts first because NULL values come first in an ascending ORDER BY in both SQLite and MySQL.

Now the same query in MySQL 8.4.8:

ERROR 1064 (42000) at line 1: You have an error in your SQL syntax; check the manual that corresponds to your MySQL server version for the right syntax to use near 'FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY o.id, c.id' at line 3

MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN. PostgreSQL does, and its table expressions documentation covers all the outer join types, but I only tested MySQL and SQLite here.

How to do a FULL OUTER JOIN in MySQL

The standard workaround: take the LEFT JOIN, then add only the right-side rows that had no match. The WHERE c.id IS NULL on the second half is what stops the matched rows appearing twice:

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
UNION ALL
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.total
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.id IS NULL
ORDER BY order_id, name;

MySQL 8.4.8:

+--------+----------+-------+
| name   | order_id | total |
+--------+----------+-------+
| Dev    |     NULL |  NULL |
| Ayesha |      101 | 25.00 |
| Ayesha |      102 | 40.00 |
| Ben    |      103 | 15.50 |
| Chloe  |      104 | 60.00 |
| NULL   |      105 | 12.00 |
+--------+----------+-------+

The same six rows SQLite gave with a real FULL OUTER JOIN. I ran this exact query in SQLite too and got the same six rows, so it's a portable pattern.

You'll often see this written with plain UNION and no WHERE. That also removes the duplicated matches, but it removes any identical rows, including real duplicates in your data, and it makes the database do extra work comparing every row to find duplicates. UNION ALL with WHERE c.id IS NULL keeps every genuine row and skips that deduplication step.

The MySQL "FULL JOIN" trap

This one surprised me. Write FULL JOIN (without OUTER) in MySQL and leave out the table alias, and you don't get a syntax error. You get a different, confusing error:

SELECT customers.name, orders.id AS order_id
FROM customers
FULL JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
ORDER BY order_id;

ERROR 1054 (42S22) at line 1: Unknown column 'customers.name' in 'field list'

MySQL read FULL as an alias for customers, so customers.name no longer exists. Use the alias it accidentally created, and the query runs, but as a plain inner join:

SELECT FULL.name, orders.id AS order_id
FROM customers
FULL JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = FULL.id
ORDER BY order_id;

+--------+----------+
| name   | order_id |
+--------+----------+
| Ayesha |      101 |
| Ayesha |      102 |
| Ben    |      103 |
| Chloe  |      104 |
+--------+----------+

Four rows, no Dev, no order 105. If you ever port a query from PostgreSQL or SQLite and MySQL suddenly complains about an unknown column, check for FULL JOIN. SQLite, for the record, ran the first version as a true full join and rejected the second with no such column: FULL.name.

Find rows with no match (the LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL pattern)

One of the most useful things a LEFT JOIN does is find what's missing. Join, then keep only the rows where the right side came back empty:

SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

+------+
| name |
+------+
| Dev  |
+------+

That's "customers who never ordered", and both databases returned the same single row. Check a column that can't be NULL in a real match, like the primary key o.id. The same pattern finds orphaned records before you add a foreign key, and pairs well with cleaning up data as in my guide to deleting duplicate rows in MySQL.

The WHERE clause trap that turns LEFT JOIN into INNER JOIN

Say you want every customer and their paid orders. This looks right, but it isn't:

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
ORDER BY c.id;

+--------+----------+--------+
| name   | order_id | status |
+--------+----------+--------+
| Ayesha |      101 | paid   |
| Ben    |      103 | paid   |
| Chloe  |      104 | paid   |
+--------+----------+--------+

Dev vanished. The LEFT JOIN did keep him, with o.status as NULL, but then WHERE o.status = 'paid' ran on the result, and NULL = 'paid' isn't true. So the WHERE filtered out exactly the rows the LEFT JOIN was there to keep.

Fix: move conditions on the right-hand table into the ON clause:

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
ORDER BY c.id;

+--------+----------+--------+
| name   | order_id | status |
+--------+----------+--------+
| Ayesha |      101 | paid   |
| Ben    |      103 | paid   |
| Chloe  |      104 | paid   |
| Dev    |     NULL | NULL   |
+--------+----------+--------+

Rule of thumb: conditions on the table you're keeping go in WHERE; conditions on the optional table go in ON. If you build these queries from PHP, pass the 'paid' value as a bound parameter, as shown in my PDO prepared statements guide.

COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) after a LEFT JOIN

Counting orders per customer is a classic LEFT JOIN job, and a classic mistake:

SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS count_star, COUNT(o.id) AS count_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;

+--------+------------+--------------+
| name   | count_star | count_orders |
+--------+------------+--------------+
| Ayesha |          2 |            2 |
| Ben    |          1 |            1 |
| Chloe  |          1 |            1 |
| Dev    |          1 |            0 |
+--------+------------+--------------+

COUNT(*) counts rows, and Dev still has one row (the one full of NULLs), so it says 1. COUNT(o.id) skips NULL values and correctly says 0. Always count a column from the optional table. If you'd rather list the order IDs in one cell, GROUP_CONCAT with ORDER BY works on the same join.

Why joins can multiply rows (and what CROSS JOIN does)

Every join returns one row per matching pair. Ayesha has two orders, so she shows up twice, and if you joined a third table where she also had two rows, you'd get four Ayesha rows. That's why a SUM() over a join with two "many" tables can come out too high: rows are repeated before the sum runs. Aggregate each child table first in a subquery, then join the totals.

A CROSS JOIN takes that to the extreme. It has no ON condition and pairs every row with every row:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS cross_rows FROM customers CROSS JOIN orders;

+------------+
| cross_rows |
+------------+
|         20 |
+------------+

4 customers × 5 orders = 20. Forgetting the ON clause gives you this by accident: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers JOIN orders; with no ON also returned 20 in both MySQL 8.4.8 and SQLite 3.46.1, with no error or warning. That's how a query on two 10,000-row tables suddenly tries to return 100 million rows. Microsoft's guide to how joins are processed explains how engines execute these, if you want to go deeper.

Which join should you use?

  • You need only rows that exist on both sides (orders with a known customer): INNER JOIN.
  • You need every row from one table, plus extra details where they exist (all customers and any orders): LEFT JOIN, with the "keep everything" table first.
  • You're tempted to write RIGHT JOIN: swap the table order and use LEFT JOIN instead. Same result, easier to read.
  • You need to compare two lists and see what's missing on either side (reconciling two exports): FULL OUTER JOIN, or LEFT JOIN + UNION ALL + RIGHT JOIN ... WHERE left.id IS NULL in MySQL.
  • You need every combination (sizes × colours): CROSS JOIN.

Need quick helpers while working on a database-backed site, like a slug generator or UUID generator? They're on the free tools page.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?

INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table and fills the right table's columns with NULL when there's no match. In my test, INNER JOIN returned 4 rows and LEFT JOIN returned 5, because the customer with no orders was kept.

Is LEFT JOIN the same as LEFT OUTER JOIN?

Yes. OUTER is optional, so LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN are identical. The same applies to RIGHT JOIN and RIGHT OUTER JOIN, and to FULL JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN in databases that support it.

Does MySQL support FULL OUTER JOIN?

No. MySQL 8.4.8 returned ERROR 1064 for FULL OUTER JOIN. Emulate it with a LEFT JOIN, then UNION ALL, then a RIGHT JOIN filtered with WHERE left_table.id IS NULL.

Does SQLite support RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN?

Yes, since SQLite 3.39.0. Older versions only supported INNER, LEFT and CROSS joins. Run SELECT sqlite_version(); to check which version you have.

Is RIGHT JOIN ever necessary?

Not really. Any RIGHT JOIN can be written as a LEFT JOIN by swapping the order of the tables, and the MySQL manual recommends LEFT JOIN for portability.

Why did my LEFT JOIN return fewer rows than expected?

Usually a WHERE condition on the right-hand table. Unmatched rows have NULL there, and the WHERE filters them out, turning the query into an INNER JOIN. Move that condition into the ON clause.

Is a plain JOIN an INNER JOIN?

Yes. JOIN on its own means INNER JOIN in standard SQL, MySQL and SQLite. In MySQL, JOIN, INNER JOIN and CROSS JOIN are syntactic equivalents.

Which join is fastest?

It depends on indexes, data size and the query plan, not the join keyword. Index the columns in the ON clause (such as orders.customer_id) and check the plan with EXPLAIN. INNER JOIN can return fewer rows, which helps, but choose the join for correctness first.

Last checked: 1 November 2026. Figures, settings and guidance can change, so confirm anything important with the sources linked above.

title: What JavaScript using disposes after returns and exceptions: nine checks
description:
using registers an object with a disposal method in a scope and calls cleanup when that scope ends. When several resources were registered, they were disposed in reverse acquisition order. An early return followed the same rule.

Nine conditions in Node.js covered disposal order, retained exceptions, and asynchronous waiting. Before using it, check which object supplies disposal and which scope exit triggers cleanup.

Disposal finishes before the caller receives a return value

This code ran as an .mjs file in Node.js 24.15.0, without a transpiler or polyfill:

const events = [];
function open(name) {
  events.push(`open:${name}`);
  return { [Symbol.dispose]() { events.push(`close:${name}`); } };
}
function work() {
  using first = open('A');
  using second = open('B');
  events.push('body');
  return 'done';
}
const value = work();
console.log(JSON.stringify({ value, events }));

The result contained value: "done", with events open:A → open:B → body → close:B → close:A. Both disposals had finished when the caller received the return value.

open only returns a fixture object. The log records calls to Symbol.dispose; it is not a measurement of real files or connections. The ECMAScript declaration and scope specification also describes disposing resources registered through using when scope processing finishes.

The comparison included failures as well as normal completion:

Condition Observed order or result
Acquire A and B, finish normally Dispose B, then A
Acquire A and return Dispose A before returning to the caller
Throw in the body Dispose A before entering catch
Acquire A, then throw while acquiring B Dispose registered A; no disposal call for B
Body and both A/B disposals throw Attempt both disposals and retain errors through SuppressedError
Register A and B with await using Finish B's asynchronous disposal before disposing A
Pass an asyncDispose-only value to using TypeError; asynchronous disposal is not called
Pass null and undefined to using Execute the body without disposal methods
Throw while using a temporary directory Directory no longer exists after entering catch

When acquiring B throws, using does not dispose B afterward. If the acquisition function allocated something before failing, that function needs to clean up its partial acquisition.

Where does the body error go if cleanup fails too?

A deliberately failing disposer tested this case. The body threw body failed, B threw close failed:B, and A threw close failed:A.

The caught exception's error.message was close failed:A. The body failure was still retained:

Reference Recorded message
error.error.message close failed:A
error.suppressed.error.message close failed:B
error.suppressed.suppressed.message body failed

Both the outer and inner wrappers were SuppressedError objects. Cleanup continued after a disposal failed, with earlier errors retained in a related chain. The explicit resource management design material explains this relationship.

Logging only the outer message can miss the body failure. The experiment followed both error and suppressed and checked each message.

Use await using for asynchronous disposal

The asynchronous fixture recorded the start and end of Symbol.asyncDispose separately. Registering await using a = ... and await using b = ... produced body → close start:B → close end:B → close start:A → close end:A → after work.

The wait in this fixture was Promise.resolve(). It did not measure network or disk I/O duration. It did verify that A's disposal started after B's completed, and that the caller continued after both finished.

Passing an object with only Symbol.asyncDispose to using without await produced a TypeError. An asynchronously disposable value cannot simply be placed in an ordinary using declaration.

Check a real Node.js temporary directory

The next example uses an actual temporary directory rather than only a logging object:

import { existsSync, mkdtempDisposableSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os';
import { join } from 'node:path';

let path;
try {
  using temporary = mkdtempDisposableSync(join(tmpdir(), 'article-using-example-'));
  path = temporary.path;
  writeFileSync(join(path, 'sample.txt'), 'fixture');
  console.log('inside:', existsSync(path));
  throw new Error('work failed');
} catch (error) {
  console.log('caught:', error.message);
}
console.log('after:', existsSync(path));

The output was inside: true, caught: work failed, and after: false. The directory, including sample.txt, was removed when the exception left the scope.

Node.js 24.15.0's mkdtempDisposableSync returns an object with a path and a disposal method for removal. This API was added in 24.4.0. An arbitrary path string does not acquire that deletion behavior merely by being used in a using declaration.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with Node.js 24.15.0 on macOS arm64. The nine-condition fixture and results are available. Other Node versions, browsers, transformed code, and forced process termination were not tested. These results cover disposal when JavaScript can execute the scope-exit steps.

title: Integrate Node.js Error Tracking Using a Backend API for Safe Checkout Rollbacks
description:
Rollback-Safe Checkout Error Capture Through a Reproducible Backend Data Contract

Short answer: capture checkout failures at the backend boundary, send a small redacted event to /v1/errors/capture, and judge the integration by whether an operator can make the same rollback decision from the same fixture. The least complex implementation is a bounded Node.js request with a release marker, checkout identifier, privacy-safe user identifier, timestamp, message, and stack trace. Payment execution must remain independent of telemetry delivery.

That is the important design choice. A dashboard is useful later. A stable event contract comes first.

Start with the rollback decision

Checkout failure tracking has a deceptively small job: tell the team what broke, in which release, and whether the new release should be reversed. It should not decide whether a card charge succeeds. It should not store a payment token. It should not turn a slow telemetry service into a second checkout failure.

For a fintech workflow, I would define one event fixture before choosing a backend. Each sanitized event needs a release identifier, checkout identifier, privacy-safe user identifier, timestamp, failure class, message, and stack trace when available. It also needs an expected rollback action. The fixture should include a timeout, validation failure, dependency failure, inference failure, and a failure after a payment attempt.

Keep the fixture versioned. A useful evaluation changes when the inputs change; changing the inputs silently makes the comparison meaningless.

Keep it boring.

Infrai fits this capture leg when a team wants error tracking beside adjacent backend capabilities behind one REST contract. Its discovery surface is public, and the documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, so the team can inspect the request shape before committing to the experiment.

The concrete advantage is breadth behind one contract: Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so adjacent backend work can stay on the same HTTP integration.

The pass rule is concrete: every event is attributable to a release, sensitive payment data is absent, repeated capture does not create a duplicate that changes the decision, and an operator can answer “which release should we roll back?” from the retained event. A missing release, an unbounded retry, or an event that can only be understood by opening raw customer data is a fail.

Which backend fits this reliability boundary?

The options have different centers of gravity. Pick the one that matches the decision you need to make repeatedly, not the one with the longest feature page.

Option Pick this when Boundary to verify
Unified observability API You want error capture beside other backend capabilities through one REST contract You must build alert polling and accept that it has no distributed trace query, source-map deobfuscation, Session Replay, or synthetic uptime checks
Sentry You need specialist exception grouping and release-oriented debugging Inference context and any adjacent backend capability require another integration
Datadog Your team already operates a broad logs, metrics, traces, and alerting platform The operational surface is wider, so validate the configuration and ownership required for a checkout rollback
Rollbar You want hosted application-exception grouping and workflow around errors Cross-system checkout and inference context still needs careful correlation

OpenTelemetry is also relevant when instrumentation portability matters. Its logs signal model provides a common vocabulary; it is not, by itself, a hosted error workflow or an alerting policy.

A unified REST backend is a reasonable leg of this experiment for a small Node.js checkout service that values breadth behind a simple surface. Live discovery describes 295 routes across 20 modules, including 23 observability routes, under one key. Its practical advantage here is one REST API, one key, and one bill for the covered backend capabilities, with plain HTTP and no SDK required. That lets a team inspect the contract before writing capture code instead of guessing a payload shape. It also means the same interface can cover adjacent backend capabilities without adding a second client library to this workflow.

My recommendation is narrow: try this unified API for the capture leg when one REST contract should cover checkout errors and adjacent backend capabilities, and when your team is willing to own polling-based alert decisions. Choose Sentry, Datadog, or Rollbar when specialist release workflows, alert routing, trace exploration, or replay are the acceptance criteria.

How do you integrate Node.js error tracking using a backend API?

Put the capture call in the catch path or an error event listener after the checkout operation has reached its own failure decision. The example below keeps telemetry bounded, uses the documented capture route, reads the key from the environment, checks response bodies, and retries a rate-limited request with an idempotency key derived from the event identity.

type CheckoutFailure = {
  eventId: string;
  message: string;
  stack?: string;
  timestamp: string;
  userId?: string;
  checkoutId: string;
  release: string;
  failureClass: string;
};

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

export async function captureCheckoutFailure(
  failure: CheckoutFailure,
): Promise<void> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/capture", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": failure.eventId,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(failure),
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2500),
    });

    if (response.ok) return;

    const responseText = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 2) {
      throw new Error(`Capture failed (${response.status}): ${responseText}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
}

export async function recordCheckoutFailure(
  cause: unknown,
  checkoutId: string,
  userId: string | undefined,
): Promise<void> {
  const error = cause instanceof Error ? cause : new Error(String(cause));
  const eventId = `${checkoutId}:${process.env.RELEASE ?? "unknown"}:${error.name}`;

  await captureCheckoutFailure({
    eventId,
    message: error.message,
    stack: error.stack,
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
    userId,
    checkoutId,
    release: process.env.RELEASE ?? "unknown",
    failureClass: error.name,
  });
}

The Idempotency-Key protects the capture retry from becoming an operational duplicate. It does not make the payment operation safe to repeat. The 2,500 ms timeout is a deliberate ceiling for telemetry work, not a payment SLA. Keep the charge call outside this retry loop, and decide whether capture failure should be logged locally, queued for later, or surfaced to the service owner. The customer-facing payment result should already be determined.

Redaction belongs before serialization. Do not put card numbers, payment tokens, full request bodies, or unnecessary personal data in the event. A user identifier helps with correlation, but it is still personal data and needs a retention policy.

What does a reproducible comparison actually test?

Run the same versioned fixture through the unified API, Sentry, Datadog, and Rollbar only where each product supports the same event meaning. Keep the inputs constant. Record pass or fail, fixture version, and date. This is an integration evaluation, not a latency or uptime benchmark; the available facts do not establish those measurements.

For each event, verify four things: the release is searchable, the checkout is identifiable without payment secrets, a repeated capture remains operationally idempotent, and the resulting record contains enough context to choose rollback or continuation. Then test the unpleasant cases: a 429, a malformed response, a timeout, and a backend outage. The checkout path must retain its original outcome in all four.

This is where the products separate. A specialist error platform may pass the release-debugging test while requiring a separate path for inference metadata. A broad operational platform may pass alert and correlation requirements while demanding more configuration than a small service wants to own. A plain REST surface may minimize client integration work while leaving alert evaluation to the application team.

The decision rule is therefore simple: select the smallest option that passes every rollback criterion and whose missing capabilities are outside the current incident process. Do not select an option because it has the shortest capture snippet.

Limits that change the choice

The main limitation of the unified API leg is that it is not a complete incident-management system. There is no alert or notification route for threshold rules, phone, SMS, or webhook delivery, so a team needing that behavior must poll a query API and build the decision loop or pair this capture path with a specialist. There is no distributed trace query or span tree; trace_id and span_id fields can help correlate records, but they do not provide trace navigation. That is the central trade-off: less client integration work in exchange for more application-owned alert policy.

It also does not provide source-map deobfuscation, crash symbolication, Session Replay, synthetic uptime checks, or heartbeat monitoring. Silent failures such as “the scheduled task did not run” need a Healthchecks-class tool. Flags have no change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, or deletion recovery. Logs have no user-deletion interface, bulk export, or subscription interface, which matters for privacy and retention requirements.

Those are decision boundaries, not footnotes. If the rollback process depends on replay, symbolication, or push alerts, use the specialist that passes those tests. Teams should try Infrai when the immediate job is consistent backend error capture plus adjacent backend calls through one REST contract, and when they accept owning polling-based alert decisions. If that boundary fits your system, start with the Node.js Express error-tracking capture guide.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • OpenTelemetry, “Logs signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • Sentry, “Error Monitoring”: https://sentry.io/for/error-monitoring/
  • Datadog, “Error Tracking”: https://docs.datadoghq.com/tracing/error_tracking/
  • Rollbar, “Error Monitoring”: https://rollbar.com/platform/error-monitoring/

title: Generated Image Buffers: Private S3-Compatible Object Storage Upload and Access
description:
Short answer: In a Node.js backend, save each OpenAI-generated image buffer with one upload to private S3-compatible object storage, then persist only its immutable object key and metadata; grant access after the application authorizes the reader.

For a marketplace that stores AI-generated training artifacts, the main trade-off isn't the mechanics of moving bytes. It is access control versus delivery simplicity. Browser-to-bucket upload looks direct, but it puts CORS policy in the critical path and makes credential handling harder to audit. A backend-to-storage write keeps the credential on the server and gives the application one place to enforce tenant ownership, retention, and deletion rules.

The result is deliberately boring. That's good.

How should Node.js save an OpenAI-generated image buffer for private object storage access?

Treat the generated image as an opaque byte buffer. The backend receives or decodes those bytes, chooses a content type, creates a unique key, uploads once, and commits a database row only after the write succeeds. The row should contain the key, marketplace tenant, generation job, content type, generator label, creation time, and retention deadline. It should not contain the image body or a permanent URL.

A useful key is generations/{userId}/{date}/{jobId}.png. Prefixes make listing and deletion predictable: an operator can enumerate one user's artifacts or one date without asking object metadata to behave like a database index. Metadata can still carry content type or generator information, but server-side listing filters by prefix rather than metadata queries. Keep searchable and compliance-relevant fields in the database.

Use a fresh jobId for every successful generation, including a rerun. There is no object versioning, object lock, or conditional If-Match write in this storage model, so overwriting a familiar name such as latest.png creates ambiguity under concurrent workers and removes the recovery path after an accidental replacement. Unique keys turn a retry into the same intended write and turn a regenerated artifact into a new record.

Here is the upload boundary in Python. A Node.js service follows the same HTTP contract with its Buffer; the important details are the raw bytes, an explicit method, server-side credentials, a stable idempotency key, status checking, and patient handling of HTTP 429.

import os
import time
from datetime import date
from urllib.parse import quote

import requests

BASE_URL = os.environ["STORAGE_API_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
BUCKET = "marketplace-training"


def upload_generated_image(
    image_buffer: bytes,
    user_id: str,
    job_id: str,
    generator: str,
) -> dict[str, str]:
    if not image_buffer:
        raise ValueError("image_buffer must contain generated image bytes")

    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    created_on = date.today().isoformat()
    key = f"generations/{user_id}/{created_on}/{job_id}.png"
    bucket_path = quote(BUCKET, safe="")
    key_path = quote(key, safe="")
    url = f"{BASE_URL}/storage/object/put/{bucket_path}/{key_path}"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "image/png",
        "Idempotency-Key": f"generation:{user_id}:{job_id}",
    }

    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(
            method="PUT",
            url=url,
            headers=headers,
            data=image_buffer,
            timeout=60,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429 and attempt < 4:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay_seconds = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay_seconds)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"image upload returned HTTP {response.status_code}: {response.text[:300]}"
            )

        return {
            "storage_key": key,
            "content_type": "image/png",
            "generator": generator,
            "created_on": created_on,
        }

    raise RuntimeError("image upload remained rate limited after five attempts")

The returned dictionary is the database payload, not proof of a public object. The bucket and object remain private. A read path should authenticate the marketplace user first and then provide time-limited access rather than persist a public link; never attach the platform Bearer token to a returned presigned URL. The signature itself is the access credential.

Don't make the client guess.

Validate the media type and size before this function, then write the returned record in the same application workflow that marks the generation job complete. If the database commit fails after the object write, the deterministic key and idempotency key let a worker retry the intended upload without manufacturing a second filename. A scheduled cleanup can later compare the generation prefix with committed records and remove unreferenced artifacts according to policy.

Implement deletion as a two-clock state machine

A reproducible retention policy needs two clocks. The database records when an artifact becomes eligible for deletion; object-storage lifecycle provides a coarse backstop. Here, lifecycle expiry has a minimum of one day, so it cannot enforce an hourly training-artifact window. If a marketplace promises deletion within hours, an application worker must select due database rows, delete their unique keys, and record the outcome. The lifecycle rule can remain as defense against missed application work, but it isn't the primary timer.

This separation also helps with consent and moderation. A filename tells you where bytes live. The database tells you why they exist, which user controls them, which training run referenced them, and when policy says they should disappear. Stuffing those answers into object metadata is tempting — one write, one apparent source of truth — but metadata isn't searchable on the server in this model. A prefix list can find generations/user-42/2026-08-14/; it cannot answer “show artifacts from generator X whose retention expires before midnight.”

There is a sharper edge for regulated training data. No object versioning or object lock means this pattern is not suitable for WORM retention or a financial-grade immutable archive. Stick with an external storage solution that supplies the required immutability controls when legal hold or recovery from overwrite is non-negotiable. Likewise, strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database because conditional writes are unavailable.

I'm not sure every team needs cross-region replication for generated marketplace images; the answer depends on its recovery objective and data-placement obligations. What is clear is that this surface does not provide automatic cross-region replication or a cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Its covered storage vendors are R2, S3, OSS, and COS, not GCS or B2. If either excluded provider or automated migration is a fixed requirement, use that provider directly and design the exit path before the first production object.

One day is coarse. Policy language shouldn't pretend otherwise.

Retry failure defines the delivery ceiling

Provider selection should follow the artifact contract. Start with private access, immutable names, prefix listing, deletion granularity, recovery requirements, and the actual runtime that performs the upload. Then compare operating surface. A marketplace already standardized on Amazon S3 or Cloudflare R2 may gain little by adding an abstraction. A team required to use Backblaze B2 should call B2 directly because it is outside Infrai's vendor coverage. A team that wants to operate its own storage can evaluate MinIO, accepting that self-management becomes part of the job.

Option Sensible shortlist condition Reason to choose another path
Amazon S3 The marketplace already owns an S3 integration and its credential controls Another contract would add operating surface without simplifying delivery
Cloudflare R2 R2 is already the approved object destination The workload must remain with a different mandated provider
Backblaze B2 B2 itself is a firm storage requirement A unified layer is required and cannot route to B2
MinIO Self-managed object storage is an explicit organizational choice The team does not want storage operations in its ownership boundary
Infrai Private artifacts benefit from plain HTTP and a consistent backend contract Public hosting, WORM, native GCS/B2 routing, or automatic cross-cloud migration is required

Infrai fits the middle lane: a team wants private object writes through one REST API, without installing another storage SDK, and expects to add other backend capabilities behind the same consistent contract. Infrai uses one credential across 295 routes in 20 modules, so the marketplace's storage worker can share the established authentication and billing boundary instead of adding a separate key and invoice. The supporting advantage here is discoverability: its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas and provides runnable examples before a key is supplied.

The catch is real. Infrai has no public or public-read ACL, and public_url stays null. That is appropriate for authenticated training artifacts but a poor fit for static-site hosting, a permanent image CDN link, or a public image host. Browser-direct upload also deserves an early proof because bucket CORS configuration is not available as an independent self-service route. Keep the upload behind the backend when predictable credential and origin handling matters more than shaving one hop.

Access control wins here, at the cost of simpler public delivery.

Rollout by one dated prefix

Start with one tenant and one dated prefix. Upload a generated image through the backend, persist its key and retention deadline, confirm an authorized read path, and list by prefix to verify that the naming rule is observable. Then run deletion against synthetic expired records after the promised interval. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes, so this validation needs an account eligible for storage writes.

Do not rewrite legacy objects just to make every key pretty. New generations can adopt the immutable convention immediately while existing rows keep their current pointers. A reader can resolve both forms during a bounded transition, and a cleanup worker can process old and new prefixes separately. This rollout makes rollback small: stop new writes, leave existing object keys intact, and keep the database as the authority for retention state.

Before widening the rollout, test a rate-limited retry, two workers receiving the same generation job, a database commit retry, a one-day lifecycle boundary, and an unauthorized download attempt. Also decide who owns abandoned multipart fragments if future image artifacts become large enough for multipart upload, because there is no automatic fragment cleanup rule. These checks are less glamorous than a storage benchmark, but they map directly to duplicate artifacts, privacy exposure, and deletion commitments.

For this marketplace, the decision rule is compact: choose the backend buffer upload and private key pattern when training artifacts must be access-controlled and policy-driven; stay with a direct incumbent when its native controls or provider mandate outweigh integration simplicity; choose an immutable external store when overwrite recovery or WORM is part of the contract.

References

  • MDN, Content-Disposition response header: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • Backblaze B2 pricing and service overview: https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage/pricing

title: Modern Web Guidance (MWG): Google Chrome's Gold Standard for Modern Web Implementation
description:
TL;DR: Modern Web Guidance (MWG) is an official skill pack + CLI from the Google Chrome team that embeds web platform best practices and browser compatibility data directly into the workflow of developers and AI coding agents. It's not about content strategy. It's about writing modern web code the right way.

1. What Is Modern Web Guidance?

Modern Web Guidance (MWG) is a curated collection of technical implementation guides for modern web features, maintained in the GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance repository. It was introduced at Google I/O 2026, released under the Apache 2.0 license, and is backed by the Google Chrome team, the Microsoft Edge team, and the web developer community.

Its core goal: stop developers (and especially AI coding agents) from generating outdated JavaScript patterns and hacky workarounds, and steer them toward native HTML/CSS APIs that are secure, performant, and match your browser support target.

2. Installation

The recommended path is the interactive wizard:

npx modern-web-guidance@latest install

Or install it for a specific agent:

Agent / Tool Command
Claude Code /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance → /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome → /reload-plugins
GitHub Copilot CLI /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance → /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome
Gemini CLI gemini extensions install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance --auto-update
Antigravity CLI agy plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance
GitHub CLI gh skill install GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance
Vercel Skills npx skills add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance

The npm package is self-contained with no extra dependencies, which keeps latency low and reduces supply-chain risk.

3. Core CLI Commands 

# Search for relevant guides
npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest search "<query>" --skill-version <version>

# Retrieve the full guide (comma-separate multiple IDs)
npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "<id>"

# List every available guide
npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest list

Windows tip: if npx fails, use npx.cmd instead.

4. When You Should Use It

Check MWG at these three moments:

  1. Before implementing any web feature.
  2. Before building a new component, to see whether a standard pattern already exists.
  3. Whenever you're tempted to write an ad-hoc solution or pull in a heavy dependency you don't really need.

5. The Three-Step Workflow

Step 1: Search

Use action-oriented queries (describe what you want to achieve, not just a feature name):

npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest search "optimize largest contentful paint image loading" --skill-version 2026_05_16-c5e7870

The output is JSON containing id, description, category, featuresUsed, and similarity. If every similarity score is low (< 0.5) or the result is empty, treat it as not relevant and browse manually with list.

Step 2: Retrieve

Fetch the full guide using an id from the search results:

npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "optimize-image-priority"

Step 3: Adapt

Guides are framework-agnostic. Adapt the code samples to your stack (React, Vue, vanilla JS, etc.), and always check the fallback and browser support sections before shipping.

6. How the Guides Work

  • Framework-agnostic: you adapt them to your stack.
  • Baseline-aware: every guide states its browser support status using Baseline. With no explicit config, MWG defaults to Baseline Widely Available. If a feature isn't there yet, follow the guide's fallback recommendation, unless your project has its own browser support policy (e.g. "Safari 17.4+" or "no polyfills").
  • Declare your Baseline target in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, for example: This project's Baseline target is Baseline 2024. That lets your agent use newer features while still generating fallbacks for older browsers.
  • Treat it as your project's preferred standard: don't ignore it, and don't make up what it says.

7. What's Covered

MWG ships 100+ expert-verified use cases spanning more than a hundred web platform features, grouped into these categories:

Category What's inside
accessibility Semantic HTML, focus management, ARIA, form accessibility
built-in-ai On-device browser AI: Prompt API, Summarizer, Translator, Language Detector
canvas WebGL shaders, exporting media from canvas, HTML in 3D scenes
css Scrollbar styling, dark mode, clip-path, container-based styling
css-layout Flexbox, grid, subgrid, container queries, anchor positioning, fluid scaling
datetime Duration math, time zones, recurring intervals, non-Gregorian calendars
forms Autofill (address/payment/sign-in), custom select, validation after interaction
html Dialog/Popover/Details APIs, invoker commands, resource prioritization
motion View transitions, physics-based easing, cross-document transitions
overlays Dialogs, popovers, tooltips, navigation drawers, context menus
passkeys WebAuthn: registration, authentication, passkey management
performance Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS), long tasks, image/script priority
privacy Data minimization, third-party audits, security headers
scroll Scroll-snap, parallax, scrollytelling, infinite scroll UX
security XSS, CSP, cookies, Cross-Origin Isolation
typography Stable font fallbacks, text balancing, precise alignment
webmcp Exposing client-side functions as tools for AI agents (Web Model Context Protocol)

There's also a separate skill for Chrome Extensions (Manifest V3), which you can select with npx modern-web-guidance@latest install --choose.

8. Why Use It

  • No reinventing the wheel: technical patterns (accessibility, performance, form validation, and more) are already curated by the Chrome team.
  • Fewer common bugs: guides cover the edge cases people usually miss. For example, autofill-address-form prevents wrong autocomplete attributes, and required-field-feedback stops errors from showing before the user has even interacted.
  • Lighter bundles: it pushes you toward native browser features instead of large libraries.
  • Cross-browser safety: every guide lists its Baseline status and fallbacks.
  • Consistency across projects and teams: one shared standard instead of everyone's personal style.
  • Measurable impact: Google's internal benchmark showed roughly a 37 percentage point improvement in agents' adherence to web best practices when equipped with MWG.

9. What Goes Wrong Without It

  • Repeated ad-hoc solutions: every developer or agent solves the same problem (custom select, dialog, form validation) differently, which makes the codebase inconsistent and hard to maintain.
  • Dependency bloat: installing a big library when the browser already has a native API (e.g. a dialog library when <dialog> does the job).
  • Missing native features: falling behind on more efficient, safer APIs (Popover API, View Transitions, on-device Prompt API) that are already Baseline.
  • Accessibility and security regressions: critical details like ARIA, focus management, CSP, XSS prevention, and autofill attributes slip through quick testing but hurt real users.
  • Ignored fallbacks: cutting-edge features without fallbacks break on older Safari or minority browsers, and you only find out when users complain.

10. A Note on Scope: MWG Is Not an SEO Tool

MWG is about code implementation (performance, accessibility, layout, security), not content strategy or SEO/GEO. At the time of writing, it doesn't include a dedicated guide for structured data / schema.org (searches return similarity scores below 0.4). For JSON-LD and schema markup, go straight to schema.org.

11. Keeping It Updated

The examples in this post use version 2026_05_16-c5e7870. The CLI warns you automatically when a newer version is available. See the updating instructions in the repo.

Resources

  • GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance on GitHub
  • Modern Web Guidance on Chrome for Developers

Have you tried MWG with your coding agent yet? I'd love to hear how it changed the code it writes.

title: Houdini GLB to USDZ with Blender, Three.js and Three-Live
description:
Originally published by Alicia Lu on 5 November 2026 at Digital Garden. Alicia is a 3D technical artist, TA and independent developer. Codex assisted with this study.

I converted the same textured Houdini plant with Three.js r187, Three-Live 1.2.3 and Blender 5.2 LTS. All three exports reopened in Houdini with 1,056 triangles. Blender preserved the original world bounds, two textures and the double-sided leaves. Three.js preserved the bounds and textures. Three-Live produced the smallest package, with a shifted bounding box and no linked textures.

One input and three export paths

The 947,652-byte input is the owned 512-pixel GLB from the Copernicus bake study. It has 628 vertices, 1,056 triangles, a normal map, a packed occlusion-roughness-metallic map and a double-sided material.

  • Three.js r187. In Chrome 156 on an RTX 5070 Ti, I loaded the GLB with GLTFLoader and ran USDZExporter with maxTextureSize 1024. I exported three times per Quick Look option.
  • Three-Live 1.2.3. The verified Windows x64 CLI read the same GLB and exported USDZ directly.
  • Blender 5.2.0 LTS. A factory-startup background session imported the same GLB and exported a Y-up, meter-scale USDZ with USD Preview Surface. A fresh Blender scene then imported the USDZ, recovering 628 vertices, 1,056 faces and two packed images. 
three-live-cli.exe convert input/houdini-plant.glb -f usdz -o evidence/plant-three-live.usdz
blender --background --factory-startup --python-exit-code 2 --python export_blender.py

const { scene } = await new GLTFLoader().loadAsync('/input/houdini-plant.glb');
const bytes = await new USDZExporter().parseAsync(scene, {
  quickLookCompatible: true,
  maxTextureSize: 1024
});

What survived when I reopened the packages

Path USDZ bytes Stored ZIP members Resolved image files Points / triangles Double-sided World Y range (m)
Three-Live 1.2.3 66,910 1 0 628 / 1,056 false −0.9923 to 1.1887
Three.js r187, option off 364,858 4 2 628 / 1,056 false 0.0000 to 2.0287
Three.js r187, option on 364,858 4 2 628 / 1,056 false 0.0000 to 2.0287
Blender 5.2 LTS, Y up 957,384 3 2 628 / 1,056 true 0.0000 to 2.0287

Houdini 22.0.429's OpenUSD 0.26.5 reopened all four packages. All entries passed CRC, store-method and 64-byte alignment checks. Each stage declared Y up and one meter per unit. Three.js and Blender preserved the GLB world bounds to within 0.000001 m per component. The Three-Live file had one USDA layer and a bound UsdPreviewSurface with no linked texture files.

The Blender package used a binary USDC layer and two PNG textures. Its normal PNG accounts for most of its 957,384 bytes. The result supports a desktop handoff where the leaf backs and floor position matter. The smaller Three.js result is another candidate when the mesh's single-sided export is acceptable for the intended camera.

What the Quick Look option changed on this plant

All six Three.js exports were byte-identical, across both settings. The exporter warned about the double-sided input in each run. Every Three.js USD mesh reopened with doubleSided false. The result is specific to this asset and exporter build.

The included device checklist links the saved USDZ files. A physical iPhone can then check texture appearance, back-facing leaves, initial scale and placement. This release reports the desktop export and reopen. Apple documents the device playback path separately. Apple Quick Look, Three.js USDZExporter, Three-Live 1.2.3, Blender USD manual.

Alicia is a 3D technical artist, TA and independent developer. Codex assisted with the test harness, evidence checks and editing.

Related studies

  • Houdini Copernicus bake for Three.js
  • Houdini USD vs glTF for Three.js

Data and reproduction

  • openusd.json
  • blender-reopen.json
  • three-usdz-desktop-reproduction.zip

title: 서비스 중단 없이 데이터베이스 구조를 변경하는 방법: Expand–Migrate–Contract 설계
description:
운영 중인 웹서비스에서 데이터베이스 구조를 변경하는 작업은 생각보다 위험하다.

개발 환경에서는 컬럼 이름을 변경하고 애플리케이션 코드를 수정한 다음 다시 실행하면 끝나는 경우가 많다.

하지만 프로덕션 환경은 다르다.

기존 버전의 애플리케이션이 계속 요청을 처리하고 있을 수 있고, 여러 서버가 서로 다른 시점에 배포될 수도 있다. 백그라운드 작업자나 예약 작업이 여전히 이전 데이터 구조를 참조하고 있을 가능성도 있다.

이 상황에서 기존 컬럼을 바로 삭제하면 어떤 일이 발생할까?

새로운 애플리케이션은 정상적으로 작동하더라도 이전 버전의 서버에서는 데이터베이스 오류가 발생할 수 있다.

이번 글에서는 운영 중인 웹서비스를 중단하지 않고 데이터베이스 구조를 변경하기 위해 사용할 수 있는 Expand–Migrate–Contract 패턴을 살펴본다.

특히 PostgreSQL 기반 서비스를 예시로 실제 배포 과정과 실패 시나리오를 정리한다.

1. 데이터베이스 변경이 서비스 장애로 이어지는 이유

먼저 웹사이트 정보를 저장하는 간단한 데이터베이스 테이블을 생각해 보자.

CREATE TABLE sites (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    url TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

애플리케이션은 url 컬럼에 저장된 주소를 조회해 사용자에게 제공한다.

SELECT id, name, url
FROM sites
WHERE id = 100;

그런데 서비스 구조를 개선하면서 url 컬럼 이름을 destination_url로 변경하기로 결정했다.

개발자가 다음 SQL을 실행했다고 가정해 보자.

ALTER TABLE sites
RENAME COLUMN url TO destination_url;

데이터베이스의 컬럼 이름은 변경된다.

문제는 기존 애플리케이션이다.

기존 서버가 여전히 다음 쿼리를 실행하면 오류가 발생한다.

SELECT url FROM sites WHERE id = 100;

PostgreSQL에서는 존재하지 않는 컬럼을 참조했기 때문에 오류를 반환한다.

즉, 데이터베이스 변경 자체는 성공했지만 서비스는 정상적으로 작동하지 않을 수 있다.

배포 시점에 발생하는 버전 충돌 

[Application V1]
      |
      | SELECT url
      v
 [Database V2]
      |
      v
[컬럼 없음 오류]

이 문제는 배포 순서와 관련이 있다.

  • 데이터베이스를 먼저 변경하면 기존 애플리케이션이 실패할 수 있다.
  • 애플리케이션을 먼저 변경하면 새로운 코드가 아직 없는 컬럼을 참조할 수 있다.
  • 여러 서버를 순차적으로 배포하면 이전 코드와 새로운 코드가 동시에 실행될 수 있다.

따라서 데이터베이스 구조 변경은 애플리케이션 배포와 분리해 설계해야 한다.

2. Expand–Migrate–Contract 패턴이란?

Expand–Migrate–Contract는 기존 구조를 즉시 제거하지 않고 새로운 구조를 단계적으로 도입하는 방법이다.

핵심은 일정 기간 기존 구조와 새로운 구조를 동시에 지원하는 것이다.

세 단계는 다음과 같다.

단계 작업 목적
Expand 새로운 컬럼이나 테이블 추가 기존 코드와 신규 코드의 호환성 확보
Migrate 데이터 이전 및 애플리케이션 전환 새로운 구조로 점진적 이동
Contract 사용하지 않는 기존 구조 제거 최종 구조 정리

전체적인 흐름은 다음과 같다.

[기존 데이터베이스]
        |
        v
      EXPAND
        |
        v
[기존 컬럼 + 신규 컬럼]
        |
        v
      MIGRATE
        |
        v
[데이터 이전 + 코드 전환]
        |
        v
      CONTRACT
        |
        v
[신규 컬럼만 유지]

여기서 중요한 것은 세 단계 사이에 충분한 검증 시간을 두는 것이다.

모든 작업을 한 번의 배포에서 끝낼 필요는 없다.

오히려 각각을 독립적으로 배포하고 검증하는 편이 장애 위험을 줄이는 데 도움이 된다.

단, 이 패턴을 사용한다고 모든 데이터베이스 변경이 자동으로 무중단 처리되는 것은 아니다.

DDL 작업의 잠금, 데이터 규모, 애플리케이션 동작, 배포 환경 등을 함께 검토해야 한다.

3. Expand: 기존 컬럼을 유지하면서 새 컬럼 추가하기

첫 번째 단계에서는 기존 url 컬럼을 삭제하지 않는다.

대신 새로운 destination_url 컬럼을 추가한다.

ALTER TABLE sites
ADD COLUMN destination_url TEXT;

변경 후 테이블은 다음 구조를 갖는다.

sites
├── id
├── name
├── url
├── destination_url
└── created_at

기존 애플리케이션은 여전히 url을 사용할 수 있다.

새로운 애플리케이션은 destination_url을 사용할 준비를 할 수 있다.

왜 처음부터 NOT NULL을 설정하지 않을까?

기존 데이터에는 새로운 컬럼 값이 존재하지 않기 때문이다.

기존 행이 있는 테이블에 값을 준비하지 않은 상태로 NOT NULL 제약을 추가하면 문제가 발생할 수 있다.

우선 nullable 컬럼으로 추가하고, 데이터를 이전한 뒤 제약을 강화하는 방식이 일반적으로 안전하다.

하지만 새로운 컬럼을 추가하는 SQL도 테이블 잠금과 관련이 있다.

PostgreSQL의 ALTER TABLE은 작업 유형에 따라 서로 다른 잠금 수준을 요구한다.

따라서 단순한 컬럼 추가라도 운영 환경에서 잠금 대기 시간이 발생할 수 있다.

운영 시 주의사항

  • 트래픽이 높은 시간대인지 확인한다.
  • 오래 실행되는 트랜잭션이 있는지 점검한다.
  • 변경 쿼리의 잠금 특성을 확인한다.
  • 실제 데이터 규모에 가까운 환경에서 미리 테스트한다.
  • 백업과 복구 절차를 준비한다.

4. Migrate 1단계: 신규 데이터부터 이중 쓰기 적용하기

새로운 컬럼이 생성됐다고 해서 모든 데이터가 자동으로 이전되는 것은 아니다.

먼저 새롭게 발생하는 쓰기 작업이 두 컬럼을 동시에 갱신하도록 변경한다.

이를 Dual Write라고 한다.

          [Application V2]
                  |
                  v
            [DB Transaction]
               /      \
              v        v
           [url]  [destination_url]
               \      /
                v    v
             [Commit]

예를 들어 다음과 같은 SQL을 사용할 수 있다.

BEGIN;

UPDATE sites
SET
    url = 'https://example.com',
    destination_url = 'https://example.com'
WHERE id = 100;

COMMIT;

두 컬럼을 하나의 데이터베이스 트랜잭션에서 갱신하면 둘 중 하나만 저장되는 문제를 줄일 수 있다.

다만 모든 쓰기 경로가 이 규칙을 따라야 한다.

예를 들어 관리자 페이지는 두 컬럼을 갱신하지만 백그라운드 작업자는 기존 url만 갱신한다면 데이터가 다시 불일치할 수 있다.

또한 순차 배포 중에는 이전 버전 서버가 잠시 남아 있을 수 있다.

따라서 이중 쓰기 코드 배포 직후부터 두 컬럼이 항상 일치한다고 가정해서는 안 된다.

반드시 확인해야 할 쓰기 경로

  • 웹사이트 등록 API
  • 웹사이트 수정 API
  • 관리자 페이지
  • 예약 작업
  • 데이터 가져오기 작업
  • 외부 시스템 연동
  • 백그라운드 Worker

모든 쓰기 경로가 전환되었는지 확인한 뒤 기존 데이터 이전을 진행하는 것이 안전하다.

5. Migrate 2단계: 기존 데이터를 점진적으로 이전하기

이제 기존 url 데이터를 새로운 destination_url 컬럼으로 복사한다.

데이터가 적다면 다음 SQL로도 가능하다.

UPDATE sites
SET destination_url = url
WHERE destination_url IS NULL;

하지만 운영 중인 테이블에 수백만 건의 데이터가 있다면 한 번의 대규모 UPDATE는 부담이 될 수 있다.

많은 행을 동시에 수정하면 트랜잭션이 길어지고, WAL 생성량과 디스크 사용량이 증가하며, 다른 작업과의 잠금 경합도 발생할 수 있다.

따라서 대규모 데이터에서는 배치 처리(Backfill)를 고려한다.

PostgreSQL 배치 업데이트 예시 

WITH batch AS (
    SELECT id
    FROM sites
    WHERE destination_url IS NULL
    ORDER BY id
    LIMIT 500
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE sites AS s
SET destination_url = s.url
FROM batch
WHERE s.id = batch.id;

이 SQL은 한 번에 최대 500개 행을 선택해 처리한다.

SKIP LOCKED를 사용하면 다른 트랜잭션이 잠근 행을 기다리지 않고 건너뛸 수 있다.

다만 이 예시는 모든 쓰기 경로의 이중 쓰기 전환이 완료됐다는 전제를 가진다.

그리고 SKIP LOCKED로 건너뛴 행은 이후 반복 실행에서 다시 처리해야 한다.

실제 운영에서는 다음 사항을 고려한다.

  1. 배치 크기를 설정한다.
  2. 배치마다 짧게 트랜잭션을 완료한다.
  3. 데이터베이스 부하를 관찰한다.
  4. 미처리 행이 남아 있는지 반복 확인한다.
  5. 마지막에 누락 데이터와 불일치를 검증한다.

이전 완료 여부 확인 

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM sites
WHERE destination_url IS NULL;

이 값이 0이면 NULL 상태로 남은 데이터가 없다는 뜻이다.

그러나 두 컬럼의 값이 일치한다는 뜻은 아니다.

정확한 비교를 위해 다음 쿼리를 사용할 수 있다.

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM sites
WHERE url IS DISTINCT FROM destination_url;

IS DISTINCT FROM은 NULL까지 고려해 두 값을 비교한다.

최종 목표는 두 컬럼의 불일치 건수가 0이 되는 것이다.

이중 쓰기와 데이터 이전 과정에서 불일치가 발견되면 해당 행을 재검증하고 복구해야 한다.

6. Migrate 3단계: 읽기 경로를 새로운 컬럼으로 전환하기

데이터 이전이 끝났다면 애플리케이션이 새로운 컬럼을 읽도록 변경할 수 있다.

하지만 모든 서버를 한 번에 전환할 필요는 없다.

Feature Flag를 이용하면 새로운 읽기 경로를 단계적으로 적용할 수 있다.

읽기 경로 예시 

def get_site_url(site, use_new_column):
    if use_new_column:
        return site["destination_url"]

    return site["url"]

이 예시에서는 use_new_column의 값에 따라 서로 다른 컬럼을 사용한다.

실제 운영에서는 애플리케이션 설정이나 Feature Flag 시스템과 연결할 수 있다.

단계별 전환 전략 

[기존 읽기 100%]
        |
        v
[신규 읽기 일부 적용]
        |
        v
[오류율 및 데이터 일치 확인]
        |
        v
[신규 읽기 확대]
        |
        v
[신규 읽기 100%]

이 과정에서는 다음 지표를 확인해야 한다.

  • 데이터 조회 오류율
  • 응답 지연 시간
  • NULL 데이터 발생 여부
  • 구버전과 신버전의 결과 불일치
  • 데이터베이스 쿼리 성능

특히 신규 컬럼 읽기를 확대하는 동안에도 기존 컬럼에 대한 이중 쓰기를 유지해야 한다.

그래야 애플리케이션을 이전 버전으로 되돌려야 하는 상황에 대응하기 쉽다.

7. Contract: 기존 컬럼을 제거하기 전 확인할 사항

신규 컬럼으로 읽기와 쓰기 전환이 완료되었다고 해서 기존 컬럼을 즉시 삭제하면 안 된다.

운영 중인 시스템에는 이전 코드를 사용하는 프로세스가 남아 있을 수 있기 때문이다.

대표적으로 다음 요소를 확인해야 한다.

  • 이전 버전의 API 서버
  • 배포가 늦어진 백그라운드 Worker
  • 오래 실행되는 예약 작업
  • 외부 데이터 처리 프로그램
  • 데이터 분석용 SQL
  • 이전 버전으로 되돌리는 롤백 절차

삭제 전 점검 순서 

[신규 컬럼 전환 완료]
          |
          v
[구버전 프로세스 존재 여부 확인]
          |
          v
[기존 컬럼 참조 코드 검색]
          |
          v
[데이터 일관성 검증]
          |
          v
[백업 및 복구 가능성 확인]
          |
          v
[기존 컬럼 제거]

이전 버전과의 호환성이 더 이상 필요하지 않다는 것을 검증한 후 기존 컬럼을 제거한다.

ALTER TABLE sites
DROP COLUMN url;

이 작업 이후에는 이전 컬럼을 사용하는 애플리케이션으로 단순 롤백할 수 없게 된다.

따라서 Contract 단계는 Expand나 Migrate 단계보다 더 신중하게 진행해야 한다.

실제 운영에서는 기존 컬럼을 제거하는 작업을 별도 배포로 분리하는 것이 적절하다.

8. 실패 시나리오: 배포 중간에 문제가 생기면?

서비스 중단 없는 마이그레이션을 설계할 때 중요한 것은 정상 경로만 고려하지 않는 것이다.

각 단계에서 실패했을 때 어디까지 되돌릴 수 있는지 정의해야 한다.

시나리오 A: 신규 컬럼 추가가 실패한 경우

Expand 단계에서 DDL 작업이 실패했다면 신규 코드를 배포하지 않는다.

데이터베이스 상태를 확인하고 잠금이나 제약 조건 문제를 해결한 뒤 다시 시도한다.

시나리오 B: 데이터 이전 중 Worker가 종료된 경우

배치 처리 도중 Worker가 종료되었다면 마지막으로 커밋된 상태부터 미처리 데이터를 확인한다.

일반적으로 배치마다 독립적으로 커밋하고, 다시 실행해도 안전한 방식으로 설계하는 것이 좋다.

이 예시에서는 destination_url IS NULL 조건을 사용하므로 이미 값이 채워진 행을 반복적으로 갱신하지 않는다.

다만 데이터 불일치까지 자동으로 해결하는 것은 아니므로 별도의 검증 작업이 필요하다.

시나리오 C: 신규 읽기에서 오류가 증가한 경우

새로운 컬럼을 읽는 과정에서 오류가 발생하면 Feature Flag를 통해 기존 읽기 경로로 되돌릴 수 있다.

이때 기존 컬럼에 대한 쓰기가 계속 유지되어야 한다.

[신규 읽기 활성화]
         |
         v
[오류율 증가 감지]
         |
         v
[기존 읽기로 전환]
         |
         v
[문제 분석 및 수정]

시나리오 D: 기존 컬럼을 삭제한 뒤 롤백이 필요한 경우

Contract 단계에서 기존 컬럼을 이미 삭제했다면 상황이 복잡해진다.

이전 애플리케이션은 삭제된 컬럼을 참조할 수 있다.

이 경우 단순한 코드 롤백만으로 문제를 해결할 수 없다.

필요하면 새로운 컬럼을 이용해 이전 호환 구조를 복원하는 별도의 마이그레이션이 필요하다.

따라서 이전 버전의 애플리케이션이 다시 실행될 가능성이 있는 동안에는 기존 컬럼을 제거하지 않는 것이 중요하다.

9. PostgreSQL 잠금과 DDL 작업에서 주의할 점

Expand–Migrate–Contract 패턴이 애플리케이션 호환성 문제를 줄여주더라도 데이터베이스 수준의 잠금 문제가 사라지는 것은 아니다.

PostgreSQL에서는 ALTER TABLE의 세부 작업에 따라 서로 다른 잠금 수준이 적용된다.

예를 들어 일부 컬럼 추가 작업은 테이블 전체를 다시 작성하지 않고 처리할 수 있지만, 작업에 필요한 잠금은 여전히 고려해야 한다.

또한 컬럼의 데이터 타입을 변경하는 작업은 테이블 재작성이나 인덱스 재구축이 필요할 수 있다.

이 때문에 마이그레이션 실행 전에 실제 SQL이 어떤 작업을 수행하는지 확인해야 한다.

배포 전 검토 항목

검토 항목 확인 내용
테이블 크기 전체 행 수와 저장 용량
잠금 수준 읽기·쓰기 요청에 미치는 영향
데이터 변경량 UPDATE로 발생할 수 있는 부하
실행 시간 운영 환경에서 예상되는 처리 시간
롤백 전략 실패 시 이전 상태로 복구 가능한지
의존성 View, Trigger, 외래키, 외부 프로그램 영향

마이그레이션 도구가 SQL을 자동으로 생성하더라도 실제 실행되는 SQL을 검토하는 과정은 필요하다.

자동화된 도구가 프로덕션 환경의 모든 위험을 알아서 해결해 주는 것은 아니다.

10. 실무에서 사용할 수 있는 배포 순서

지금까지 설명한 내용을 실제 배포 순서로 정리하면 다음과 같다.

배포 1: Expand

  • 새 컬럼 추가
  • 기존 컬럼 유지
  • 이전 애플리케이션의 정상 동작 확인

배포 2: Dual Write

  • 새로운 코드에서 두 컬럼을 함께 기록
  • 모든 쓰기 경로가 전환됐는지 확인
  • 구버전 서버 및 Worker 종료 여부 확인

배포 3: Backfill

  • 기존 데이터 배치 이전
  • 데이터 불일치 검사
  • 미처리 행 재시도
  • 완료 후 최종 검증

배포 4: Read Switch

  • 새로운 컬럼 읽기 적용
  • 오류율 및 성능 점검
  • 문제가 발생하면 기존 읽기로 복구

배포 5: 신규 구조 안정화

  • 읽기와 쓰기를 새로운 컬럼 중심으로 통일
  • 이전 컬럼에 대한 쓰기 제거
  • 더 이상 구버전이 실행되지 않는지 확인

배포 6: Contract

  • 이전 컬럼 참조 제거 확인
  • 백업과 복구 절차 확인
  • 기존 컬럼 삭제
  • 최종 모니터링

위 순서는 예시이며 서비스 구조에 따라 여러 단계를 분리하거나 통합할 수 있다.

중요한 것은 각 단계가 검증 가능하고, 전환 도중에도 호환성이 유지되도록 설계하는 것이다.

11. 운영 환경 적용 전 체크리스트

스키마 변경

  • [ ] 변경 대상 테이블과 컬럼의 사용처를 확인했는가?
  • [ ] 기존 코드가 새 스키마에서도 정상 작동하는가?
  • [ ] 신규 컬럼의 NULL 허용 여부를 검토했는가?
  • [ ] DDL의 잠금 수준을 확인했는가?
  • [ ] 실제 규모의 데이터로 테스트했는가?

데이터 이전

  • [ ] 신규 쓰기 경로가 모두 전환되었는가?
  • [ ] Backfill 작업을 재실행해도 안전한가?
  • [ ] 대규모 트랜잭션을 피하도록 설계했는가?
  • [ ] 미처리 데이터와 불일치를 측정하는가?
  • [ ] 데이터 이전 완료 조건이 명확한가?

배포와 롤백

  • [ ] 구버전과 신버전이 일정 기간 공존할 수 있는가?
  • [ ] 신규 읽기를 단계적으로 적용할 수 있는가?
  • [ ] 장애 발생 시 이전 읽기 경로로 되돌릴 수 있는가?
  • [ ] 오래 실행되는 작업자의 호환성을 확인했는가?
  • [ ] Contract 단계 이전에 롤백 가능성을 검증했는가?

운영 모니터링

  • [ ] 데이터베이스 오류율을 확인하는가?
  • [ ] 마이그레이션 진행 상태를 기록하는가?
  • [ ] 데이터베이스 잠금과 처리 지연을 관찰하는가?
  • [ ] 배포 후 일정 기간 오류율을 점검하는가?
  • [ ] 최종적으로 사용하지 않는 컬럼과 코드를 정리하는가?

12. 모든 스키마 변경에 이 패턴이 필요할까?

모든 데이터베이스 변경을 복잡한 단계로 나눌 필요는 없다.

개발 중인 프로젝트이거나 서비스 중단이 허용되는 환경에서는 직접 변경하는 방식이 더 간단할 수 있다.

반면 다음 조건에 해당한다면 Expand–Migrate–Contract 패턴을 고려할 가치가 있다.

  • 운영 중 서비스 중단을 최소화해야 한다.
  • 애플리케이션 서버가 여러 대다.
  • 배포 과정에서 구버전과 신버전이 공존한다.
  • 데이터베이스에 많은 데이터가 저장되어 있다.
  • 기존 데이터 구조를 변경해야 한다.
  • 배포 실패 시 안전한 복구가 필요하다.

중요한 것은 복잡한 아키텍처 자체가 아니다.

데이터베이스 구조와 애플리케이션 코드의 호환성을 유지하면서 새로운 구조로 이동할 수 있도록 만드는 것이다.

결론

운영 중인 웹서비스에서 데이터베이스 구조를 변경할 때 가장 중요한 것은 새로운 SQL을 실행하는 속도가 아니다.

기존 애플리케이션과 새로운 애플리케이션이 서로 다른 구조를 기대하는 상황에서도 서비스가 정상적으로 동작하도록 설계하는 것이다.

Expand–Migrate–Contract 패턴은 이러한 문제를 해결하기 위해 변경 작업을 여러 단계로 나누는 접근법이다.

새로운 구조를 추가하고, 데이터를 이전하고, 애플리케이션을 전환한 뒤, 마지막에 기존 구조를 제거한다.

이 과정에서 버전 호환성, 데이터 일관성, 잠금, 모니터링, 롤백 전략을 함께 고려해야 한다.

무중단 데이터베이스 마이그레이션의 핵심은 변경을 한 번에 끝내는 것이 아니라, 변경 과정 전체가 안전하도록 설계하는 것이다.

웹사이트 디렉터리 서비스에 적용해 생각해 보기

레이더 링크모음과 같이 여러 웹사이트의 주소와 카테고리 정보를 안내하는 서비스도 데이터 구조를 설계할 때 참고할 수 있는 사례다.

이러한 유형의 서비스에서 웹사이트 주소를 저장하는 필드나 카테고리 관리 구조를 변경한다면 기존 데이터를 유지하면서 새 구조로 전환하는 방법을 고려할 수 있다.

다만 실제 데이터베이스 구성과 배포 방식은 서비스마다 다르므로 필요한 마이그레이션 전략도 달라진다.

참고 자료

  • PostgreSQL 공식 문서: ALTER TABLE
  • Prisma Data Guide: Expand and Contract Pattern
  • Prisma ORM v7: 데이터 마이그레이션 가이드

title: Why Database Schema Design Should Come Before Backend Development
description:
When starting a backend project, it is easy to focus immediately on creating APIs, writing controllers, and implementing business logic.

But before writing backend code, one important step deserves attention: database design.

A well-planned database structure helps developers understand how information is stored, how different entities are connected, and how the application will manage data.

During my development experience, working with ERP modules helped me understand why database schema design is an important part of backend development.

Here are some things I learned.

1. Understand the Requirements Before Designing Tables

The first step in database design is understanding what the application needs to do.

For example, consider a simple billing application. It may need to manage:

  • Customers
  • Invoices
  • Invoice items
  • Payments

Before creating tables, it is important to understand how these entities interact.

Questions worth considering include:

  • Can one customer have multiple invoices?
  • Can an invoice contain multiple items?
  • Can an invoice have multiple payment records?
  • Which information should be stored in each table?

Understanding these requirements helps avoid unnecessary changes later.

2. Identify Entities and Their Relationships

Once the requirements are clear, the next step is identifying the main entities and their relationships.

For example, in a billing system:

  • One customer can have multiple invoices.
  • One invoice can contain multiple invoice items.
  • One invoice can have multiple payment records.

These relationships help determine how tables should be structured.

A simplified relationship diagram might look like this:

Customer
   |
   | One-to-Many
   |
 Invoice
   |
   | One-to-Many
   |
Invoice Items

Invoice
   |
   | One-to-Many
   |
 Payments

Visualising these relationships makes it easier to understand the database structure before implementation.

3. Understand Primary Keys and Foreign Keys

Primary keys and foreign keys are fundamental to relational database design.

A primary key uniquely identifies a record in a table.

A foreign key establishes a relationship between records in different tables.

For example:

  • customer_id can be the primary key in the Customer table.
  • invoice_id can be the primary key in the Invoice table.
  • customer_id in the Invoice table can reference the Customer table.

This relationship helps maintain data integrity and ensures that an invoice is associated with a valid customer.

4. Consider Constraints and Data Integrity

Database design is not only about creating tables and connecting them.

It is also important to decide what data should be accepted and what rules should be enforced.

Some commonly used constraints include:

  • NOT NULL: Prevents a column from storing NULL values.
  • UNIQUE: Prevents duplicate values in a column or combination of columns.
  • PRIMARY KEY: Uniquely identifies each record.
  • FOREIGN KEY: Maintains relationships between tables.
  • CHECK: Ensures that values satisfy a specified condition.

For example, an invoice amount should not be negative if the business rules do not allow it.

Applying suitable constraints helps prevent invalid data from entering the database.

5. Use ER Diagrams to Visualise the Structure

An Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) is a useful way to represent database entities and their relationships.

Instead of trying to understand the entire structure from table definitions, developers can view the relationships visually.

During my development work, I explored ER diagram design using dbdiagram.io.

It helped me organise entities, identify relationships, and understand how foreign keys connect different parts of the application.

Tools such as dbdiagram.io are particularly useful when planning relational database structures.

6. How Database Design Helps Backend Development

A clear database structure makes backend implementation easier to organise.

For example, when working with NestJS and TypeORM, database entities and their relationships influence how developers structure their models and database operations.

A well-planned schema can help with:

  • Defining TypeORM entities.
  • Establishing entity relationships.
  • Writing queries and joins.
  • Implementing API operations.
  • Maintaining data consistency.
  • Understanding how information flows across modules.

It also makes it easier to discuss the system structure with other developers before implementation begins.

7. Lessons I Learned

Working with database-driven ERP applications helped me appreciate the importance of planning before coding.

Some key takeaways:

  • Understand the business requirements first.
  • Identify entities and relationships clearly.
  • Plan primary keys and foreign keys.
  • Consider constraints and data integrity.
  • Visualise the schema using an ER diagram.
  • Review the structure before implementing backend logic.

Database design is not a one-time activity. As application requirements change, the schema may also need to evolve.

Final Thoughts

A good backend application starts with a clear understanding of its data.

Taking time to plan the database structure before implementing APIs can make development more organised and help reduce avoidable changes later.

My experience working with PostgreSQL, TypeORM, and ERP modules has helped me understand how important database design is to building maintainable applications.

Do you usually create an ER diagram before starting backend development, or do you design the database as you build the application?

I'd love to hear how other developers approach it.

Further Reading

  • PostgreSQL Documentation - Constraints
  • dbdiagram.io
  • TypeORM Documentation - Entities

The examples in this article are simplified illustrations of relational database concepts.
