title: Stop Listening to scroll for Progress Bars. CSS Scroll Timelines Are Baseline
description:
TL;DR: animation-timeline: scroll() and view() drive a normal CSS animation with scroll position instead of time. Firefox 159 turned them on by default on October 27, 2026, so scroll-driven animations are now Baseline Newly available.

The listener everyone has written

You want a reading progress bar. A thin line at the top that fills as the reader scrolls. So you write this:

const bar = document.querySelector(".progress");

window.addEventListener("scroll", () => {
  const max = document.documentElement.scrollHeight - innerHeight;
  bar.style.transform = `scaleX(${scrollY / max})`;
}, { passive: true });

Then someone resizes the window, and you add a resize listener. Then the bar stutters on a busy page, and you add requestAnimationFrame. Then a fade-in effect on cards shows up in the design, and you add an IntersectionObserver with ten thresholds. It works. It is also a small physics engine for a 4px line.

What it is

A CSS animation normally runs on the document timeline, which moves with time. animation-timeline lets you swap that for a timeline that moves with scrolling:

  • scroll() follows the scroll position of a scroll container, from 0% at the top to 100% at the bottom.
  • view() follows one element as it travels through its scroll container's visible area.

Your keyframes stay exactly the same. Only the clock changes.

The minimal one: a reading progress bar 

.progress {
  position: fixed;
  inset: 0 0 auto 0;
  height: 4px;
  background: rebeccapurple;
  transform-origin: 0 50%;
  animation: grow linear both;
  animation-timeline: scroll(root);
}

@keyframes grow {
  from { scale: 0 1; }
  to { scale: 1 1; }
}

No duration, no JavaScript. scroll(root) means "the document's own scroller", and the animation's progress is the scroll progress.

I tested it in Chrome 156 in a 400 by 300 px frame with a 1300 px tall page, so 1000 px of scroll. The computed scale was 0.25 1 at 250 px, 0.5 1 at 500 px, and 1 at the bottom. It maps one to one, which is exactly what the listener was trying to do.

The realistic one: reveal cards as they enter

The fade-in-on-scroll effect is where view() and animation-range earn their keep:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  @supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
    .card {
      animation: reveal linear both;
      animation-timeline: view();
      animation-range: entry 0% entry 100%;
    }
  }
}

@keyframes reveal {
  from { opacity: 0; translate: 0 40px; }
  to { opacity: 1; translate: 0 0; }
}

view() tracks the card through the viewport. animation-range: entry 0% entry 100% squeezes the whole animation into the entry phase: it starts when the card's top edge touches the bottom of the viewport, and ends when the card is fully inside.

In the same test frame, I placed a 100 px tall card 600 px down the page. At 300 px of scroll its top touched the bottom of the 300 px viewport, and its opacity was 0. At 350 px, halfway in, opacity was 0.5 and translate was 0px 20px. At 400 px, fully in, opacity was 1.

No observer, no thresholds, no class toggling. The wrappers keep it polite: motion only for people who did not ask for less, and only where the browser understands view().

Can I use it?

Where Status
Baseline Newly available since October 27, 2026
Chrome and Edge 115
Safari (macOS and iOS) 26
Firefox 159
Tested Chrome 156, where every number in this post was measured
Spec Scroll-driven Animations (W3C CSS Working Group)

Firefox was the last one in. Its 159 release notes say scroll-driven animations are now enabled by default. MDN lists both animation-timeline and animation-range as Baseline 2026. If you still support older browsers, the @supports check above keeps them on the static design.

Gotchas

  1. The animation shorthand resets the timeline. animation-timeline is a reset-only part of the animation shorthand, so writing the shorthand after it puts the timeline back to auto. With animation-timeline: scroll(root) first and animation: grow linear both second, Chrome reported animation-timeline: auto, a duration of 0s, and a plain DocumentTimeline. The bar did not follow the scroll at all; it jumped to its last keyframe and stayed full width. Always put animation-timeline after the shorthand.

  2. scroll() picks the nearest scroller, and overflow: hidden counts. Plain scroll() means scroll(nearest). I put the bar inside a fixed wrapper with overflow: hidden, which makes that wrapper a scroll container with nothing to scroll. The timeline was inactive, and the computed scale stayed none at every scroll position. For page-level effects, write scroll(root) and stop guessing.

  3. It is still an animation, so it still moves. Scroll-linked motion is exactly the kind of effect people turn on reduced motion to avoid. Keep decorative ones inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference), as in the card example. A progress bar that only changes scale is usually fine to leave on.

Wrap-up

The scroll listener was never wrong, just a lot of code standing between a scroll position and a number between 0 and 1. Find one in your codebase, delete it, and give the keyframes a scroll timeline instead.

Sources

  • Firefox 159 release notes for developers (MDN)
  • Scroll-driven animations (web-features explorer, Baseline status)
  • animation-timeline (MDN)
  • animation-range (MDN)

This article was written with the help of AI and checked against the sources above.

title: Designing an image-review workflow: five decisions to make before building
description:
An image-review screen looks simple until two people review different versions of the same file. One approves it, another requests a change, and the team has to work out which decision counts.

For developers building ecommerce or creative-production tools, the difficult part is making those decisions clear. Here are five questions I would settle before building the interface.

1. What exactly is being approved?

An approval should refer to a particular file version. A filename alone is a weak reference: the name can stay the same while the pixels change.

Give each version its own identifier. Keep the original file separate, and make it clear which version a reviewer is viewing. When a replacement arrives, show the earlier approval as part of the history rather than treating it as approval of the new file.

2. Where does feedback belong?

“Fix the edge on the left” is easy to misunderstand when several images are open. Attach feedback to the file version and, when useful, a position on the image.

If comments use image coordinates, decide how those coordinates behave when the preview is resized. A comment should still point to the same detail on a phone and a desktop. If a new version changes the crop, show the old comment against its original version rather than silently moving the pin.

3. Who can approve the work?

Separate permission to upload, edit, review and approve. These are different responsibilities, even when a small team gives one person several roles.

If your quality process requires an independent reviewer, enforce that rule on the server. Hiding the approval button from an editor is helpful interface design, but it does not enforce the permission.

4. What happens when decisions overlap?

A reviewer can leave a tab open while somebody else replaces the file. Before accepting an approval, check that the version being approved is still the version awaiting review.

If it has changed, explain what happened and ask the reviewer to inspect the replacement. Avoid a success message that leaves them believing they approved something they never saw.

5. Does the final export meet the brief?

Visual approval and delivery checks answer different questions. An image can look right while having the wrong dimensions, file format or filename.

Keep a small delivery checklist alongside the review: required dimensions, format, background, naming pattern and the expected number of files. Check what you can automatically, and leave subjective judgements, such as whether retouching looks natural, for a person.

Start with one complete path

Map one file from upload through a revision, approval and download. Include an outdated browser tab and a failed upload in that walkthrough. It is a useful way to expose ambiguous states before adding a batch interface.

I am Chandran, founder of Rupato, a product photo and video editing business operated by Liditech Ltd in the UK. This is our brand account. I am sharing the product questions behind clearer editing and review workflows, and would welcome other approaches.

How do you handle approval when a file changes during review?

title: How to change location on the Windows 11 taskbar
description:
With a recent update, Windows 11 now supports repositioning the taskbar natively via the Settings UI.

Microsoft has explicitly omitted drag-and-drop support, characterizing the classic lock-and-unlock interaction as unnecessary complexity that often leads to accidental user error.

While the developer community has introduced various mods and tools to bypass this limitation, these implementations face potential stability issues with future OS updates.

The current approach remains open to future iterations based on feedback.

Why Microsoft removed the ability to move with the mouse

The company chose not to allow dragging of the taskbar to protect users from accidental moves that occurred while using the computer. According to Diego Baca, Microsoft's vice president of design, adding a setting to "lock" the bar to avoid these mistakes was considered unnecessary complexity.

Microsoft clarifies that this particular design decision is not final and may change in the future.

Third-party programs

Users who wish to restore the ability to move the bar with the mouse can use external tools, such as Taskbar Location Options or add-ons from the Windhawk platform. However, using such utilities comes with risks, as they may stop working properly after future Windows updates.

title: # Windows Found My Bug Before I Did. I Just Had to Read the Error Message.
description:
Sometimes, the hardest part of debugging isn't finding the bug. It's actually paying attention to what the error message is telling you.

Today, I was working on a simple Java task: splitting a string like name=Kwame into a key and a value.

The idea was straightforward:

  1. Find the position of =.
  2. Extract everything before it as the key.
  3. Extract everything after it as the value.

Here's the code:

String text = "name=Kwame";

int index = text.indexOf('=');

String key = text.substring(0, index);
String value = text.substring(index + 1);

System.out.println(key);
System.out.println(value);

Expected output:

name
Kwame

Simple enough, right?

Where I went wrong

My first implementation looked like this:

String value = text.substring(index);

I thought I was extracting the value after =.

But there was one problem.

substring(index) starts extracting at the index you provide. It doesn't skip that character.

So instead of getting:

Kwame

I got:

=Kwame

Java didn't complain. The code compiled and ran perfectly fine. It simply returned something I wasn't expecting.

Then Windows stepped in.

I eventually passed that value into a file path, and Windows threw this exception:

Illegal char <:> at index 2: =C:/Documents

At first, I was looking everywhere except the actual problem.

But look closely:

=C:/Documents
^

The unwanted = was still there.

The error message had practically pointed at the problem. I just hadn't paid enough attention to it.

What I learned

1. Java's substring indexing starts at zero.

String text = "name=Kwame";
int index = text.indexOf('=');

String key = text.substring(0, index);
String value = text.substring(index + 1);

Remember:

  • substring(start, end) includes start but excludes end.
  • substring(start) extracts from start to the end.
  • index + 1 skips the delimiter.

2. Code can compile and still be logically wrong.

A successful compilation doesn't guarantee that your program is producing the expected result.

3. Read the error message before rewriting your code.

Error messages often contain valuable clues, including the exact input that caused the failure.

Sometimes the answer is already there.

I'm back on the learning streak, and these little debugging experiences are teaching me more than I expected.

Your turn

What's an off-by-one error or silly debugging mistake that cost you way more time than it should have?

I'd love to hear your stories.

Java #Programming #Debugging #SoftwareEngineering #LearningInPublic

title: Responsible Design Patterns for Gambling-Related Calculator Tools
description:
Developers build calculators for all kinds of regulated or risky domains: loans, crypto, insurance, betting. The code is usually the easy part. The harder question is what the tool encourages people to do. A wagering requirement calculator, for example, can be built to help someone see that a bonus is expected to cost them money, or it can be built to make the bonus feel like a puzzle worth solving at any cost. Same formulas, very different outcomes.

This article collects design patterns for building gambling-adjacent tools that inform rather than push. It draws on general UX ethics, accessibility practice and the principles behind responsible gambling guidance. The examples come from wagering calculators, but most of the patterns apply to any tool where the user's money and wellbeing are on the line.

Start with the purpose statement

Before writing any UI, write one sentence describing what the tool is for. For example: "Help adults understand the real turnover and expected cost of a bonus offer before they accept it." Every later design decision should be checked against this sentence. If a feature makes accepting offers more likely without making understanding better, it fails the test.

Write a second sentence describing what the tool is not for: "This tool does not recommend offers, rank operators or suggest strategies to clear requirements faster." Making non-goals explicit protects the product from slow drift toward becoming a marketing funnel.

Pattern 1: lead with cost, not with the bonus

Most promotional copy leads with the bonus amount, in the largest font, in a celebratory color. A responsible tool inverts this hierarchy. The first result a user sees should be the required turnover and the expected cost.

Bad:   YOU GET 500!  (small print: 35x on deposit + bonus)
Good:  Required turnover: 35,000
       Expected cost of clearing: about 1,225
       Bonus value: 500
       Expected result: about -725

Visual weight is an argument. Give the largest type to the number that best describes reality.

Pattern 2: no dark patterns in inputs

Avoid defaults that flatter the offer. Common offenders:

  • Defaulting the wagering base to "bonus only" when many terms use "deposit + bonus."
  • Defaulting game contribution to 100% without saying so.
  • Defaulting RTP to an unusually high value.
  • Hiding the max-bet field under "advanced options."

A neutral default is either a realistic, documented value or no default at all, forcing an explicit choice. If you show a default, label where it came from.

Pattern 3: make time visible

Turnover is abstract; time is concrete. Converting a requirement into number of bets and bets per day makes it tangible. "7,000 bets in 14 days, or 500 per day" communicates intensity far better than "14,000 turnover." It also invites the question every responsible design should invite: is this how I want to spend my time?

function intensityMessage(betsPerDay) {
  if (betsPerDay == null) return null;
  if (betsPerDay > 300) return "This pace is very high. Consider whether this fits your limits.";
  if (betsPerDay > 100) return "This requires sustained daily play.";
  return null;
}

Pattern 4: say what EV hides

Expected value is an average. Most individual outcomes will differ, sometimes wildly. A short, plain-language note under the result helps:

This is an average. Many people will lose their balance before completing the requirement; a few will finish ahead. The average is negative.

If you have a simulation mode, show a distribution rather than a single number: for example, "In 10,000 simulated sessions, 71% ended with zero balance before completion."

Pattern 5: age gating and the 18+ notice

Any tool in this domain should state clearly that it is intended for adults (18+, or the local legal age). A permanent footer notice is the minimum. Do not use playful styling for it; it should read as a fact, not a decoration.

For content sites, avoid targeting content at minors: no cartoon mascots, no game-like rewards for using the tool, no streaks or badges. These mechanics are designed to create habits, which is exactly what you do not want here.

Pattern 6: always-visible help

A responsible gambling link should be present on every result screen, not buried in a footer menu. It should lead to practical information: how to set deposit limits, how self-exclusion works, how to recognize warning signs and where to find support. A good example of this kind of resource is the sorumlu oyun (responsible gaming) page on bahisbonusu.com, which collects warning signs and support options in Turkish.

<aside class="rg-notice" role="note">
  <strong>18+</strong> Gambling can be harmful.
  <a href="https://bahisbonusu.com/sorumlu-oyun/">Responsible gaming resources</a>
</aside>

Keep the notice readable: sufficient contrast, normal font size, and never dismissible in a way that hides it permanently.

Pattern 7: no calls to action toward operators

A calculator page is not a landing page. Do not place "Claim now" buttons, operator logos or affiliate offers next to results. When the result says "expected cost exceeds bonus value," and a button beside it says "Get this bonus," the design is contradicting itself, and users notice which message the page actually wants them to follow.

If a site does have commercial content elsewhere, keep it clearly separated and clearly labeled, and keep tools neutral.

Pattern 8: neutral, precise language

Words shape decisions. Prefer:

  • "Expected cost" over "investment."
  • "Required turnover" over "play-through challenge."
  • "Bonus terms" over "rewards."
  • "You are expected to lose about X" over "You could win up to Y."

Avoid urgency language ("only today", "hurry") and any wording implying gambling is a way to earn income. A glossary of terms helps users decode jargon in the offer itself.

Pattern 9: privacy by default

A calculator needs no personal data. Do not require accounts, do not store inputs server-side and do not send inputs to analytics with user identifiers. Spending data is sensitive: a series of large deposit amounts entered into a calculator can reveal financial distress. Calculate on the client, and if you need analytics, aggregate it.

// Calculation happens entirely in the browser.
// Only an anonymous event name is sent, never the values.
analytics?.track("calculator_used");

Pattern 10: accessibility is part of responsibility

People in vulnerable situations include people using screen readers, high zoom or keyboard navigation. Ensure:

  • Every input has a visible label.
  • Results are announced with aria-live="polite".
  • Warnings are not conveyed by color alone; use text and icons.
  • Error messages say what to fix, in plain language.

An inaccessible responsible gambling notice does not exist for the people who cannot perceive it.

Pattern 11: honest limits of the tool

State what the tool does not model. For example: "This calculator does not account for maximum cashout caps, sticky bonus rules or game-specific restrictions. Always read the full terms." Honesty about limitations builds more trust than false precision.

Pattern 12: friction where it helps

Most UX work removes friction. In this domain, a little friction in the right place can be protective. Examples:

  • After a calculation with strongly negative expected value, show the summary sentence before any detail.
  • When a user enters a very large deposit, display a gentle note about setting limits.
  • Never auto-advance from the calculator to anything else.

The goal is not to lecture but to create a moment to pause.

A checklist for reviews

Use this in code review or design review:

[ ] Purpose and non-goals written down
[ ] Cost shown before or with bonus value, same visual weight or more
[ ] No flattering defaults; defaults are documented
[ ] Time and intensity shown (bets, bets/day)
[ ] EV caveat in plain language
[ ] 18+ notice always visible
[ ] Responsible gaming link on result screen
[ ] No operator CTAs or affiliate buttons beside results
[ ] Neutral language; no urgency or income framing
[ ] No personal data collected; client-side calculation
[ ] Accessible labels, live regions, non-color warnings
[ ] Limitations stated

Testing the ethics, not just the math

You can write automated tests for some of these rules. For example, a snapshot test can check that the result panel always contains the responsible gaming link, and a unit test can assert that a negative expected value always produces a warning:

test("result view always includes RG notice", () => {
  const html = renderResult(sampleResult);
  assert.match(html, /sorumlu-oyun/);
  assert.match(html, /18\+/);
});

test("negative EV always warns", () => {
  const r = calculate({ ...inputs, multiplier: 50 });
  assert.ok(r.bonusEV < 0);
  assert.ok(r.warnings.length > 0);
});

Encoding values in tests means they survive redesigns and new team members.

Conclusion

Tools in gambling-adjacent domains carry extra responsibility because the people using them may be making decisions under pressure. The patterns here are not complicated: lead with cost, avoid flattering defaults, make time visible, keep the 18+ notice and support resources close, stay away from calls to action and respect privacy and accessibility. A calculator built this way is genuinely useful, and it is also the kind of tool you can be comfortable putting your name on.

For a Turkish-language example of a reference site that pairs tools with responsible gaming information, see bahisbonusu.com and its responsible gaming section.

title: Training Artifact Storage: Browser Uploads and the Large-Object Transfer Boundary
description:
Short answer: use a presigned single request for small training artifacts, and use presigned multipart when the object size or expected upload time makes restarting the whole object an SLO risk. Presigned POST is a useful policy-shaped single request, but it does not create a smaller retry boundary.

That rule is for a B2B SaaS product where browsers send training artifacts directly to S3-compatible object storage. The application should authorize the upload and retain its state; the browser should carry the bytes. The important choice is the size of the failure domain, not which verb looks nicest in a code sample.

Should browser uploads use presigned POST, PUT, or multipart for large files?

Begin with the object lifecycle. The application authenticates the user, selects an object key, and issues short-lived permission. The browser then uploads directly to storage. A single PUT is easy to observe and easy to explain: one request, one progress stream, one final result. A presigned POST fits a form and policy workflow, but it still has one whole-object transfer boundary.

Multipart changes that boundary. The client splits the object, records the result for each part, and completes the object only after the required part results are present. If a connection disappears after several successful parts, the client can retry the missing part instead of replaying the entire training artifact. That is the useful property.

The trade is operational state. Multipart needs an upload identifier, part numbers, returned part results, a completion step, and an abort path. It also creates more requests and more signing work. A low part size improves retry granularity but raises request volume; a high part size reduces orchestration while making each retry more expensive. I've seen teams pick a fixed threshold from a blog post, then discover that their mobile users have a very different completion-time distribution.

Capacity planning should use the object-size distribution, upload duration, concurrency, retry count, browser memory, and target completion SLO. I don't know a universal byte threshold that survives those variables. Measure the p95 and p99 path you actually operate, then choose the threshold where whole-object retries threaten the SLO.

The failure exercise that exposes the real design

The useful rehearsal is bounded: upload a large artifact, interrupt the connection after several parts have succeeded, reconnect, and restart the browser before completion. This is a test of state ownership, not a benchmark. The invariant is simple: acknowledged parts are not uploaded again without a reason, an incomplete object is never announced as complete, and an abandoned upload has an explicit cleanup decision. I want the exercise to include the awkward transitions that a happy-path test skips — the tab closes, the authorization expires, the completion call is repeated, or the browser reports success before the application has persisted its own record. Those transitions are where an apparently successful upload turns into an object the user cannot find, a duplicate, or a cleanup obligation with no owner.

Pull the network.

On recovery, the client should compare its durable part records with the source file and continue from missing work. The completion request belongs after that comparison. If the operation cannot finish, the client or control plane should abort the multipart upload; otherwise, unfinished fragments become an accounting and capacity problem that the happy-path dashboard will not show.

Measure first.

The application boundary can stay provider-neutral. This Go example makes the decision and records the retry scope; the provider-specific signing and completion calls remain behind an adapter whose contract can be tested independently.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "strconv"
)

type UploadPlan struct {
    Mode       string
    RetryScope string
    AbortOnFailure bool
}

func planUpload(sizeBytes, thresholdBytes int64, unstableNetwork bool) UploadPlan {
    if sizeBytes >= thresholdBytes || unstableNetwork {
        return UploadPlan{
            Mode:           "presigned-multipart",
            RetryScope:     "missing-part",
            AbortOnFailure: true,
        }
    }

    return UploadPlan{
        Mode:           "presigned-put",
        RetryScope:     "whole-object",
        AbortOnFailure: false,
    }
}

func requiredInt64(name string) int64 {
    value, err := strconv.ParseInt(os.Getenv(name), 10, 64)
    if err != nil || value <= 0 {
        panic(name + " must be a positive integer")
    }
    return value
}

func main() {
    plan := planUpload(
        requiredInt64("FILE_BYTES"),
        requiredInt64("MULTIPART_THRESHOLD_BYTES"),
        os.Getenv("UNSTABLE_NETWORK") == "true",
    )
    fmt.Printf("mode=%s retry_scope=%s abort_on_failure=%t\n",
        plan.Mode, plan.RetryScope, plan.AbortOnFailure)
}

The adapter should make completion idempotent at the application boundary and should distinguish authorization retries from data retries. A throttled authorization request needs bounded exponential backoff and respect for Retry-After; a failed part needs a part-level retry policy; a canceled operation needs cleanup. Those are different clocks and should not share one generic retry loop.

Buy versus build is an on-call decision

The storage API is only one part of the ownership decision. I put signing, CORS policy, multipart state, cleanup, provider credentials, observability, and incident response in the same review because a small upload demo hides most of that work.

Approach Useful when What the team owns Main limitation
Native storage integration The company has standardized on one storage estate Provider SDK behavior, credentials, CORS, signing, and lifecycle policy Moving providers becomes an application project
Self-hosted signing service Policy control and deployment control matter more than staff time Availability, key rotation, API compatibility, and the complete upload state machine The maintenance and on-call load does not disappear
Generic HTTP control plane Several storage backends must share one application contract The adapter contract, upload records, cleanup policy, and browser origin configuration Backend-specific controls still need an explicit mapping

There is no universally correct buy decision. A small platform team with one backend may rationally keep a native integration because the extra abstraction has no operational payoff. A team supporting several compatible backends may value one HTTP contract and one credential boundary because every service can use it without installing a language-specific SDK. That benefit is about integration surface and ownership, not a claim that the storage layer has identical semantics everywhere.

Where this recommendation does not fit

Multipart is a poor default for tiny objects, short-lived uploads, or systems that cannot persist upload state. The extra requests and state machine add failure modes without shrinking a meaningful retry domain. Stick with a single presigned request when the whole-object retry is comfortably inside the completion SLO.

This browser-direct pattern is also unsuitable when the product requires public object delivery, public-read ACLs, object versioning, object lock or WORM retention, conditional If-Match writes, automatic cross-region replication, hourly expiration, or server-side metadata search beyond prefix-based listing. Those requirements need a storage integration and policy model that explicitly provides them, or an additional coordinator and delivery layer.

Browser CORS is another launch gate. The bucket's origin policy must permit the browser's actual method and headers; a presigned URL cannot make a forbidden browser origin legal. Test preflight behavior from the deployed origin, with the same headers and credentials mode used by the application. A successful server-side upload test proves very little about this path.

The decision rule is therefore narrow and practical: keep a single request while its restart cost is small, move to multipart when the retry domain threatens the SLO, and refuse the browser-direct design when the required object controls are outside its contract. That leaves a measurable architecture instead of a slogan about large files.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage/pricing

title: How to Deploy a Hybrid Cloud: A Step-by-Step Plan, Security Risks, and When to Choose Public or Private
description:
Deploy a hybrid cloud by placing each workload where its data, latency, compliance, cost, and elasticity needs are best met, linking sites over private encrypted connections with one identity provider, and deploying through one policy layer so on-premises and cloud locations are operated the same way. Control Plane runs the same workloads on your own servers and on AWS, GCP, and Azure under one API, one set of policies, and one observability stack.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

A hybrid cloud works when each workload runs where its requirements are best met and every environment is operated the same way.

  • Decide placement per workload. Evaluate data gravity, latency, compliance, burst demand, and hardware needs before choosing public or private for each application.
  • Connect environments securely. Use dedicated interconnects or IPsec VPN tunnels between sites, and never send unencrypted traffic across the public internet.
  • Establish one identity and policy layer. A single identity provider and policy-as-code framework reduce credential sprawl and configuration drift.
  • Run Kubernetes or a platform across both. Whether you manage clusters yourself or use a platform layer, consistent orchestration lets you operate every environment the same way.
  • How Control Plane fits. Control Plane’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a set of locations a workload runs across, can combine AWS, GCP, and Azure regions with your own servers joined through Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), Control Plane’s way of turning your own servers into managed locations, and existing clusters connected through Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), Control Plane’s option for connecting a cluster you already run. Workloads run active-active across all of them.

How Do I Decide Between Public and Private Cloud Hosting?

The right placement depends on the workload. Two applications in the same company can have opposite requirements.

Workload Trait Points Toward Public Cloud Points Toward Private / On Premises Why
Demand pattern Bursty or seasonal Steady, predictable baseline Public cloud scales on demand without idle hardware. Steady workloads at high utilization are often cheaper on owned capacity.
Data gravity and residency Data already lives in a cloud region or is generated there Large datasets stored on premises, or sovereignty rules mandate a specific physical location Moving large datasets is slow, and egress fees make moving data out of a cloud expensive. Keep compute near the data.
Latency to users or systems Users are distributed globally Users or dependent systems are in one facility Public cloud regions and CDNs cover the globe. On-premises placement keeps traffic between co-located systems off the WAN.
Regulatory requirements Standard compliance frameworks satisfied by major providers Strict data-handling rules, air-gapped environments, or audit regimes that require physical control Public clouds carry broad certifications, but some regulators require infrastructure you control.
Hardware specificity General-purpose compute, standard GPUs Mainframes, specialized appliances, or custom hardware already installed Cloud providers offer GPUs, FPGAs, and managed HSMs. Mainframes and custom appliances often have no cloud equivalent.
Team skills Strong cloud-native skills, limited infrastructure ops capacity Deep infrastructure expertise, limited cloud experience Public cloud offloads hardware ops. On-premises requires hands-on infrastructure management.

Most organizations land on a mix. A workload that handles regulated patient data might stay on premises while a customer-facing API with global traffic runs in the public cloud. For a deeper look at the cost side of this decision, see the cloud vs. on-premises vs. hybrid cost comparison.

What Are the Best Steps for Deploying a Hybrid Cloud for My Company?

A phased approach reduces risk and keeps the project aligned with business outcomes. This plan is vendor neutral and works with one cloud provider or several.

Phase 1: Inventory Workloads and Data Flows

Catalog every application, database, message queue, and batch job. Record data flows between systems, network dependencies, current owners, and SLAs.

Phase 2: Classify and Decide Placement

Apply the decision table above to each workload. Assign a target environment (public region, on-premises cluster, or both for active-active). Document the rationale so future teams understand why a workload lives where it does. Define recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO) for critical systems.

Phase 3: Design Network Connectivity

Connect environments with dedicated interconnects or encrypted tunnels. The major providers each offer a dedicated link product:

  • AWS Direct Connect
  • Azure ExpressRoute
  • Google Cloud Interconnect

Dedicated links are private but not encrypted by default, so add MACsec or IPsec over the link for regulated traffic. If dedicated links are not justified by bandwidth or latency requirements, site-to-site VPN over IPsec is the minimum.

Phase 4: Establish One Identity Provider and Workload Identity

Federate a single identity provider (such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, or Google Workspace) across every environment. Use workload identity federation instead of long-lived API keys so services authenticate with short-lived tokens. For a deeper look at this pattern, see workload identity federation explained.

Phase 5: Pick One Deployment and Policy Layer

Choose a deployment mechanism that works the same way in every location. This could be a GitOps pipeline, a platform layer, or a combination. A change to a workload definition must produce the same result whether the target is a cloud region or an on-premises cluster.

Phase 6: Set Up Observability Across Environments

Centralize metrics, logs, and traces from every location into one system. Split observability makes incidents that span environments easy to miss. Define alerting thresholds and on-call ownership per workload.

Phase 7: Migrate in Waves

Start with a low-risk workload to validate connectivity, latency, security controls, monitoring, and rollback procedures. Expand only after each wave is stable, secure, and documented. Avoid migrating everything at once.

Phase 8: Test Failover Between Environments

Simulate a location failure and verify that traffic shifts to the surviving environment within your RTO. Test backup integrity and restoration procedures in a clean environment.

Phase 9: Operate and Review

Monitor costs, permissions, configurations, and security posture continuously. Reassess workload placement at least annually and after major business or architectural changes.

What Security and Compliance Risks Are Unique to Hybrid Cloud, and How Can I Mitigate Them?

These risks come from operating across environment boundaries, on top of generic cloud security.

Hybrid-Specific Risk Why It Exists Concrete Mitigation
Expanded attack surface across network boundaries Every link between environments is a potential entry point. Restrict cross-environment traffic to documented paths. Use dedicated interconnects or encrypted tunnels. Apply deny-by-default firewall rules at both ends.
Inconsistent policy between environments Different tools and teams manage each environment. Adopt policy as code (for example, Open Policy Agent) applied to both environments from one repository.
Fragmented identity and long-lived credentials Services in one environment need keys to reach another. Use workload identity federation with short-lived tokens. Eliminate static API keys crossing environment boundaries.
Data in transit between sites Traffic crosses networks you do not fully control. Enforce mTLS between services. Encrypt all cross-site traffic with IPsec, MACsec, or TLS.
Visibility gaps and split logging Each environment has its own logging stack. Centralize logs and security alerts into one SIEM or observability platform. Correlate events across environments.
Configuration drift Manual changes in one environment are not replicated. Manage all infrastructure and workload configuration as code. Run drift detection on a schedule.
Shared responsibility confusion Teams assume the cloud provider or the on-premises team owns a control, and neither does. Document the shared responsibility model for every layer. Assign explicit owners for each control.
Compliance scope creep Regulated data moves to an environment that was not in audit scope. Tag data by classification. Enforce placement policies that prevent regulated data from landing in unapproved locations. Maintain a data flow map.

The Cloud Security Alliance’s hybrid cloud risk analysis provides additional depth on several of these vectors. Treat all connections as untrusted until authenticated and authorized, segment networks to limit lateral movement, and conduct regular incident response drills that span both environments.

How Do I Run Kubernetes Across On Premises and Public Cloud for Hybrid Cloud Application Deployment?

Teams typically use separate clusters managed with GitOps, a hyperscaler hybrid Kubernetes product, or a platform layer that abstracts the clusters.

Separate Clusters Managed with GitOps

The simplest model is one cluster per environment with a GitOps controller such as Argo CD or Flux deploying the same manifests to each. This keeps clusters independent and avoids dependencies between clusters’ management layers. The trade-off is that you own upgrades, etcd backups, storage provisioning, and CNI management for every on-premises cluster.

Hyperscaler Hybrid Kubernetes Offerings

Each major provider offers a way to run or manage Kubernetes on your own hardware under its tooling:

  • Amazon EKS Anywhere runs Kubernetes clusters built on EKS Distro on your own infrastructure, and Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes attaches on-premises servers as worker nodes to an EKS cluster whose control plane AWS manages.
  • Google Distributed Cloud brings GKE to on-premises and edge locations.
  • Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes projects existing clusters into Azure’s management plane.

These products reduce the operational load of running Kubernetes on premises but tie management to a single provider’s tooling.

Cross-Cluster Networking and Service Discovery

Services in one cluster often need to reach services in another. Solutions include service mesh federation, DNS-based service discovery, or a platform layer that provides a global endpoint. Whichever approach you choose, enforce network policy with a deny-by-default posture and require mTLS for all cross-cluster traffic.

Operational Load of On-Premises Kubernetes

Running Kubernetes on your own hardware adds node OS patching and hardware lifecycle to the upgrade, etcd, storage, and CNI work above, and typically requires dedicated platform engineers. Teams that want the flexibility of on-premises Kubernetes without the full operational burden often adopt a platform layer that handles these concerns.

Which Tools Best Manage Hybrid Cloud Infrastructure as Code and Policy Governance Across Environments?

Hybrid governance requires several tool categories working together. No single tool covers every layer.

Category Examples What It Covers Where Gaps Remain
Infrastructure as code Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi Provisioning cloud resources, networks, and clusters declaratively Not designed for continuous workload delivery or runtime policy enforcement
Configuration management Ansible OS-level configuration, package installation, on-premises server setup Less suited to cloud-native workload orchestration
Policy as code Open Policy Agent, Kyverno Admission control, resource validation, compliance guardrails Requires integration into every cluster and pipeline
GitOps Argo CD, Flux Continuous delivery of Kubernetes manifests from Git Does not provision infrastructure or enforce cross-cluster policy
Secrets management HashiCorp Vault, cloud-native secret stores Storing and rotating secrets, issuing short-lived credentials Must be integrated into every environment separately

The gap that remains across all of these tools is a unified view of workloads, policies, and observability spanning every environment. For a deeper look at how these tools fit together, see the hybrid cloud management guide.

What Solutions Help Manage Container Orchestration Complexity While Maintaining Security?

The core trade-off is between operating Kubernetes yourself and using a managed or platform layer. Self-managed clusters give full control but require dedicated platform engineering staff. Managed services reduce operational load but may limit customization. A platform layer can abstract clusters entirely, letting teams deploy workloads without managing infrastructure.

Regardless of which model you choose, these security controls should be on by default:

  • Network policy with deny-by-default traffic. No service should be reachable unless explicitly allowed.
  • mTLS between services. Encrypt and authenticate all service-to-service communication.
  • Workload identity. Services authenticate with short-lived tokens instead of static credentials.
  • Secrets management. Secret values stay out of code, images, and environment variables in plain text.
  • Image provenance. Only signed, scanned images from trusted registries are admitted.
  • Audit logs. Every API call and configuration change is recorded in a tamper-evident log.
  • Least-privilege RBAC. Users and service accounts receive only the permissions they need, scoped to the narrowest possible resource set.

How Control Plane Approaches Hybrid Cloud

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into one GVC. A GVC can mix AWS, GCP, and Azure regions, servers in your own data center joined with MK8s, and existing clusters connected with BYOK. With MK8s, Control Plane operates the Kubernetes layer on servers you join, and the hardware stays yours. MK8s and BYOK locations give full Kubernetes access for teams that want operators or Helm charts. Many teams run Control Plane in a single cloud as well, for the same Day 2 operations.

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, Capacity AI (Control Plane’s right-sizing of CPU and memory based on historical usage), built-in observability, and security. On Control Plane-managed compute there is no cluster at all. On MK8s locations Control Plane operates the Kubernetes layer. With BYOK, you keep running the cluster you connected and Control Plane runs the workloads on it. Built-in observability covers metrics, logs, and traces for every location in one place.

A workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location, so on-premises and cloud locations back each other up. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Those locations can be two regions of one cloud or locations on different providers, for example an on-premises MK8s location and a cloud region.

On Control Plane, location routing options include priority routing tiers, where a lower-priority tier receives traffic only when every location in the higher-priority tier is unavailable, and latency offsets that make a location appear closer or farther. Teams use these to keep traffic on preferred locations and define which locations take over when they fail.

Security defaults are built in. Workloads are closed by default behind a deny-by-default internal firewall, traffic between them uses mTLS, and Control Plane’s built-in secrets management keeps secret values out of code and images. A tamper-proof audit trail records changes made through the Control Plane API. Each workload is isolated with cgroups, namespaces, and restricted syscalls and capabilities. One set of org-scoped policies controls access to every Control Plane resource.

Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code, including workloads running on your own servers. Cloud Wormhole, Control Plane’s built-in way to give workloads private access to services in VPCs and on-premises networks behind firewalls, works without VPN clients to install. For lift-and-shift of on-premises VMs, VM workloads run on MK8s locations with the KubeVirt add-on and KVM-capable nodes.

Control Plane ships its own Terraform and Pulumi providers, so it complements the infrastructure as code you already run. Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

For a comparison of hybrid cloud platforms, see the 9 best hybrid cloud platforms in 2026. For teams looking to consolidate multiple clouds onto one platform, the same GVC model applies across providers.

FAQ

What is a hybrid cloud and how does it work?

A hybrid cloud combines private infrastructure, either on premises or in a dedicated environment, with public cloud services from providers like AWS, GCP, or Azure. Workloads and data are distributed across both environments based on requirements such as compliance, latency, cost, and scalability. Secure networking and a shared identity model connect the environments so they operate as one system.

How do I decide which workloads should run on premises versus in the public cloud?

Evaluate each workload against six criteria: data gravity and residency, latency to users or dependent systems, regulatory requirements, demand pattern (steady versus bursty), hardware specificity, and team skills. Workloads with large on-premises datasets or strict data sovereignty rules stay on premises. Workloads with global users or unpredictable demand fit the public cloud. Most organizations end up with a mix.

What are the first steps to deploy a hybrid cloud?

Start by inventorying every application, database, and data flow. Classify each workload against the placement criteria and set RTO and RPO targets for critical systems. Then design network connectivity between environments with dedicated interconnects or IPsec VPN tunnels, and federate one identity provider across all locations.

What security risks are unique to hybrid cloud deployments?

The risks specific to hybrid include an expanded attack surface across network boundaries, inconsistent security policies between environments, fragmented identity with long-lived credentials crossing sites, data exposure in transit between environments, visibility gaps from split logging, configuration drift, shared responsibility confusion, and compliance scope creep when regulated data moves to unapproved locations.

How do I keep security policies consistent across on-premises and cloud environments?

Adopt policy as code using tools like Open Policy Agent or Kyverno, stored in a single Git repository and applied to every environment through your CI/CD pipeline. Pair this with a single identity provider, workload identity federation for service-to-service authentication, and centralized logging so policy violations are detected regardless of where they occur.

Can I run Kubernetes across both on-premises and public cloud?

Yes. Options include running separate clusters in each environment managed with GitOps tools like Argo CD, using hyperscaler hybrid Kubernetes products such as Amazon EKS Anywhere or Google Distributed Cloud, or adopting a platform layer that abstracts cluster management. Whichever option you choose, enforce consistent policy, mTLS on cross-cluster traffic, and centralized observability.

What tools do I need for hybrid cloud infrastructure as code and governance?

You need infrastructure as code tools (Terraform, OpenTofu, or Pulumi) for provisioning, policy-as-code tools (Open Policy Agent, Kyverno) for guardrails, GitOps controllers (Argo CD, Flux) for deployment, and a secrets management system (HashiCorp Vault or cloud-native secret stores). No single tool covers every layer, so integration between them is essential.

How does Control Plane help with hybrid cloud deployment?

Control Plane lets you define a GVC that spans AWS, GCP, and Azure regions, on-premises servers joined with MK8s, and existing clusters connected with BYOK. Each workload runs in every location of its GVC behind one global endpoint, so a failed site’s traffic goes to the surviving locations. Security defaults like deny-by-default firewalls, mTLS, and built-in secrets management apply to workloads in every location of a GVC. Control Plane handles Day 2 operations including autoscaling, Capacity AI right-sizing, and observability.

How do I test failover between on-premises and cloud environments?

Simulate a location failure by taking down one environment and verifying that traffic shifts to the surviving location within your defined recovery time objective. Test backup integrity by restoring data in a clean environment. Run these drills on a regular schedule and document results for compliance audits.

What is the biggest mistake organizations make when deploying a hybrid cloud?

Treating hybrid cloud as a one-time migration rather than an ongoing operating model. Workload placement, security policies, cost optimization, and compliance posture all require continuous review. Organizations that deploy and forget end up with configuration drift, credential sprawl, and environments that are hybrid in name but siloed in practice.

title: Kubernetes in Production: Reference Architecture, Zero-Downtime Upgrades, Autoscaling, and Running Postgres in Containers
description:
A production-ready Kubernetes cluster starts with a managed control plane, worker nodes across three availability zones, an ingress controller or gateway behind a cloud load balancer, cluster and pod autoscaling, and stateful data either in a managed database or in an operator-managed database with replicas across zones. The hard part is Day 2: upgrades, scaling, failover, and security patches, which is why many teams run workloads on a platform that operates Kubernetes for them; Control Plane runs containers across AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own servers with autoscaling, failover, and Day 2 operations handled, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

  • Architecture. Use a managed control plane (EKS, GKE, or AKS), separate system and workload node pools, an ingress controller or Gateway API implementation behind a cloud load balancer, cert-manager for TLS, and network policies for isolation.
  • Upgrades. Read release notes, check for deprecated APIs, upgrade staging first, upgrade the control plane, then roll through node pools one at a time with surge nodes and PodDisruptionBudgets.
  • Autoscaling. Layer the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) for replica count, the Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) for right-sizing, and a node autoscaler (Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter) for capacity. KEDA adds event-driven triggers.
  • Stateful data. Managed databases are the simplest path. When you need Postgres in Kubernetes, use an operator such as CloudNativePG with replicas across zones, automated failover, and rehearsed backup and restore.
  • When not to run it yourself. If your team spends more time operating Kubernetes than shipping product, a platform that handles Day 2 for you is the faster path.

What is a simple Kubernetes cluster architecture for production, including ingress and load balancer traffic flow?

A production cluster has three layers: the control plane, the node pools, and the networking stack that carries traffic from the internet to your pods.

Reference architecture

Managed control plane. Use a managed Kubernetes service so the cloud provider runs etcd, the API server, and control plane upgrades. The three major options are Amazon EKS, Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS).

Node pools. Create at least two node pools. A small system node pool runs cluster add-ons (CoreDNS, metrics-server, the ingress controller). A workload node pool runs your application pods. Spread both pools across three availability zones. Use topology spread constraints or pod anti-affinity rules so replicas land in different zones. Set resource requests and limits on every pod so the scheduler can place pods accurately.

Ingress and gateway layer. An ingress controller or a Gateway API implementation sits behind a cloud load balancer and routes external HTTP and HTTPS traffic to Kubernetes Services. Use cert-manager to issue and renew TLS certificates from Let’s Encrypt or an internal CA. Use external-dns to keep DNS records in sync with your routes. Apply network policies to restrict traffic between namespaces.

Secrets management. Store secrets in an external secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, or HashiCorp Vault) and sync them into the cluster with the External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI Driver.

Request path from DNS to pod

  1. DNS resolution. The client resolves your domain. The record, kept current by external-dns, points to the cloud load balancer.
  2. Cloud load balancer. The load balancer accepts the connection, optionally terminates TLS, and forwards traffic to the ingress controller’s pods, either through node ports or directly to pod IPs (IP target mode on the AWS Load Balancer Controller, container-native load balancing on GKE). The load balancer’s health checks decide which ingress targets receive traffic.
  3. Ingress controller or gateway. The controller terminates TLS if the load balancer did not, matches the host and path, and forwards the request to the right Kubernetes Service. Most ingress controllers read the Service’s endpoints and send traffic directly to pod IPs.
  4. Service. The Service selects ready pods by label. kube-proxy or a CNI plugin such as Cilium balances connections across pod IPs.
  5. Pod. The container handles the request. Readiness probes decide whether a pod is listed as a Service endpoint. Liveness probes restart a container that has stopped responding.

Component table

Component Purpose Common open-source choice
Gateway or ingress controller HTTP routing, TLS termination Gateway API implementations (Envoy Gateway, Cilium, Istio, Contour)
TLS certificates Automated certificate issuance and renewal cert-manager
DNS automation Sync DNS records with routes external-dns
CNI plugin Pod networking, network policy Cilium, Calico
Metrics Cluster and application metrics Prometheus
Tracing Traces, metrics, and logs OpenTelemetry
Secrets sync External secrets into Kubernetes External Secrets Operator
Policy engine Admission control, compliance OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno

The community ingress-nginx controller was retired in March 2026 and receives no further releases or security fixes. The Kubernetes project recommends migrating to the Gateway API.

How do I plan zero downtime Kubernetes upgrades and migrations while keeping AI infrastructure compliant and stable?

Kubernetes ships about three minor releases a year, and the project maintains release branches for the three most recent minor versions; the Kubernetes releases page lists the current versions and their end-of-life dates. Each release can remove APIs and change defaults, so a repeatable upgrade process keeps routine upgrades from turning into incidents.

Upgrade runbook

  1. Read the release notes. The release notes and the deprecated API migration guide list every removal and behavior change.
  2. Check API deprecations. The API server exposes the apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis metric, and managed services such as EKS and GKE flag deprecated API usage before an upgrade. Fix manifests and Helm charts before you upgrade.
  3. Respect version skew. Upgrade one minor version at a time; the control plane cannot skip minor versions, and kubelets may lag the API server by up to three minor versions. Upgrade add-ons (CNI, CoreDNS, CSI drivers, kube-proxy) to versions that support the target.
  4. Upgrade a staging cluster first. Apply the new version to a non-production cluster that mirrors production. Run integration and smoke tests, and confirm every controller, operator, and custom resource still works.
  5. Upgrade the control plane. On a managed service this is a console action, a CLI command, or a Terraform change. Running pods keep serving while the control plane updates.
  6. Upgrade node pools one at a time. Add surge nodes on the new version, then cordon and drain old nodes. PodDisruptionBudgets limit how many replicas of an application can be evicted at once. Readiness probes keep traffic off replacement pods until they can serve. Give pods a preStop delay and a termination grace period so endpoint removal finishes before shutdown. Single-replica applications still drop traffic, and a PodDisruptionBudget that allows zero disruptions blocks the drain.
  7. Validate after each pool. Check pod health, error rates, and latency before moving to the next pool.

Blue/green cluster upgrades

For large version jumps, or when an in-place rollback is unacceptable, build a new cluster on the target version, deploy workloads to it, shift traffic at the load balancer or DNS layer, and retire the old cluster. This costs more while both clusters run and removes in-place upgrade risk. Stateful data must be replicated or restored into the new cluster, and DNS TTLs set how fast traffic moves.

GPU and AI workload considerations

The NVIDIA driver on the node, the CUDA version in the container image, and the framework version must be compatible. Validate the combination in staging before you roll GPU node pools.

Compliance and change management

Keep a change record for every upgrade: what changed, who approved it, what was tested, and how to roll it back. Store cluster configuration in version control so auditors can see the history of every change.

Which managed Kubernetes solution is best for autoscaling EC2 nodes and automatically scaling pods?

Kubernetes autoscaling works at two layers. Pod autoscaling changes how many pods run or how large they are. Node autoscaling changes the compute underneath them. On AWS, the usual answer is EKS with the HPA for pods and either Karpenter or EKS Auto Mode, which runs Karpenter for you, for EC2 nodes. GKE and AKS offer managed node provisioning of their own.

Pod autoscaling

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA). The HPA adjusts replica count from CPU, memory, or custom metrics. HPA computes CPU utilization as a percentage of the pod’s request, so accurate requests matter. Stabilization windows prevent flapping during short spikes.

Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA). The VPA recommends or sets resource requests from observed usage. Do not let VPA and HPA act on the same CPU or memory metric; running VPA in recommendation mode alongside HPA avoids the conflict.

KEDA. KEDA scales pods from event sources such as queue depth, stream lag, cron schedules, or Prometheus queries. It manages HPA objects for you and can scale a workload to zero.

Node autoscaling

Cluster Autoscaler. The Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled and removes underused nodes. It works with node groups and managed node pools on all three major clouds.

Karpenter. Karpenter is an open-source node provisioner first built for AWS. It launches right-sized instances directly from the cloud API instead of scaling fixed node groups, and it consolidates workloads onto fewer or cheaper nodes when demand drops.

GKE Autopilot and node auto-provisioning. GKE Autopilot manages nodes for you and bills general-purpose pods by the resources they request; pods that select specific hardware, such as GPUs or a machine series, are billed by node. On GKE Standard, node auto-provisioning creates and deletes node pools as needed.

AKS node autoprovisioning. AKS node autoprovisioning, built on Karpenter, picks VM sizes from pending pod requests so you don’t predefine a node pool for each VM size.

Autoscaling comparison

What scales Trigger Typical reaction time Caveats
HPA (pod replicas) CPU, memory, custom metrics Seconds to low tens of seconds Needs accurate requests; new pods still need scheduling, image pull, and readiness, which takes minutes if nodes must be added
VPA (pod resources) Observed usage Minutes; may recreate pods unless in-place resize is enabled Conflicts with HPA on the same metric
KEDA (pod replicas) Queue depth, stream lag, cron, external metrics Seconds to low tens of seconds Adds a controller to operate; supports scale to zero
Cluster Autoscaler (nodes) Unschedulable pods Minutes Limited to the instance types in each node group
Karpenter (nodes) Unschedulable pods, consolidation Usually faster than node-group scaling GPU instances launch slower; spot interruptions need fallback capacity
GKE Autopilot (nodes) Pod scheduling Minutes Less control over node configuration

On Control Plane, each workload autoscales per location between a minimum and maximum, targeting concurrent requests, requests per second, CPU, memory, or latency depending on workload type, and KEDA is available for event-driven scaling. Capacity AI, Control Plane’s right-sizing of CPU and memory based on historical usage, adjusts resource allocation over time. Capacity AI is not used for GPU workloads or for workloads that autoscale on CPU or on multiple metrics.

Best platforms for running stateful workloads like Postgres in containers

Running Postgres in production needs durable storage, replication with automated failover, rehearsed backups, and a plan for major version upgrades. There are three broad options.

Managed database services

The cloud provider handles replication, failover, backups, and minor-version patching, and provides tooling for major version upgrades that you schedule.

  • AWS: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL
  • GCP: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL and AlloyDB
  • Azure: Azure Database for PostgreSQL

You give up some control and portability in exchange for a lighter operational load.

Kubernetes operators

Operators turn Postgres lifecycle tasks (provisioning, replication, failover, backup, restore) into Kubernetes resources. The established open-source operators are:

  • CloudNativePG
  • Zalando’s Postgres Operator
  • Crunchy Data’s PGO

They run Postgres pods with persistent volumes, configure streaming replication, promote a replica when the primary fails, and archive WAL to object storage for point-in-time recovery.

Platforms with packaged Postgres templates

On Control Plane, the template catalog includes highly available Postgres (a Patroni cluster of at least three members with one leader and streaming replicas) and Postgres Multi-Location (one Patroni cluster stretched across locations with a single primary, streaming replicas in other locations, automatic promotion when a location is lost, and a leader-routing proxy per location). pgEdge and CockroachDB templates are also available. Stateful workloads on Control Plane use volume sets: persistent volumes with a performance class, snapshots, and restore from snapshot.

Key operational considerations

Synchronous vs. asynchronous replication. With synchronous replication, the primary confirms a commit only after a replica has it, so failover to that synchronous replica loses no committed transactions. The cost is added write latency, and writes stall when no synchronous replica is available unless the operator falls back to asynchronous mode, which drops the guarantee. Asynchronous replication is faster and can lose the most recent transactions during failover. Most operators let you choose.

Backups and point-in-time recovery. Take base backups to object storage and archive WAL continuously. Rehearse restores on a schedule.

Storage classes and volume performance. Use SSD-backed storage classes sized for your IOPS and throughput. Block volumes such as Amazon EBS and Persistent Disk are zonal, so a pod cannot follow its volume to another zone; replica failover is what survives a zone loss. Test what happens when a volume detaches, a node dies, or a zone goes down.

Major version upgrades. pg_upgrade needs a short outage. Copy mode scales with data size; link mode takes minutes but leaves no fallback once the new cluster starts. Run ANALYZE afterward. Logical replication to a new cluster shortens the cutover, but it does not carry DDL or sequence values, and tables need primary keys or a replica identity.

Do not autoscale database replicas with HPA. Replication topology and consistency rules make reactive scaling unsafe. Change replica counts deliberately through the operator.

Decision table

Factor Managed service Kubernetes operator Platform template
Operational burden Lowest Highest Low to moderate
Portability Tied to one cloud Any conformant cluster Any cloud or location Control Plane runs on, including your own clusters and servers
Customization Limited Full Template values
Failover Automatic when high availability is enabled Operator-managed Automatic Patroni promotion (Postgres templates)
Backup and PITR Built in Operator-configured Optional logical or WAL-G backups, off by default; restore is manual
Major version upgrades Managed or semi-managed Declarative in CloudNativePG and PGO; needs planning Manual, needs planning

Why is Kubernetes considered complex for AI infrastructure teams and what are the biggest operational pain points?

AI and ML teams face every standard Kubernetes challenge plus problems specific to GPUs, large models, and fast-moving frameworks.

  1. GPU scheduling and node pools. Kubernetes treats GPUs as extended resources, and a pod gets whole GPUs unless you add sharing such as MIG, time-slicing, or MPS, or allocate devices through Dynamic Resource Allocation. Mitigation: isolate GPU node pools with labels and taints, and use the NVIDIA GPU Operator to manage drivers and the device plugin.
  2. Driver and CUDA version management. A mismatch between the node driver, the CUDA version in the image, and the framework causes crashes or silent failures. Mitigation: pin driver versions in node images and test the full stack in CI.
  3. Image sizes and pull times. AI images often run to several gigabytes, and pulling one onto a cold node can take minutes. Mitigation: pre-pull or cache images on GPU nodes and trim images with multi-stage builds.
  4. Autoscaling GPU nodes with slow cold starts. GPU instances take longer to launch than CPU instances and are often capacity-constrained, so a scale-up can leave pods pending. Mitigation: keep a warm GPU node or reserved capacity for latency-sensitive inference.
  5. Multi-tenant isolation. Teams sharing a GPU cluster can starve each other. Mitigation: use namespaces, ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges, and priority classes.
  6. Networking and egress costs. Moving large datasets between zones or out of a cloud adds transfer charges. Mitigation: keep data and compute in the same zone and use topology-aware scheduling.
  7. Storage for models and datasets. Model checkpoints and datasets need high-throughput storage that many pods can read at once. Mitigation: use shared file storage through CSI drivers (Amazon FSx for Lustre, Filestore, Azure Files) or object storage, and cache hot models on local disks.
  8. Skills gap. Most ML engineers are not Kubernetes operators. Mitigation: give them a platform layer that hides cluster details.

On Control Plane, workloads can attach NVIDIA GPUs, and the pricing page lists models from T4 to B200. Control Plane handles scheduling, autoscaling, and rolling updates for those workloads.

Where can I find the best in class container management and networking tools?

The CNCF Landscape is the most complete directory of cloud native projects.

Service mesh. Istio and Linkerd add mutual TLS, traffic management, and service-to-service telemetry.

CNI plugins. Cilium is eBPF-based and covers network policy, observability, and service mesh features. Calico is widely deployed and supports network policy and BGP.

Ingress and Gateway API. The Gateway API is the successor to the Ingress resource, with richer routing, traffic splitting, and role-based configuration. Implementations include Cilium, Istio, Contour, and Envoy Gateway; cloud options include the AWS Load Balancer Controller and GKE Ingress.

Observability. Prometheus for metrics, OpenTelemetry for traces, metrics, and logs, and Grafana with Alertmanager for dashboards and alerting.

Policy engines. OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno enforce admission policies such as required labels, no privileged containers, and mandatory resource limits.

For a comparison of platforms that manage Kubernetes for you, see the best Kubernetes management platforms roundup.

When not to run Kubernetes yourself, and how Control Plane fits

If your engineers spend more hours on cluster upgrades, node patching, autoscaler tuning, and incident response than on your product, operating Kubernetes is costing you delivery time.

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into what Control Plane calls a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a set of locations a workload runs across. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads on AWS, GCP, and Azure; on existing Kubernetes clusters, through Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), Control Plane’s option for connecting a cluster you already run; and on your own servers, including on premises, through Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), Control Plane’s way of turning your own servers into managed locations. Many teams run it in one cloud as well.

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, Capacity AI right-sizing, built-in observability, and security, with no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate. With MK8s, Control Plane operates the Kubernetes layer on the servers you join; with BYOK, you keep running the cluster you connected.

Every workload update is a rolling update: the previous version keeps serving until the new version reports ready. Readiness and liveness probes decide when a replica takes traffic and when it restarts. A workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Those locations can be two regions of one cloud or locations on different providers. For the cost side of that design, see active-active vs. active-passive costs.

Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. Control Plane ships Terraform and Pulumi providers, so workloads fit the same infrastructure-as-code review process as the rest of your stack, plus an MCP server for AI assistants.

Teams weighing whether to build a platform team at all can read the guide to production-grade infrastructure without a platform team.

FAQ

Short answers to common production Kubernetes questions.

What is a simple Kubernetes cluster architecture for production, including ingress and load balancer traffic flow?

A managed control plane (EKS, GKE, or AKS), worker nodes across three availability zones, and an ingress controller or Gateway API implementation behind a cloud load balancer. Traffic flows from DNS to the load balancer, through the ingress or gateway where TLS usually terminates, to a Kubernetes Service, and then to pods that pass their readiness probes.

How do I plan zero downtime Kubernetes upgrades and migrations while keeping AI infrastructure compliant and stable?

Read the release notes and fix deprecated APIs, upgrade a staging cluster, upgrade the production control plane, then roll node pools one at a time with surge nodes and PodDisruptionBudgets. For AI workloads, validate GPU driver and CUDA compatibility before touching GPU node pools, and keep a change record for every upgrade.

Which managed Kubernetes solution is best for autoscaling EC2 nodes and automatically scaling pods?

On AWS, EKS with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for pods and Karpenter, or EKS Auto Mode, which runs Karpenter for you, for EC2 nodes. Karpenter launches right-sized instances directly instead of scaling fixed node groups. Add KEDA if workloads scale on queue depth or event streams.

What are the best platforms for running stateful workloads like Postgres in containers?

Managed database services (RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Azure Database for PostgreSQL) carry the lightest operational load. Inside Kubernetes, operators such as CloudNativePG, Zalando’s Postgres Operator, and Crunchy Data’s PGO handle replication, failover, and backup. Control Plane’s template catalog includes Patroni-based highly available and multi-location Postgres.

Why is Kubernetes considered complex for AI infrastructure teams?

GPU scheduling, driver and CUDA compatibility, large image pulls, slow GPU node launches, multi-tenant contention, and the gap between ML engineering and cluster operations are the main sources. Many AI teams adopt a platform layer to absorb them.

How does pod autoscaling work with node autoscaling in Kubernetes?

The HPA adds or removes pod replicas based on metrics. When new pods cannot be scheduled, the node autoscaler (Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter) adds nodes, and it removes nodes that become underused after pods scale down. Configure both layers together.

What are the biggest operational pain points of running Kubernetes in production?

Upgrade churn across Kubernetes versions, node images, and add-ons is the most persistent. Autoscaler tuning, secrets management, network policy, observability, and incident response for stateful workloads follow. Teams without platform engineers often find Day 2 work takes more time than the initial setup.

Can I run production Kubernetes workloads without managing a cluster myself?

Yes. On Control Plane-managed compute in AWS, GCP, and Azure regions there is no cluster to operate, and autoscaling, rolling updates, observability, and security are built in. You can also connect existing clusters with BYOK, which you keep operating, or join your own servers with MK8s, where Control Plane operates the Kubernetes layer.

How do I run Postgres with high availability across multiple cloud regions?

Run a Patroni cluster with a single primary, streaming replicas in other regions, and leader-aware routing in each location, and decide whether replication to the remote regions is synchronous or asynchronous; synchronous commits across regions add a network round trip to every write. Control Plane’s Postgres Multi-Location template packages this design.

Where can I find the best container management and networking tools for Kubernetes?

Start with the CNCF Landscape. For CNI, look at Cilium and Calico; for service mesh, Istio and Linkerd; for observability, Prometheus and OpenTelemetry; for policy, OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno.
