title: AI can generate the interface. What makes it worth caring about?
description:
As more product work is generated from shared patterns, designers need to decide where an experience should surprise, celebrate, or simply leave someone alone.

Imagine asking an AI tool to design a task-completion state.

The result has a checkmark, a friendly message, and a small burst of confetti. It uses the right components. The spacing matches the system. The animation is polished.

Now imagine that same response after two different tasks.

In one, someone has finished setting up a business they have spent months trying to launch. In the other, an administrator has updated the forty-seventh record of the morning.

The component is consistent. The experiences should probably be different.

Nothing in the confetti explains which moment deserves it. That decision depends on what the person has done, how often they do it, and whether they want the product to make an occasion of it.

As AI becomes more capable of assembling interfaces from established patterns, this distinction deserves more attention. We are getting better at telling tools what belongs to our product. We also need to decide what belongs to the moment.

Matching the system is an incomplete definition of quality

There are good reasons to care about consistency. People should not have to relearn familiar actions on every screen. Teams should not spend their time reconstructing decisions already made elsewhere.

Figma’s guidance on working with its agent describes how components, guidelines, examples, and task-specific context help generated work reflect a team’s product. That is useful progress. It also makes clear that consistency depends on the context supplied to the tool.

But a faithful rendering of a system can still be an emotionally inappropriate response.

A success message can be correct and patronizing. An illustration can match the brand and occupy space someone needs for their work. A playful loading state can be charming until it appears during a time-sensitive task.

These failures are difficult to identify by inspecting the component alone. They emerge from the relationship between the component and the person encountering it.

In my earlier article about design-system judgment, I explored the distinction between enforcing rules and deciding whether a pattern is appropriate. Expression brings another version of that problem into view: a detail can follow every rule we wrote and still misunderstand the occasion.

I want software to have room for color, humor, beauty, and small surprises.

I want an interaction to feel satisfying, even when satisfaction cannot be reduced to a shorter completion time.

I also want the product to recognize when I have work to do.

Pleasure has a history beyond the AI conversation

Designers were studying this long before generative interfaces.

Don Norman’s work on emotional design considers appearance, the experience of using something, and the meaning people attach to it. That gives us a broader vocabulary than “add delight.” Pleasure can come from how something looks, how well it responds, or what owning and using it means to someone.

Therese Fessenden’s distinction between surface and deep delight is useful here too. An amusing detail can create a moment of pleasure, while a well-considered workflow can produce a quieter satisfaction that lasts through the task.

The second does not make the first disposable.

A product can be dependable and exuberant. A useful tool can have a peculiar illustration or a lovely transition simply because someone cared about making it enjoyable. We do not have to defend every expressive choice by pretending it saves three seconds.

But we do have to understand what it asks of the person.

A color choice might make a screen more inviting without adding a step. A celebration might demand attention. A joke might require cultural familiarity. A transition might make a relationship easier to understand — or force someone to wait.

“Delight” is too generous a label to apply before finding out which of those things happened.

A playful product still needs restraint

Duolingo offers an instructive example because expression is already central to its identity.

In its account of redesigning the app’s core tabs, the team describes experimenting with several visual directions, then finding tensions between consistency and purpose. An illustrated header on every tab created uniformity, but some illustrations occupied space without communicating anything useful.

The solution included different header sizes for different purposes, with titles kept in consistent positions.

That is a more useful lesson than “make every screen playful.” A recognizable product can vary its emphasis while preserving familiar structure. The team’s own account shows that even an expressive brand needs to ask where an illustration earns its space.

This matters when a design becomes an example for AI to reuse.

If the reference screen has a large illustration, should the next screen have one too? Is the illustration a general rule, a possibility, or a response to a particular situation?

A tool can reproduce the visible answer while missing the reason for it. So can a designer working from an incomplete specification.

As generation becomes easier, that missing explanation can travel further. A choice made for one meaningful moment becomes the default for several ordinary ones.

The expressive detail survives. Its purpose does not.

Consistency can include a change in tone

Mailchimp’s voice-and-tone guidance makes an important distinction: its voice remains recognizable, while its tone responds to the reader’s circumstances.

The guide welcomes humor but gives clarity priority. It asks writers to consider whether someone has finished a campaign or is confused and looking for help, and warns against forcing a joke.

This is a practical way to preserve personality without requiring the same emotional performance everywhere.

A product’s identity can live in how sensitively it changes.

Warmth during onboarding might mean encouragement. Warmth after an error might mean a direct explanation, preserved work, and a clear next step. The writing can sound like the same company without treating both situations as opportunities for comedy.

That distinction should also shape instructions given to AI.

“Make it friendly and playful” leaves a great deal unresolved. Friendly to whom? Playful at what point? What has just happened?

A more useful instruction describes the situation: the user’s work is safe; they need to understand why the action failed; avoid humor; make the recovery path obvious.

There is still room for good writing within those constraints. The constraints establish what the writing owes the person.

Expression can make an interface clearer

It is tempting to organize this debate as a negotiation between expressive design and usable design. Google’s research on Material 3 Expressive complicates that framing.

In its published research account, Google describes an email interface where the Send button became larger, more prominent, and closer to the keyboard. Participants located it faster. The expressive treatment also changed hierarchy and placement; its benefit cannot be attributed to decoration alone.

The same report includes a less successful experiment: a playlist replaced familiar rows with a scattered arrangement of album artwork. Participants found it visually exciting, but usability suffered.

These are findings from Google’s tested designs, not evidence that every product should adopt the same aesthetic. Together, they show why the actual interaction matters more than the adjective attached to it.

Color can establish emphasis. Shape can distinguish actions. Motion can show where something went. An expressive decision may help people understand a product while making it more pleasurable.

The question is what remains legible after we introduce it.

A familiar control can carry considerable character. A surprising arrangement can remove the very cues someone needs to use it. Designers have to examine both effects, rather than accepting “on brand” or “more delightful” as sufficient explanations.

The same delight can become someone else’s interruption

Asana’s celebrations show why preference belongs in this discussion.

Its 2016 introduction of an expanded celebration system described occasional animated characters appearing after task completion, with celebrations enabled through settings.

A 2018 community discussion captures the other side: a customer found the characters intrusive and asked how to disable them. A reply explained the setting.

That exchange does not establish how most users felt. It does show that the same detail can be welcome to one person and unwelcome to another.

This is where the word “delight” can hide an assumption. We describe our intention as though it were already the user’s response.

A celebration designed to recognize accomplishment may become an obstacle during repetitive work. Something enjoyed privately may feel inappropriate during a presentation. Someone may like the character and still prefer to finish without watching it.

Giving people control is part of designing the experience well.

For motion, the stakes can extend beyond preference. W3C’s guidance for Animation from Interactions, a Level AAA criterion, explains why people need ways to disable nonessential interaction-triggered movement, including the potential for vestibular symptoms.

An expressive experience should have a considered reduced-motion version. Removing movement should leave clear feedback, meaningful hierarchy, and an understandable result.

There are many ways to make something feel good. Movement is one of them.

AI changes how easily the wrong detail can spread

None of these problems began with AI. Teams have copied patterns without understanding them for years.

What AI introduces is another way to reproduce those decisions — and an opportunity to be more explicit about them.

A library might describe a celebration’s colors, duration, and animation curve. That describes the asset. It says little about whether a celebration should happen after someone completes a tutorial, pays a bill, or removes an account.

Those are different events even if the system labels all three “success.”

Here is a hypothetical rule worth testing: a fuller acknowledgment for a meaningful first achievement; brief feedback for repeated routine actions; direct, restrained language for sensitive outcomes.

That rule will not fit every product. Its value is that it gives the team something concrete to question.

Is the first achievement actually meaningful to the person, or merely valuable to our onboarding metrics? Does a repeated action become meaningful when it completes a larger goal? Are we assuming we know how someone feels because we know which button they pressed?

A good specification should leave those questions visible.

AI can help explore expressive alternatives: different copy, motion treatments, layouts, and levels of emphasis. There is no need to claim that surprise or beauty belongs exclusively to human production.

But producing an alternative and establishing when it is welcome are different kinds of work.

If we evaluate generated interfaces mainly by how closely they match the library, we will favor what is easiest to compare. If we ask whether the experience suits the occasion, we need examples, use over time, and feedback from the people living with it.

That is a broader evaluation than a screenshot review can provide.

“Worth caring about” should not mean harder to leave

There is another complication: products can use expression to serve goals people did not choose.

A cheerful character might encourage a useful habit. It might also make declining an offer feel like disappointing someone. A reward animation might acknowledge progress, or distract from how little progress actually occurred.

Those possibilities need to remain in the argument. Emotional design is capable of persuasion as well as pleasure.

The appropriate question is whose purpose the detail advances.

Does it help someone enjoy an activity they value? Does it acknowledge something they accomplished? Or does it make the product’s preferred behavior harder to refuse?

Time spent and repeat visits cannot answer that on their own. Someone may return because the product is useful, because leaving is costly, or because a mechanic creates pressure. Those explanations have different implications for design.

I am interested in software people appreciate using. That requires taking their ability to dislike a detail seriously, even when it is the detail the team loves most.

Give the expressive decision a proper review

In a product team, this work needs a place before the final polish pass.

For a proposed expressive moment, I would want to see it in three conditions: the first encounter, repeated use, and a situation where the person is rushed or something has gone wrong.

The same animation may behave beautifully in isolation and become tiring in a sequence. The same line of copy may be reassuring on a quiet afternoon and dismissive during a failure.

Research should make room for those differences. Watch whether people can continue. Ask what they think the response means. Find out whether they want to see it again. Include people who prefer less motion or sound, and test whether the experience still communicates clearly.

These observations will not produce a universal delight score. They can help us distinguish a detail people value from one they tolerate.

This also changes what we document.

Alongside the approved example, record the circumstance it serves, when to scale it back, and a case where it should not be used. Give both people and AI tools a reason to choose differently.

A system with that kind of guidance can protect character. It can make room for an unusual illustration, a distinctive rhythm, or a moment of celebration while keeping everyday work dependable.

The alternative is to encode only what is easy to repeat and hope the rest survives delivery.

I want the products we build with AI to have more room for pleasure: a color choice that lifts a screen, a response that acknowledges effort, a transition that feels unusually right. I also want that pleasure to survive actual use, beyond the first demo and the designer’s own preferences.

Return to the two completed tasks. The new business owner and the administrator may both need confirmation. One might welcome a moment to take in what they have accomplished. The other might want the next record ready.

AI can generate both responses.

We still have to notice that the occasions are different.

title: What AI has changed in Design Systems, and what is still up to us
description:
Three design experts told me how AI is changing the way we build and maintain Design Systems. And led me to think that “the future” is already happening now.

You’ve probably read, or even written, one of those LinkedIn posts about someone building a complete Design System in 20 minutes with Claude. Or in 15 minutes with Gemini. Or… you get the idea.

Those posts made me curious. I had never built a full Design System, although I had set up the basic elements of one before I really dug into AI, and it was as interesting as it was painful. So the promise of building a full one in minutes was appealing.

My mistake? Confusing a UI kit with a Design System, and believing the whole process could really be done in minutes.

At UXDX Berlin last May, two talks about Design Systems made me want to know more about how AI has changed them in the day-to-day of product teams. That curiosity led me to interview three design experts, and to get to the essential part of what a Design System actually is: Marianne Ashton-Booth, Head of Product Design at ITV; David Sward, Chief Design Officer at Siemens; and Nicolas Chatelain, freelance Senior Designer and specialized in Design System and Ops.

Three experts, three different approaches. Nicolas Chatelain bets on a frame that bends without breaking, flexible with teams and ready for AI. David Sward bets on speed with guardrails, with AI as a tool and a human in the loop. Marianne Ashton-Booth bets on people and process, treating the Design System like a product.

The last two had both just given a talk at UXDX when I talked with them, so what follows draws on two different moments with each of them: what they said on stage, and what they told me one-on-one afterwards.

1. AI automates the easy part, but the hard part still belongs to humans

One-on-one after her talk, Marianne Ashton-Booth said something that felt particularly on point to me: “Anybody can spin up prototypes in minutes, and that’s great. But then that gap between what’s actually feasible, what’s actually close to the brand, or close to the actual components that we’ve got, can be quite distant.”

Nicolas Chatelain, whom I interviewed in July, put the same idea in other words: the UI is the easy part of a Design System. “The hardest part, the one that makes a DS work or not, is governance and adoption.”

Neither of them sees the components as the problem; Nicolas even says anyone could, indeed, build a kit while we were talking. What matters is consistency across teams, and across a whole company, and that is the human part of a Design System. A Zeroheight report on the state of Design Systems, published in early 2026, points the same way: 59% of practitioners credit communication and community for their system’s adoption.

On stage, Marianne Ashton-Booth had already named what breaks instead. When a design system fails, she said, “it’s almost never just [the design system’s core operations]. The components are usually fine.” What breaks are the invisible layers underneath: trust, communication, prioritisation, relationships, and shared belief.

2. The bottleneck has moved from production speed to review

“My biggest problem is trying to slow people down with AI,” David Sward told me. Indeed, AI has sped up a lot of processes, all the way to delivery.

Here, he does not mean slowing his team down so that they get used to AI, but keeping them inside the security and compliance rules of a large enterprise. With hundreds of products relying on his system, a mistake would take several hundred million euros to fix. His operating principle: “don’t break things.”

But the fact remains: productivity has risen. And once speed is there, the bottleneck shifts from production to the people who review, validate and keep everything coherent. Nicolas Chatelain and Marianne Ashton-Booth ran into this too.

During Nicolas Chatelain’s mission for an international group, for example, AI-boosted product teams started to outpace the central Design System team, whose original strategy was to lock everything down. His verdict:

“With AI, it’s a total rollback. We have to become much more flexible, because tomorrow people could create a kit in five minutes. If we become useless, they’ll find an even easier way to bypass us.”

Figma’s slots, which let teams put their own content inside a standardised component, are one way to loosen the frame.

At ITV, Marianne Ashton-Booth’s team takes another route and relies on “design system reps” in both design and engineering: “They tend to be the go-to people that have a little bit more prominence and involvement in things like final decisions. It just means that things can keep moving rather than just becoming a bit of a bottleneck.” On stage, she added that rather than treating AI as a separate topic, ITV asked the right question: “What does that mean for the design system? How should our processes evolve?”

These three approaches suggest that there is no single way to handle the bottleneck: it depends on the context, the level of risk, and how far AI has advanced, and been accepted, in the organisation. That is precisely where humans remain useful: understanding at what moment, and to what extent, everyone who holds decision-making power over the Design System should step in, and when they should let go.

3. The Design System is becoming something AI reads

This is the part that sounds most like “the future”, but is actually already the present: making the system readable for machines.

Nicolas Chatelain’s team started watching tools like V0 and Lovable in the second half of 2025, and concluded it was too early to adopt them. They chose to prepare the system instead: tokens migrated to the DTCG (Design Tokens Community Group) standard, a shared format for the values of a system, like colours, spacing or typography, so that every tool, and every AI agent, reads them the same way.

An MCP server (Model Context Protocol) lets an AI agent query the Design System directly, for instance to find the right component or token, instead of guessing. In a field study published in July 2026, Kaelig Deloumeau-Prigent looked at 21 open-source Design Systems: 20 of them offer an MCP server (official or community-built), but only 3 have set up Figma Code Connect, which ties a Figma component to its real code counterpart. Plenty of systems let AI read them, far fewer tie their components back to design.

David Sward’s team uses AI on the other side of the process: a large language model (LLM) compares what teams have implemented with what the Design System is supposed to be, and, in his words, “systematically tells you what to fix.” In his own Design System, AI stays “a tool just like anything else” (an engine harmonises thousands of icons, for instance), and his broader principle holds: “You can’t remove a human from the loop and then expect them to step back in to operate the system if they don’t understand the state the system is in.”

Marianne Ashton-Booth, on her end, is adamant: “There might be parts of [a design system] that become more AI-generated or automated. But a design system isn’t just that part, you know, it’s the people and it’s the process as well. And that’s the bit that I think we’ll still retain.”

Where I think we’re heading: code as the source of truth

These insights led me to believe this is where Design Systems are heading: the code, rather than the design file, is becoming their source of truth. We might already be there. Designers who use AI seem to open Figma less and less (that’s my case), and in teams where shipping and iterating beat perfecting details, the blurring of roles (I talked about it here) doesn’t help.

Nicolas Chatelain said it: “Today, the source of truth has to be the code. Absolutely.” Working in the code removes a layer of abstraction between AI and production, and “tomorrow, when this documentation lives directly in the code, we won’t need Figma anymore.” He admits he may be “completely wrong”, and still finds Figma useful to explore and fine-tune. And I agree with him that Figma isn’t dead. But for me its place in the process has definitely changed.

Concretely, it means that whatever is merged into the code becomes the standard, and design files, documentation and AI agents all read from it. Every review then becomes a governance decision. But as Tony Ward wrote in his recent article “Code as the Source of Truth”, the key is to keep “a subject-matter expert in the loop at every step of the way.” Which leaves the real question: in this new process, who gets to say what goes into the truth?

As for me, meeting these three experts showed me there is no single answer to that question. Each built theirs from their own environment, and in that richness I found keys to meet my own challenges. I hope you will too.

Thanks to UXDX for providing access to the event, and to David Sward, Marianne Ashton-Booth and Nicolas Chatelain for their time.

All of Nicolas Chatelain’s quotes were translated from French.

title: The Fonts app.onepassapps.com Ships: 7 WOFF2 Files, 218,512 Bytes, and the One Your Browser Actually Downloads
description:
I work on OnePassApps, so this is our own product and everything below is a measurement of our own build, taken today from outside the browser and from one tab of the visible Chrome, signed out, with the network cache switched off.

On 4 November 2026 at about 21:40 UTC I fetched the stylesheet our home page loads and read the font files it points at as bytes. This post is about the layer I had not looked at before: the seven web fonts the site ships.

The route

The home page links two stylesheets. One is /shell-fallback.css, 3,054 bytes, the static crash fallback that renders when the bundle fails to load. It carries no font rules at all - I checked, there are zero @font-face blocks in it.

The other is /assets/index-B_evf03w.css, fetched with crossorigin and an explicit content type of text/css; charset=utf-8. Uncompressed it is 242,648 bytes. Asked for Brotli it comes back at 40,833 bytes, with the header content-encoding: br. Both times it answers HTTP 200 with the same ETag, "89dd32c00a2e009fc0329349dbbccb70", and the same cache rule: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.

One family, seven files, fourteen declarations

The stylesheet declares 14 @font-face blocks. They are not 14 different fonts: they are 7 unique declarations, each written out twice, and the two copies of each are byte-for-byte identical. Every block names the same family, Inter Variable, the same style, normal, the same weight range, 100 900, the same display mode, swap, and the same format, woff2-variations.

The only thing that differs between the seven is the file it points at and the unicode-range that file covers:

  • inter-vietnamese-wght-normal - 10,252 bytes
  • inter-greek-ext-wght-normal - 11,232 bytes
  • inter-cyrillic-wght-normal - 18,748 bytes
  • inter-greek-wght-normal - 18,996 bytes
  • inter-cyrillic-ext-wght-normal - 25,960 bytes
  • inter-latin-wght-normal - 48,256 bytes
  • inter-latin-ext-wght-normal - 85,068 bytes

That is 218,512 bytes of font on the server, in seven files with seven different SHA-256 digests.

What a browser actually downloads

Here is the part worth knowing: a first-time visitor downloads one of them.

I opened the home page in a fresh tab with the cache disabled and recorded every network request. Exactly one font was fetched:

/assets/inter-latin-wght-normal-Dx4kXJAl.woff2 - HTTP 200, font/woff2, 48,256 bytes, over HTTP/3.

Not the Vietnamese, not the Greek, not the Cyrillic, not even the Latin Extended. The unicode-range on each block is what decides this: the Latin file declares U+0-FF plus a list of punctuation and symbol blocks, so a page whose text is Latin never needs the other six. I repeated the same measurement on the Text Studio route and got the same single font request.

The browser's own font API agrees. document.fonts reports 14 faces - one per @font-face block, including the duplicates - and exactly two of them read as loaded. The other twelve sit at unloaded, waiting for a character they cover to appear on the page. Nothing is preloaded: there is no link rel=preload for a font anywhere in the page, so the font arrives when the CSS is parsed and the text needs it.

So the 218,512 bytes are the catalogue, and 48,256 bytes is what an English page actually pays for.

Why the weights are a range and not seven files

font-weight: 100 900 with a single woff2-variations file is the variable-font path. One file per script, and the browser interpolates the weight inside it - which is why the family is Inter Variable rather than Inter, and why the computed font-family on the body reads "Inter Variable", Inter, system-ui, sans-serif at a 15px body size. There is no static bold file to fetch.

The fallback chain after the family name matters more than it looks. Inter and system-ui are both there, so if the font file is slow the page still paints in the operating system's own UI face and swaps the real family in when font-display: swap allows it.

The cache rule is the same on every file

All seven font files answer HTTP 200 with content-type: font/woff2 and cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. Each carries its own ETag:

  • inter-vietnamese-wght-normal - "2759cd7f277af7bf9c94ee261d4757f5"
  • inter-greek-ext-wght-normal - "fc33e0f42efd31375bbe011350f72430"
  • inter-cyrillic-wght-normal - "ad67b369dcdfde0a7119965c5f0c2273"
  • inter-greek-wght-normal - "b51265eb3dde6cb9caae832f0d1410dd"
  • inter-cyrillic-ext-wght-normal - "8b5589cbc08333c62904b58b187c1401"
  • inter-latin-wght-normal - "6d816f85b659cca213b3dff1d5fcdfd3"
  • inter-latin-ext-wght-normal - "25e6c942560690c572feb4fbdbca3e"

The names are content-hashed, so a new build gets a new URL and the old one stays valid for a year. Fonts are the one asset class where that pattern is safe to lean on: change a glyph and you change the bytes.

The files are served uncompressed. Asking for Brotli on the Latin subset returns the same 48,256 bytes, because a WOFF2 is already compressed - there is nothing left for the HTTP layer to squeeze.

What the stylesheet says about the family

The design token resolves to one declaration, found once in the file:

--font-sans: "Inter Variable", "Inter", system-ui, sans-serif

and the body inherits it. The Inter name is a second chance for a machine that has Inter installed but not our variable build; system-ui is the last stop.

Limits

One build, one snapshot (4 Nov 2026, about 21:40 UTC), one network, signed out, cache disabled for the browser measurement. I read the seven files the stylesheet names today - if a later build changes the set, these counts change with it. I measured what the browser requested on two routes, the home page and the Text Studio, both in Latin; a page with Cyrillic or Vietnamese text would pull a different subset, and I did not test one. The duplicate declarations are duplicated in the shipped CSS today; whether that is deliberate or a build artefact, I cannot tell from the outside and am not going to guess.

If you want to read the app itself: app.onepassapps.com and the guides.

I work on OnePassApps, the team behind app.onepassapps.com.

title: Amazon ECS Managed Daemons can now collect json-file logs from application containers on Amazon ECS Managed Instances
description:
Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) introduces json-file log driver support for Amazon ECS Managed Instances and log driver volumes for Amazon ECS Managed Daemons. Together, these features let you collect application logs with the observability agent of your choice and forward them to any destination you choose.

With this launch, your application containers on ECS Managed Instances can write their logs as local files in standard Docker json-file format, which most observability agents read natively. Your managed daemons can directly read these files through a volume mount, without specifying host bind mount paths or requiring root privileges. As a result, one managed daemon on each instance can collect logs from every application container that uses the json-file log driver. Amazon ECS keeps each container's logs in a dedicated directory named with the container ID and retains them until the container is removed, so your managed daemon can use native file-based log collection and trace every log back to the container that produced it.

To get started, set the log driver to json-file in the logConfiguration of your application task definition. Next, register a daemon task definition that specifies a volume with logDriverVolumeConfiguration, and mount the volume into your daemon container using mountPoints. You can configure this using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, API, AWS SDKs or AWS CloudFormation. This feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon ECS Managed Instances and Managed Daemons are available, at no additional cost. To learn more, refer to our documentation page and visit Amazon ECS Managed Instances.

title: Parsing SRT subtitles in the browser: the 30-line converter that makes every WebVTT player happy
description:
Parsing SRT subtitles in the browser: the 30-line converter that makes every WebVTT player happy

Disclosure: I'm building RKMovies — an ultra-lightweight 4K media player client (0.91 MB APK, hardware-accelerated decoding, zero telemetry). Site: https://rkmovies.dpdns.org · Android APK: https://rkmovies.dpdns.org/apk · Windows app: https://rkmovies.dpdns.org/desktop

Every video player on Android that is worth using speaks WebVTT. Almost every subtitle file floating around the internet is SRT. They look identical at a glance, but the parsers do not forgive the differences.

The gap is small and annoying:

  • SRT uses a comma in timestamps (00:00:01,500), WebVTT demands a dot (00:00:01.500)
  • SRT cues start with an optional numeric index line, WebVTT does not have one
  • SRT files often ship with a BOM and CRLF line endings

So instead of pulling in a subtitle library (remember: the whole APK is 0.91 MB, every dependency is a size audit), I wrote a tiny converter that runs in the browser when a local subtitle file is loaded:

async function fileToVtt(file) {
  let t = await file.text();
  t = t.replace(/\r/g, "").replace(/^﻿/, "");
  if (/^\s*WEBVTT/.test(t)) return t;
  const out = [];
  for (const b of t.split(/\n{2,}/)) {
    const lines = b.split("\n").filter(l => l.trim() !== "");
    if (/^\d+$/.test(lines[0]?.trim())) lines.shift();
    const tl = lines.shift();
    if (!tl || tl.indexOf("-->") < 0) continue;
    out.push(tl.replace(/,/g, ".") + "\n" + lines.join("\n"));
  }
  return out.length ? "WEBVTT\n\n" + out.join("\n\n") + "\n" : "";
}

The whole thing is ~20 lines. It reuses the same cleanup pass we already run for inline captions (stripping tags like <i> and positioning junk), then hands the result to the player as a Blob URL. From the user's side: pick an .srt file, it just works.

Two edge cases that actually bit me in testing:

  1. Some SRT files use LF only, some CRLF, some have a BOM. Normalizing all three up front saves a "why are my subtitles empty" bug report.
  2. Multi-line cues must stay multi-line. If you flatten them, dialogue and sound effects merge into one unreadable line.

If you are shipping a small player and want subtitles without a dependency, this is the whole trick. WebVTT is forgiving once the commas become dots.

RKMovies runs this on Android (0.91 MB APK with hardware decoding and multi-audio support: https://rkmovies.dpdns.org/apk) and on Windows (https://rkmovies.dpdns.org/desktop). No account, no telemetry.

title: How to Handle OTP in Selenium Java with a Real SMS Number API
description:
Disclosure: I work with HeroSMS, the virtual number provider used in the examples below. Written with AI tools; code and endpoints checked against the HeroSMS API reference.

If you've tried to handle OTP in Selenium WebDriver, you know this test. It types a phone number, clicks "Send code", then sits in Thread.sleep(30000) while you read the code off your phone and type it in. That works on your own machine. In the nightly run nobody types anything, so the next explicit wait fails:

org.openqa.selenium.TimeoutException: Expected condition failed: waiting for url to contain "/welcome". Current url: "https://staging.example.com/signup/verify"
(tried for 15 seconds with 500 milliseconds interval)

The CI runner has no SIM card. This tutorial replaces the human with an API. The test rents a real number, polls for the SMS code from Java with a deadline, types the code after an explicit wait and releases the number in finally. GitHub Actions runs the whole thing on a schedule. Stack: Java 17+, Maven, Selenium 4.52 and JUnit 5.

How to automate OTP in Selenium WebDriver

Selenium can't read SMS because it drives a browser, not a phone. To automate OTP in Selenium:

  1. Rent a phone number through an SMS API and type it into your form.
  2. Poll the API from Java until the code arrives.
  3. Wait for the OTP field with WebDriverWait and type the code into it.

Your test code does the polling, and Selenium only does the typing. The same flow works for sign-up, login and SMS 2FA.

Mocks, test numbers, 2FA off for test users, or a real number

Start with the free options, since real numbers cost money. Selenium's own documentation advises against automating 2FA at all. It suggests these workarounds instead:

  • disable 2FA for test users or in the test environment
  • accept a test-only token
  • skip 2FA for requests from your test machines' IPs
Option What it proves Cost When to run
Mocked SMS sender UI and app logic Free Every PR
Provider test credentials or fictional numbers Your call to the SMS provider; UI with a fixed code Free Every PR
2FA off for test users, or a test-only token Everything after the second factor Free Every PR
TOTP secret in the test Your authenticator-app step Free Every PR
Real rented number A real SMS reaches a real number and your app accepts the code Paid per number Nightly, pre-release

Twilio's test credentials don't connect to real phone numbers. Firebase's fictional test numbers (up to 10, each with a fixed code) send no SMS. If your second factor is an authenticator app, you don't need a phone: generate the TOTP code from the shared secret.

None of these options proves that an SMS actually reaches a phone in your launch country. A real-number test fills that gap. I built the same split (mocks on every PR, real SMS on a schedule) three times before: in Python, for Playwright with a webhook and for Postman and Newman. This post is the Selenium Java version.

What you need

  • Java 17 or later (the CI job below uses 21), Maven 3.6.3 or later, and Chrome. Selenium Manager has been built in since 4.6 and downloads and caches the matching driver. Since 4.11 it can also fetch Chrome for Testing if no browser is installed.
  • A HeroSMS API key and some balance. What you buy is an activation: one number reserved for one service in one country for about 20 minutes. The exact end time is in expiredAt. Numbers cover 180+ countries, so you can usually test in the country you launch in.
  • These environment variables: 
export HEROSMS_API_KEY="<your API key>"
export OTP_SERVICE="<service code>"   # 2-4 letters
export OTP_COUNTRY="<country ID>"     # an integer
export APP_URL="https://staging.example.com"
# optional: export HEROSMS_MAX_PRICE="<price cap per number>"

Service codes and country IDs come from the getServicesList and getCountries endpoints in the HeroSMS API reference. GET /activations/offers/sms without filters returns them too: service codes are the keys of data, and country IDs are the keys inside each service.

To use JUnit 6 (which needs Java 17+), change the BOM version to 6.1.3. The test compiles unchanged because it only uses the Jupiter API. HTTP calls go through the JDK's own HttpClient, so Jackson is the only extra dependency.

Step 1: a small SMS API client in Java 

// src/test/java/com/example/otp/HeroSmsClient.java
package com.example.otp;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Minimal HeroSMS v1 client: rent a number, read the last OTP, finish or cancel. */
public final class HeroSmsClient {
    private static final String API = "https://hero-sms.com/api/v1";
    private static final ObjectMapper JSON = new ObjectMapper();

    private final HttpClient http = HttpClient.newHttpClient(); // immutable, reuse it
    private final String apiKey;

    public HeroSmsClient(String apiKey) {
        if (apiKey == null || apiKey.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("HEROSMS_API_KEY is not set");
        }
        this.apiKey = apiKey;
    }

    /** One rented number. phone is digits without the '+'. */
    public record Activation(String id, String phone, String countryPhoneCode, String expiredAt) {}

    /** Error body from the API: branch on title, not on the HTTP status. */
    public static final class HeroSmsException extends IOException {
        public final int status;
        public final String title;
        public final String details;
        public final transient JsonNode info;
        public final long retryAfter; // seconds, 0 if the header is absent

        HeroSmsException(int status, String title, String details, JsonNode info, long retryAfter) {
            super("HTTP " + status + " " + title + ": " + details);
            this.status = status;
            this.title = title;
            this.details = details;
            this.info = info;
            this.retryAfter = retryAfter;
        }
    }

    public Activation buy(String service, int country, Double maxPrice)
            throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        Map<String, Object> body = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        body.put("service", service);
        body.put("country", country);
        body.put("amount", 1);
        body.put("verificationType", "sms");
        if (maxPrice != null) body.put("maxPrice", maxPrice);

        JsonNode a = call("POST", "/activations", body).path("data").path(0);
        if (a.isMissingNode()) throw new IOException("POST /activations returned no activation");
        return new Activation(a.path("id").asText(), a.path("phone").asText(),
                a.path("countryPhoneCode").asText(), a.path("expiredAt").asText());
    }

    /** data of GET /activations/{id}/otp/last: smsCode and smsText, either may be null. */
    public JsonNode lastOtp(String id) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        return call("GET", "/activations/" + id + "/otp/last", null).path("data");
    }

    /** Closes the activation after the code was used. No refund. */
    public void finish(String id) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        call("POST", "/activations/" + id + "/finish", null);
    }

    /** Cancels an activation that got no SMS. The price is refunded. */
    public void cancel(String id) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        call("DELETE", "/activations/" + id, null);
    }

    private JsonNode call(String method, String path, Object body)
            throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        HttpRequest.Builder req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(API + path))
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(15)) // without it, send() can block forever
                .header("Authorization", "ApiKey " + apiKey)
                .header("Accept", "application/json");
        if (body != null) {
            req.header("Content-Type", "application/json")
               .method(method, HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(JSON.writeValueAsString(body)));
        } else {
            req.method(method, HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.noBody());
        }

        HttpResponse<String> res = http.send(req.build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        String text = res.body() == null ? "" : res.body();
        if (res.statusCode() >= 400) {
            JsonNode err = parse(text);
            long retryAfter = res.headers().firstValue("Retry-After")
                    .map(HeroSmsClient::seconds).orElse(0L);
            throw new HeroSmsException(res.statusCode(), err.path("title").asText(""),
                    err.path("details").asText(""), err.path("info"), retryAfter);
        }
        return parse(text); // 204 No Content -> missing node
    }

    private static JsonNode parse(String text) {
        if (text.isBlank()) return JSON.missingNode();
        try {
            return JSON.readTree(text);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            return JSON.missingNode(); // not JSON
        }
    }

    private static long seconds(String value) {
        try {
            return Long.parseLong(value.trim());
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return 0; // an HTTP date: use the caller's fallback
        }
    }
}
  • Auth is one header, Authorization: ApiKey <key>. The key is read from the environment and never touches the browser.
  • Errors come back as JSON with title and details, and sometimes info. HeroSmsException keeps all three plus the Retry-After header, so callers can branch on title.
  • Always set HttpRequest.timeout. Without it, send() can wait forever, and one stuck request hangs the whole job. With it, a slow request throws an HttpTimeoutException.
  • phone comes back as an integer without the +. asText() keeps every digit.

Step 2: poll for the code with a deadline, not Thread.sleep

A fixed Thread.sleep(30000) is the classic way to wait for an OTP, and it fails in both directions. It's too short when a carrier is slow, and it wastes 28 seconds when the SMS lands in two. Poll instead, and stop at a deadline:

// src/test/java/com/example/otp/SmsCodePoller.java
package com.example.otp;

import com.example.otp.HeroSmsClient.HeroSmsException;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

/** Polls GET /activations/{id}/otp/last until a code arrives or the deadline passes. */
public final class SmsCodePoller {
    private static final Set<String> CLOSED =
            Set.of("ACTIVATION_NOT_ACTIVE", "CANCELED", "FINISHED", "REFUNDED");
    private static final Pattern CODE = Pattern.compile("\\b\\d{4,8}\\b"); // fit it to your template

    private SmsCodePoller() {}

    public static String waitForCode(HeroSmsClient sms, String activationId, Duration timeout)
            throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        long deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos();
        long delayMs = 2_000; // backs off to 10 s
        IOException lastError = null; // becomes the cause if time runs out
        while (System.nanoTime() < deadline) {
            long sleepMs = delayMs;
            try {
                JsonNode otp = sms.lastOtp(activationId);
                lastError = null; // the API answered
                String code = extractCode(otp);
                if (code != null) return code;
                if (!text(otp.path("smsText")).isEmpty()) {
                    throw new IllegalStateException("SMS arrived without a 4-8 digit code: adjust the regex");
                }
            } catch (HeroSmsException e) {
                if (CLOSED.contains(e.title)) {
                    throw e; // closed or expired: stop polling
                } else if (e.status == 429) {
                    sleepMs = (e.retryAfter > 0 ? e.retryAfter : 5) * 1_000; // documented for offers only
                } else if (e.status >= 500) {
                    lastError = e; // server error: retry until the deadline
                } else if (e.status == 400 || e.status == 404) {
                    lastError = null; // open activation, no SMS yet
                } else {
                    throw e; // any other error: stop polling
                }
            } catch (IOException e) {
                lastError = e; // timed-out or dropped request: retry until the deadline
            }
            long leftMs = Duration.ofNanos(deadline - System.nanoTime()).toMillis();
            if (leftMs <= 0) break;
            Thread.sleep(Math.min(sleepMs, leftMs));
            delayMs = Math.min(delayMs * 3 / 2, 10_000);
        }
        throw new IllegalStateException(
                "No SMS for activation " + activationId + " within " + timeout.toSeconds() + " s", lastError);
    }

    static String extractCode(JsonNode otp) {
        String code = text(otp.path("smsCode")).trim();
        if (!code.isEmpty()) return code;
        Matcher m = CODE.matcher(text(otp.path("smsText")));
        return m.find() ? m.group() : null;
    }

    private static String text(JsonNode node) {
        return node.isMissingNode() || node.isNull() ? "" : node.asText(); // NullNode.asText() is "null"
    }
}
  • GET /activations/{activationId}/otp/last returns smsCode (the code) and smsText (the whole message). Either one can be null. When smsCode is empty, the regex takes the first 4-8 digit number from smsText, so adjust it to your SMS template.
  • The API reference doesn't document the response before the first SMS. The poller therefore treats 400, 404 and an empty data as "not yet", unless title says the activation is closed. One side effect: a 404 caused by a wrong ID looks like a timeout.
  • A 5xx response, a timed-out request or a dropped connection is retried until the deadline. If polling runs out of time, the last such error becomes the exception's cause, so a proxy or DNS problem doesn't look like a missing SMS.
  • On 429 the loop honors Retry-After. The reference documents that header only for the offers endpoint, so the loop falls back to 5 seconds when it's absent.
  • The deadline uses System.nanoTime(), which doesn't jump when the runner's clock is adjusted.

Why not use Selenium's own FluentWait? It's generic, so new FluentWait<>(activationId) can poll any object, not just a driver. But Function.apply can't throw checked exceptions, and the polling interval is fixed. The 429 and closed-activation rules would end up wrapped and hidden. A plain loop is easier to read.

Step 3: the Selenium OTP test with JUnit 5 and explicit waits 

// src/test/java/com/example/otp/OtpSignupTest.java
package com.example.otp;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.AfterEach;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Tag;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.condition.EnabledIfEnvironmentVariable;
import org.openqa.selenium.By;
import org.openqa.selenium.StaleElementReferenceException;
import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver;
import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement;
import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver;
import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeOptions;
import org.openqa.selenium.support.ui.ExpectedConditions;
import org.openqa.selenium.support.ui.WebDriverWait;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;

@Tag("real-sms")
@EnabledIfEnvironmentVariable(named = "HEROSMS_API_KEY", matches = ".+")
class OtpSignupTest {
    private static final By PHONE = By.cssSelector("[data-test=phone]");
    private static final By SEND_CODE = By.cssSelector("[data-test=send-code]");
    private static final By OTP = By.cssSelector("[data-test=otp]"); // the input, or a wrapper around one box per digit
    private static final By OTP_BOXES = By.cssSelector("[data-test=otp] input");
    private static final By VERIFY = By.cssSelector("[data-test=verify]");
    private static final By OTP_ERROR = By.cssSelector("[data-test=otp-error]");

    private WebDriver driver;
    private WebDriverWait wait;

    @BeforeEach
    void startBrowser() {
        ChromeOptions options = new ChromeOptions();
        options.addArguments("--headless=new", "--window-size=1366,900");
        driver = new ChromeDriver(options); // Selenium Manager finds or downloads the driver
        wait = new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(15)); // polls every 500 ms
        wait.ignoring(StaleElementReferenceException.class); // OTP boxes may re-render
    }

    @AfterEach
    void quitBrowser() {
        if (driver != null) driver.quit();
    }

    @Test
    void signsUpWithARealSmsCode() throws Exception {
        // Check the config before paying for a number
        String service = env("OTP_SERVICE", null);
        int country = Integer.parseInt(env("OTP_COUNTRY", null));
        String cap = env("HEROSMS_MAX_PRICE", "");
        Double maxPrice = cap.isEmpty() ? null : Double.valueOf(cap);
        String appUrl = env("APP_URL", null);

        HeroSmsClient sms = new HeroSmsClient(System.getenv("HEROSMS_API_KEY"));
        HeroSmsClient.Activation number = sms.buy(service, country, maxPrice);
        long boughtAt = System.nanoTime();
        boolean gotCode = false;
        try {
            driver.get(appUrl + "/signup");
            wait.until(ExpectedConditions.visibilityOfElementLocated(PHONE))
                .sendKeys("+" + number.phone());
            wait.until(ExpectedConditions.elementToBeClickable(SEND_CODE)).click();

            String code = SmsCodePoller.waitForCode(sms, number.id(), Duration.ofSeconds(120));
            gotCode = true;

            typeOtp(wrongCode(code)); // a wrong code must be rejected first
            wait.until(ExpectedConditions.elementToBeClickable(VERIFY)).click();
            wait.until(ExpectedConditions.visibilityOfElementLocated(OTP_ERROR));

            typeOtp(code);
            wait.until(ExpectedConditions.elementToBeClickable(VERIFY)).click();
            wait.until(ExpectedConditions.urlContains("/welcome")); // TimeoutException = test fails
        } finally {
            ActivationCleanup.release(sms, number.id(), gotCode, boughtAt);
        }
    }

    /** One input, or one box per digit: types by index, so it doesn't rely on auto-focus. */
    private void typeOtp(String code) {
        WebElement otp = wait.until(ExpectedConditions.visibilityOfElementLocated(OTP));
        if ("input".equalsIgnoreCase(otp.getTagName())) {
            otp.clear();
            otp.sendKeys(code);
            return;
        }
        wait.until(ExpectedConditions.numberOfElementsToBe(OTP_BOXES, code.length()));
        for (int i = 0; i < code.length(); i++) {
            int index = i;
            String digit = code.substring(i, i + 1);
            wait.until(d -> {
                List<WebElement> boxes = d.findElements(OTP_BOXES); // fresh lookup on every try
                if (boxes.size() <= index) return null; // mid re-render: keep waiting
                WebElement box = boxes.get(index);
                box.clear();
                box.sendKeys(digit);
                return true;
            });
        }
    }

    private static String wrongCode(String code) {
        return (code.startsWith("1") ? "2" : "1") + code.substring(1);
    }

    /** Blank counts as unset: GitHub passes an empty string for a missing variable. */
    private static String env(String name, String fallback) {
        String value = System.getenv(name);
        if (value != null && !value.isBlank()) return value.trim();
        if (fallback != null) return fallback;
        throw new IllegalStateException(name + " is not set");
    }
}

To run it locally, export the variables above and run mvn test -Dgroups=real-sms. If Surefire reports Tests run: 1, ... Skipped: 1, the key wasn't exported in that shell. Once the key is exported, a plain mvn test runs this test too and buys a number. For everyday runs, use mvn test -DexcludedGroups=real-sms.

  • @Tag("real-sms") lets Maven select or exclude the test. @EnabledIfEnvironmentVariable disables it when the key isn't set, so a PR build without the secret never buys a number.
  • The test reads all of its config before buy, and APP_URL has no fallback. A missing or malformed variable therefore fails the test before it pays for a number.
  • Every interaction goes through an explicit wait. WebDriverWait takes a Duration and polls every 500 ms. It ignores NotFoundException by default and throws TimeoutException when time runs out.
  • Use visibilityOfElementLocated for fields, elementToBeClickable for buttons, and numberOfElementsToBe to wait until every OTP box exists.
  • Don't set an implicit wait as well. The Selenium waits page warns against mixing implicit and explicit waits, because the resulting timeouts are unpredictable.
  • Split OTP inputs get one digit per box, by index, with a fresh lookup each time. If a re-render briefly leaves fewer boxes, the lambda returns null and the wait polls again. The wait also ignores StaleElementReferenceException, so a box that re-renders mid-typing is retried instead of failing the test.
  • The wrong-code check proves your app rejects bad input. If your app burns the code after one wrong attempt, drop those three lines. If it submits on the last digit, drop the Verify clicks.
  • For a login or SMS 2FA test, open your login page instead and type the code at the second-factor prompt. If your form has a separate country picker, strip countryPhoneCode (also in the purchase response) from the start of the number.
  • The Selenium Chrome docs use --headless=new. Chrome 132 removed the old headless mode, so plain --headless now does the same thing.

Step 4: finish or cancel the number in finally 

// src/test/java/com/example/otp/ActivationCleanup.java
package com.example.otp;

import com.example.otp.HeroSmsClient.HeroSmsException;

import java.time.Duration;

final class ActivationCleanup {
    private ActivationCleanup() {}

    /** Finish if the code was used, cancel otherwise. Never throws: it must not hide the test failure. */
    static void release(HeroSmsClient sms, String id, boolean gotCode, long boughtAtNanos) {
        try {
            if (gotCode) {
                sms.finish(id); // the SMS arrived: close it, no refund
                return;
            }
            try {
                sms.cancel(id); // no SMS: cancel, the price goes back to your balance
            } catch (HeroSmsException e) {
                if ("OTP_RECEIVED".equals(e.title)) {
                    sms.finish(id); // the SMS came late
                } else if ("EARLY_CANCEL_DENIED".equals(e.title)) {
                    long minSec = e.info.path("minActivationTime").asLong(120);
                    long waitNanos = boughtAtNanos + Duration.ofSeconds(minSec + 5).toNanos() - System.nanoTime();
                    if (waitNanos > 0) Thread.sleep(Duration.ofNanos(waitNanos).toMillis());
                    try {
                        sms.cancel(id); // one more try, no more waiting
                    } catch (HeroSmsException again) {
                        if (!"OTP_RECEIVED".equals(again.title)) throw again;
                        sms.finish(id);
                    }
                } else {
                    throw e;
                }
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            System.err.println("[otp] cleanup of " + id + " interrupted; check GET /activations");
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.err.println("[otp] cleanup of " + id + " failed: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

The release call sits in the test's own finally, right after the purchase, so it runs whether the assertions pass or throw. @AfterEach only quits the browser.

  • If the code arrived, finish closes the activation, with no refund. If it didn't, DELETE cancels the activation and refunds the price.
  • The API refuses a cancel during a number's first minutes. It returns EARLY_CANCEL_DENIED with info.minActivationTime, which is about 2 minutes in the reference's examples. A test that fails within seconds therefore waits out that window plus 5 seconds, then tries once more.
  • If the SMS arrives late, the cancel fails with OTP_RECEIVED and the code calls finish instead. Cleanup branches on title, not on the HTTP status.
  • Cleanup errors are only logged. Throwing from finally would replace the real failure (say, a TimeoutException on the OTP field) with a less useful one.
  • If the runner itself dies, no Java code runs at all. Unused numbers are refunded to your balance, and GET /activations lists anything still open.

Step 5: run the Selenium Java test nightly in GitHub Actions

Real numbers cost money, so run this test on a schedule rather than on every push:

# .github/workflows/otp-nightly.yml
name: otp-nightly
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '17 4 * * 1-5' # 04:17 UTC on weekdays; every run buys a number
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: otp-nightly
  cancel-in-progress: false # a canceled run may never reach the finally block

jobs:
  real-sms:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - name: Fail if the API key is missing
        env:
          HEROSMS_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.HEROSMS_API_KEY }}
        run: test -n "$HEROSMS_API_KEY" || { echo "::error::HEROSMS_API_KEY is not set"; exit 1; }
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '21'
          cache: maven
      - name: Real-SMS Selenium test
        env:
          HEROSMS_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.HEROSMS_API_KEY }}
          OTP_SERVICE: ${{ vars.OTP_SERVICE }}
          OTP_COUNTRY: ${{ vars.OTP_COUNTRY }}
          HEROSMS_MAX_PRICE: ${{ vars.HEROSMS_MAX_PRICE }}
          APP_URL: ${{ vars.APP_URL }}
        run: mvn -B test -Dgroups=real-sms
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: surefire-reports
          path: target/surefire-reports
          retention-days: 7
  • The first step fails the job if the secret is missing or misnamed. Without that step, GitHub passes an empty string, @EnabledIfEnvironmentVariable skips the test, and the nightly run goes green with Skipped: 1.
  • The key comes in through the step's env:, not the command line, as GitHub's secrets guide recommends. Surefire's forked test JVM inherits Maven's environment, so System.getenv sees the key.
  • Your PR workflow should run mvn -B test -DexcludedGroups=real-sms and not pass the key at all. GitHub doesn't pass secrets other than GITHUB_TOKEN to workflows triggered from forks, so a fork PR can't spend your balance. Don't move this job to pull_request_target, because that trigger does get secrets.
  • The ubuntu-latest image ships with Chrome and ChromeDriver, and Selenium Manager finds the driver itself, so the workflow needs no browser setup step.
  • Scheduled workflows have a few quirks:
    • They run on the latest commit of the default branch.
    • Times are in UTC unless you set a timezone.
    • Under load they can start late or be dropped, especially at the top of the hour. That's why the cron uses minute 17.
    • In a public repository, they are disabled after 60 days without activity.
  • Set HEROSMS_MAX_PRICE as a repository variable, so a price change can't quietly raise the cost of every run.
  • If you add failure screenshots, treat them as sensitive: they show the phone number and the code. Keep artifact retention short.

Troubleshooting

  • The code never arrives.
    • Check that your app accepted the number with the +.
    • Check that OTP_SERVICE matches the service that sends your SMS, since an activation is reserved for one service.
    • If your app rejects certain prefixes, phoneException in the purchase body excludes them up front.
    • POST /activations/{activationId}/replace gives you a free replacement number. If you use it, pass the activation it returns to ActivationCleanup.release, not the original ID.
  • TimeoutException on the OTP field. One of three things is usually wrong:
    • The locator is wrong.
    • The field is inside an iframe. Call driver.switchTo().frame(...) first.
    • Your app shows the field only after the send-code request returns. Raise the wait for that one step instead of adding an implicit wait.
  • StaleElementReferenceException on split boxes. Your component re-renders after each digit. Re-query each box by index, as typeOtp does, and keep ignoring(StaleElementReferenceException.class) on the wait.
  • Skipped: 1 instead of a run. HEROSMS_API_KEY isn't set in that shell, so @EnabledIfEnvironmentVariable disabled the test. In CI, the guard step fails the job instead.
  • 429 Too Many Requests. The poller honors Retry-After and backs off to 10 seconds. The concurrency group stops two scheduled runs from polling at the same time.
  • EARLY_CANCEL_DENIED in the log. This is expected when a test fails fast. Cleanup waits and retries once. If the retry is refused too, the number stays open until it expires.
  • Expired activation. Polling stops on ACTIVATION_NOT_ACTIVE, CANCELED, FINISHED or REFUNDED. A 2-minute poll sits well inside the ~20-minute activation. If you wait longer, compare against expiredAt.
  • SessionNotCreatedException about the ChromeDriver version. The usual cause is an old driver pinned with webdriver.chrome.driver, or a leftover WebDriverManager setup. Remove it and let Selenium Manager pick the matching driver.
  • Passes locally, fails headless. Headless Chrome may lay the page out differently. Set an explicit --window-size, as above, and take a screenshot on failure to see what the browser saw.

FAQ

Can I automate Selenium 2FA in Python instead? Yes, and the API calls are the same. My Python OTP post has the client and the polling loop with requests, so you can call them from a pytest Selenium test.

How do I automate email OTP in Selenium Java? It's the same loop with a different inbox. Create a test inbox with an email-testing API and poll it for the message with the same deadline loop. Then pull the code out with the same regex and type it with the same typeOtp. Only the client class changes.

Can I just skip OTP or CAPTCHA in tests? For most runs, yes. Selenium's docs recommend a test-only token, or 2FA disabled for test users. Keep one real-SMS run to check delivery. Never try to solve CAPTCHAs in automation; disable them in your test environment instead.

What about TOTP and Google Authenticator in Selenium? You don't need a phone for those. Store the shared secret as a CI secret and generate the current code at runtime with any RFC 6238 TOTP library.

How do I automate mobile OTP in Selenium Java? "Mobile OTP" usually means an SMS code sent to a phone number, which is exactly what this test handles. If the form lives in a native app rather than a web page, the same HeroSmsClient and poller work from an Appium test.

How much does a run cost? Each run pays for one number. The price depends on the service and country, and HEROSMS_MAX_PRICE caps it. A run that gets no SMS is canceled and refunded. If the cancel retry is refused too, the number stays open until it expires. A run that receives an SMS is paid even if your app then fails. A weekday schedule comes to about 22 numbers a month.

Use it on your own app only

Test only apps you own or are authorized to test. A rented number is yours only for the activation window, so don't tie it to an account you'll need later, and delete test users afterwards.

Wrap-up

Keep mocks and test tokens on every PR, and add one scheduled Selenium run against a real number. The PR runs prove the page works. The nightly run proves that a real user gets a code they can type into that page, in the country you launch in, with the SMS template you actually ship. If you'd rather have codes pushed to you than polled, the HeroSMS API reference documents an sms-incoming webhook. The Playwright post above shows that setup.

How do you handle OTP in Selenium today: a test token, a shared phone, or something else?

title: Open-source local video editor - Concat
description:
TL;DR: Concat replaces cloud-based editors by running entirely on your machine via a native Rust engine and GPU compositor. It processes local models for offline tasks like auto-captions and voice cloning without uploading raw footage.
Best for: Developers, creators, and tinkerers wanting a local, scriptable video editor.
Repository snapshot: ⭐ 14 124 stars · 🍴 1 748 forks · Rust · AGPL-3.0
Daily picks: Follow GitHub Open Source on Telegram

What it is

Concat is an open-source, local-first video editor written in Rust. It aims to provide a native alternative to cloud-dependent video editing suites, running entirely on consumer hardware with GPU acceleration and local AI integration.

How it works

The project relies on a native Rust engine paired with a GPU compositor to render effects and transitions live in the preview window. For offline intelligence, it runs local models to handle tasks like automated speech-to-text captions and voice cloning without sending data to external servers. It exposes a built-in JSON-RPC API and a Model Context Protocol server, allowing AI agents and external scripts to manipulate timelines and project structures programmatically.

Key features

  • Local execution with GPU-accelerated rendering and live preview composition
  • Offline auto-captions and voice cloning powered by local models
  • Scriptable workflow via an integrated JSON-RPC API and MCP server
  • Built-in curve editor and keyframe animation parameters
  • Export capabilities supporting H.264, HEVC, and AV1 up to 4K 60fps in 10-bit color

Getting started

Clone the repository from GitHub and ensure you have a compatible Rust toolchain installed alongside your GPU drivers. Build the project locally using Cargo:

git clone https://github.com/jub0t/Concat.git
cd Concat
cargo build --release

When not to use it

Because the software is currently in an early beta phase, you should expect potential stability issues and missing creature comforts found in mature commercial suites. It is not recommended for production environments where crashes could result in missed deadlines until the codebase matures further.

Discuss

Which video editing task do you most wish you could automate via an API?

  • Discuss this pick on Telegram
  • GitHub repository
  • Full breakdown

Curated from the repository README and metadata. No hands-on test is claimed; evaluate it in a sandbox before production use.
