title: Native Menus, File Dialogs and 3D Models
description:
A desktop app gets judged in the first ten seconds. If the menu bar is wrong, Cmd+Q does nothing or the Save dialog looks like it came from a different decade, people notice, even if they can't say what bothers them. The word processor from last Friday's post needed all of that to hold up next to a native app, so those pieces are now part of Codename One. They work with the code you already write for a phone.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

The real open and save dialogs

openFileChooser() picks one file. Desktop apps need more: several filters, a suggested name, extra options in the dialog and a preview while the user browses. showOpenDialog() and showSaveDialog() cover that:

Display.getInstance().showOpenDialog(new OpenFileRequest()
        .title("Import photos")
        .multiSelect(true)
        .addFilter(new FileTypeFilter("Images")
                .extensions("png", "jpg").mimeTypes("image/*"))
        .addOption(FileDialogOption.checkbox("strip", "Remove location data", true))
        .preview(path -> {
            try (InputStream in = FileSystemStorage.getInstance().openInputStream(path)) {
                return new ScaleImageLabel(Image.createImage(in));
            } catch (IOException err) {
                return new Label("No preview");
            }
        }),
    result -> {
        if (result.isCancelled()) {
            return;
        }
        boolean strip = "true".equals(result.getOptionValue("strip"));
        for (String path : result.getPaths()) {
            // import each file
        }
    });

The request above in the simulator, with the preview and the option.

Every platform opens and saves files. The extras appear where the platform has them, and the rest ignore them, so one request works everywhere:

Platform Open Save
macOS NSOpenPanel NSSavePanel, with format list, options and tag field
Windows IFileOpenDialog IFileSaveDialog, with options as dialog controls
Linux GtkFileChooser GtkFileChooser with overwrite confirmation
Android The system document picker, several files, folders Create document, with no storage permission
iOS The document picker, several files, folders Exported through the document picker
Browser The browser's file picker A download with the suggested name

A save request writes its content after the user has picked the location, off the EDT, and it can see which format and options were chosen. Platform hints, such as the macOS tag field or the folder Android starts in, are one call each.

A menu bar that follows each platform

A Command already knows its name, icon, and action. Tell it where it goes and it shows up in the native menu bar on macOS, Windows, Linux and in the browser build. Paths make submenus, and check and radio items work the way you'd expect:

String[] zooms = {"50%", "100%", "200%"};
for (String zoom : zooms) {
    Command c = Command.create(zoom, null, e -> setZoom(zoom));
    c.setDesktopMenu("View/Zoom").setDesktopMenuGroup(1).setDesktopRadioGroup("zoom");
    c.setDesktopChecked("100%".equals(zoom));
    form.getToolbar().addCommandToOverflowMenu(c);
}

On a phone the same commands stay in the overflow menu, so there's nothing to branch on.

The word processor's File menu on macOS.

About, Settings and Quit live in different places on every desktop, under different names. Give the command a role and each platform puts it where its own apps do, with its own shortcut:

Command settings = Command.createDesktopRole(Command.DESKTOP_ROLE_SETTINGS, e -> showSettings());
Command quit = Command.createDesktopRole(Command.DESKTOP_ROLE_QUIT, e -> quit());
Role macOS Windows Linux
About Application menu, first Help, last Help, last
Settings "Settings…" in the application menu, Cmd+, "Options" under Tools "Preferences" at the foot of Edit
Quit "Quit" in the application menu, Cmd+Q "Exit" at the foot of File "Quit" at the foot of File, Ctrl+Q

The File and Edit roles work the same way, so Redo is Cmd+Shift+Z on a Mac and Ctrl+Y on Windows without you looking it up. On macOS a role replaces the built-in item, so the menu never shows two Quit items.

Roles landing in the macOS application menu.

One more small thing that makes an editor feel right: form.setDocumentModified(true) puts the dot in the close button on macOS and an asterisk before the title on Windows and Linux, and the Save command enables itself while there's something to save.

Animated 3D models

The other big addition came from Skirmish. GltfLoader loads glTF 2.0 models, binary .glb or JSON .gltf, together with their textures, so a textured model renders with no extra setup. AnimatedModel brings them to life:

GltfScene knight = GltfLoader.loadScene(in);
AnimatedModel unit = new AnimatedModel(device, knight);
unit.play("Walking_A", true);
unit.addTo(gameView);
// later
unit.crossFade("1H_Melee_Attack_Chop", 0.15f, false);

It plays the model's animation clips, cross-fades between them, deforms skinned meshes with their skeleton and carries rigid parts, like a sword in a hand, along with their bones. Skinning runs on the CPU, so it looks identical on every port and needs nothing from the shaders. Many instances can share one loaded scene: the vertex data, clips and textures are shared, and only the posed vertices are per instance. That's how a Skirmish battle fills the arena with troops.

A textured glTF model.
Animated characters in Skirmish.

The desktop integration guide, the file system chapter and the 3D graphics chapter have the details.

Tomorrow, the last post of the week: WebRTC Calls, Key Agreement and ORM Checks at Build Time.

title: I built a language where bad edits can't reach your running process
description:
⭐ GitHub: github.com/grloper/Blaze · source on GitHub · by @grloper

grloper / Blaze

Experimental Rust incremental runtime and Cranelift JIT with executed local hot-swap workflows

Blaze 🔥

The live logic runtime. Swap functions in a running production process —
in ~500 microseconds, safety-checked, canaried against live traffic, instantly reversible.
For humans, and for AI agents

Website · Demo · How it’s safe · Category · Benchmarks · Tested · Tests

▶  Watch it in action

Every other tool makes you redeploy. Blaze rewrites live code mid‑request —
and refuses anything unsafe before a single user ever feels it.
10 seconds. One running server. Zero dropped calls in the scripted local run.

Swap a live function in ~500µs  ·  reject broken edits automatically  ·  canary on live traffic  ·  undo in one call.
▶ Video not playing? Open it directly or watch the full story on the website.


LaunchDarkly flips booleans. Blaze swaps functions — in ~500 microseconds with a safety check, a canary, and an undo button. And it is how you let…

View on GitHub

You edit a function while the process is running. The old runtime either crashes, silently corrupts state, or makes you restart. Blaze treats a live edit as a verdict, not a hope: safe, rejected, or relinked — decided before anything changes. The demo swaps a function in a running process and shows the classification happening first; the canary catches the bad edit before the swap.

It is early (version 0.1.0), tested mainly on Windows, and I want your hardest review.

A real run of cargo run -p blaze-jit --release --example living_service -- --script on my Windows machine (Rust 1.94.0). The GIF replays the dashboard's actual repaints, slowed down: the real run is over in seconds. Every beat is asserted by the example itself.

Why salsa and Cranelift: a firewall in the query graph

Blaze parses into a lossless CST, lowers each function to a small register IR inside a salsa query graph, and compiles with Cranelift. The key rule is that a function's lowered IR depends on its own text and on its callees' signatures, never their bodies. Edit a body and callers are untouched; change a signature and every caller is pulled into the recompile set. The blast radius falls out of the graph as a by-product of recompiling.

The runtime then picks a protocol from that:

What changed Class What happens
A syntax error, undefined callee, arity or type mismatch Rejected Nothing is compiled; the previous version keeps serving
Nothing at the IR level (a comment) NoEffect Nothing
Bodies only, signatures intact SafeSwap One atomic pointer store into the function's slot
A signature changed or a function was removed Relink The affected callers recompile and commit together under a quiescence barrier

Every Blaze-to-Blaze call is an acquire-load of the callee's slot plus an indirect call, so generated code has no relocations against other functions. That is why a swap can be one store.

Guardrails for bad edits

A live process should survive a bad edit, so every function threads a per-call context with a depth counter and a fuel budget (one unit per call and per loop back-edge). Unbounded recursion returns ResourceExhausted; an infinite loop returns FuelExhausted. Division by zero is guarded. The language has only int (i64) and float (f64) and no memory operations, which is part of why a script cannot corrupt the host.

Canary and rollback

canary(source, policy) compiles an isolated candidate and shadows it on a sampled fraction of live calls. The caller always receives the live answer. A candidate that diverges, faults or runs out of fuel aborts and cannot be promoted. Every reload, including rejected ones, is journaled with its class, radius, diagnostics and latency, and rollback(generation) reinstalls an earlier source through the same protocol.

The demo, and what it does and does not show

living_service is an HTTP scoring service whose logic is a .blaze file. Its scripted mode makes six live edits under load: a body edit, a broken save, a runaway loop caught by the canary, a risky rule promoted after divergence, an ABI change, and a rollback. This is what the example printed at the end of my run:

In that run 42,834 requests were served across the six edits and none were dropped; the body-edit swap committed in 336 microseconds. The README quotes a different run (51,815 requests, 496 microseconds). Those are two local runs on two machines, so read both as "same order of magnitude", not as a spec. I also ran cargo test --workspace --release on the same machine: 110 tests passed, 0 failed. Many of them hammer swaps from a second thread.

The README states the audit ran on Windows and that Linux and macOS were not re-run. My run is also Windows only.

Numbers, with caveats

I ran the repo's benchmark examples once each on my Windows machine. Single runs, release mode: treat them as orders of magnitude.

Left: bench_reload. Right: bench_vs_interpreter. Both from blaze-jit/examples, run by me on one machine; the README lists its own numbers from a shared cloud container, which differ.

On the 40-function chain, a body edit swapped in about 0.45 ms against 5.6 ms for a full cold compile. In bench_vs_interpreter, one branchy rule, cross-checked to give identical answers, ran roughly 54 times faster through a native FuncHandle than through rhai's compiled-AST call_fn. That is one rule against one interpreter; it says nothing general about interpreters. bench_calls also reports a handle-based call path at about 83 M calls/s on one thread for a trivial leaf, which measures dispatch cost, not useful work.

Quickstart 

git clone https://github.com/grloper/Blaze && cd Blaze   # needs Rust 1.94+
cargo test --workspace
cargo run -p blaze-jit --release --example living_service -- --script

The Rust 1.94 requirement is real: on 1.91 the build stops because the locked Cranelift crates need 1.94. On Windows I used the GNU toolchain (x86_64-pc-windows-gnu) with MinGW on PATH.

Embedding:

use blaze_jit::{LiveRuntime, EditClass};

let rt = LiveRuntime::new("int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }")?;
assert_eq!(rt.call("add", &[2, 3]), Ok(5));
let report = rt.reload("int add(int a, int b) { return a + a + b; }")?;
assert_eq!(report.class, EditClass::SafeSwap);
assert_eq!(rt.call("add", &[2, 3]), Ok(7));

The honest part

  • One source file and one flat namespace. No modules, strings, arrays or structs, and no implicit int/float conversion.
  • State lives in the host. Migrating script-owned data is not something Blaze does; StateMigration is reserved and cannot occur today.
  • Retired code generations are kept for the life of the runtime, so memory grows with the number of edits.
  • An active canary re-executes sampled calls, so it only suits functions without observable side effects.
  • Watch mode is mtime polling, not OS file events.
  • "Proven" in the README means tested, not formally verified. There has been no independent security review and no production use.
  • No LICENSE file yet: the workspace Cargo.toml declares Apache-2.0, but the repository has no LICENSE file, so treat the code as readable but not clearly reusable.

Try it, and help

The most useful thing is critique of the swap protocol: where could a concurrent caller observe a torn state that my tests do not cover? Run the examples on Linux or macOS and tell me what breaks. Issues and PRs welcome at github.com/grloper/Blaze. Roadmap items are richer types, explicit conversions, and script-owned state migration.

What edit would you try to sneak past it?

title: I built a Linux sensor that catches exploits by where code runs, not what it looks like
description:
⭐ GitHub: github.com/grloper/Wraith · open source (MIT) · by @grloper

grloper / Wraith

Wraith is a low-level Rust security sensor that answers a question most tools can't: "is this process being exploited right now?" By focusing entirely on anomalous runtime behavior rather than known signatures or payloads, Wraith detects live exploits and uncovers zero-day vulnerabilities completely in advance of a patch.

Runtime security, through a different lens.
Observe execution. Inspect its origin. Understand the anomaly.

Quickstart   /   Real demo   /   Design   /   Threat model   /   Contribute

Concept artwork, not telemetry. Still version · Art direction & motion

Wraith

A small Rust runtime sensor that inspects where Linux syscalls come from.

Injected code can change its bytes. It still has to execute somewhere. Wraith uses ptrace and /proc/<pid>/maps to flag sensitive syscalls from suspicious executable memory, inspect W^X requests, and correlate signals across threads. No payload signatures cloud service, or model required. Only two direct Rust dependencies: nix and libc.

Continuously developed, not a finalized endpoint product. The focus is reproducible Linux security investigation with honest coverage and workload evidence—not an antivirus or Nmap replacement. See the development program and Linux/Kali tool comparison.

Inspect the origin
Executable mappings and syscall provenance. No payload signature required. 		Follow the execution
Shared process
…
View on GitHub

The payload changed its bytes again. The hash didn't match, the signature didn't fire, and the exploit ran anyway. Every payload can change what it looks like. None of them can change where it runs from. So I built a sensor that stops a process at every syscall and asks one question: is the instruction that issued this syscall sitting in file-backed code, or in RWX memory, the heap, the stack, or nowhere at all?

That is how a sensor like this is supposed to catch a zero-day: not by targeting the exact weakness, but by flagging the one thing every exploit has to do, run code from where code should never run.

Real output of bash demo.sh, which I ran on WSL2 Ubuntu (Linux 5.15) for this post; the GIF replays the captured text line by line. Twenty per-thread log lines from one benign case are trimmed in the GIF only. The "injection" is a safe simulator that maps an RWX page and opens a socket from it. No real exploit is involved.

Six simulator cases: benign runs clean, the injection gets flagged CRITICAL with sensor exit 3, block mode returns -ENOSYS instead of running the payload syscall, and kill mode terminates the tree first.

The idea

On Linux x86-64, Wraith uses ptrace to stop a target at each syscall entry, reads the registers, and consults a cached copy of /proc/<pid>/maps. It then checks three invariants that ordinary programs normally satisfy:

  1. Provenance. The instruction issuing a sensitive syscall should sit in an accepted executable mapping, meaning file-backed code or the vDSO. If it comes from RWX memory, the heap, the stack or an anonymous mapping, that is flagged.
  2. W^X. Requests for writable and executable memory, and writable-to-executable transitions, are reported.
  3. Stack placement. A stack pointer in the heap or a file mapping is a heuristic HIGH.

A violation is a signal for review, not proof of exploitation. It needs no payload signature, but it also does not know the vulnerability, so it only sees exploitation that leaves one of these artifacts.

What it can show today

The repo ships safe local simulators, not exploits. bash demo.sh runs six cases and asserts the outcomes:

| Case | What happened |
| Benign program | No detections: 80 syscalls, 0 events, exit 0 |
| Benign multi-threaded program | No detections across worker threads |
| Shellcode simulator | HIGH wx_violation, then CRITICAL foreign_origin_syscall, then CRITICAL exploitation_chain; sensor exit 3 |
| Same on a worker thread | Detected, exit 3 |
| With --block | Syscall returns -ENOSYS (the simulator prints socket() -> -38), fixture survives |
| With --kill | Traced tree terminated before the payload syscall runs |

The script ends with PASS: both controls clean; main/worker injection detected; block and kill verified. That is the extent of the detection evidence. I have not run it against a real CVE exploit or real malware, and no false-positive rate has been established.

Quickstart

Linux 5.3+ on x86-64, Rust 1.74+, procfs mounted, and permission to trace your own child. WSL2 works; restricted containers may deny ptrace. Windows and macOS are not supported.

git clone https://github.com/grloper/Wraith.git && cd Wraith
cargo build --release --locked
./target/release/wraith doctor
bash demo.sh
./target/release/wraith run --json events.jsonl -- ./your-target

Sensor exit codes: 0 no HIGH/CRITICAL, 1 HIGH, 2 operational error, 3 CRITICAL. That is the sensor's status, not the target's.

How it is built

An engine module owns policy, map lookup and statistics; a tracer module owns ptrace and enforcement. Provenance lookup is a binary search over parsed mapping intervals. Worker threads share per-address-space state. There are two direct dependencies, nix and libc, and no async runtime or serialization crate. Output is human-readable on stderr plus JSONL evidence, with schema versions, and a strict triage helper validates complete logs.

For this post I built the repo at its current main and ran the whole Rust suite in WSL2 with WRAITH_REQUIRE_PTRACE=1, so skipped ptrace tests would fail instead of passing quietly: 134 tests passed, 0 failed. (The README and docs/verification.md still say 130; the docs have not caught up with a few newer tests.)

What broke

This is the useful part. The first real Java control completed successfully, but two handled SIGSEGV delivery stops were reported as HIGH crash events, because the JVM uses signals internally. The fix was to treat signal delivery as INFO and require a confirmed terminal status before calling something a crash. JVMs also request RWX pages, and the benign Java control still produced four HIGH findings for those RWX requests. Legitimate JITs look like attackers to this check, which is why the README says to baseline first and never to turn on --jit-critical or enforcement blindly.

Another bug: the kill path raced with queued stops while targets died, and a test using 64 alternating single-thread and worker-thread targets failed with ESRCH at iteration 5 before the fix. The repo keeps the failing-then-passing evidence in docs/verification.md.

The honest part

  • Maturity: pre-1.0, tested against its own simulators rather than real exploits.
  • Blind spots: ROP/JOP entirely inside accepted file-backed code, data-only attacks, malicious shared libraries, memfd-backed executable images and map races. The threat model lists them.
  • Overhead: every traced syscall stops the target. On two WSL workloads the median slowdown was 3.36x (loopback HTTP, 20 requests) and 3.00x (SQLite, 200 transactions); a syscall-only loop was 140x. Use it on a few high-value targets, not a whole host.
  • JIT runtimes (JVM, browsers, .NET) will produce findings. Baseline first.
  • Environment: all measurements, mine and the repo's, come from WSL2, not native Linux. No fleet compatibility claim. An eBPF backend is not implemented. A commenter asked about it, and the observation half already exists: snoop traces syscalls with eBPF tracepoints at full speed, no stop-the-world. Wraith's provenance check (where the syscall instruction lives) would still need to be layered on that feed, and block/kill enforcement would still need ptrace's synchronous stop.
  • Enforcement can break legitimate applications and is not a substitute for a sandbox.
  • A clean result means no configured signal was observed, not that an exploit is absent.
  • It is not an EDR.

Try it, and help

The most useful contributions are a benign program that trips it, a regression fixture for it, or timing numbers from a real service on native Linux. Start with CONTRIBUTING.md and docs/roadmap.md at github.com/grloper/Wraith. Please report security issues through SECURITY.md.
